🗂️ Section TOC

A jump-table of this chapter's sections goes here.

14.1 How the Scheduler Works

The kube-scheduler runs as a control plane component. When a new pod is created without a nodeName, it enters the scheduling queue. The scheduler then executes a multi-phase pipeline to find the best node.

1
Filtering

Which nodes CAN run this pod? Checks: sufficient resources, node taints, node selectors, affinity rules, port availability.

2
Scoring

Which passing node is the BEST fit? Scores based on: resource balance, affinity preference, spread, image locality.

3
Binding

The highest-scoring node wins. Scheduler sets pod.spec.nodeName and the kubelet on that node starts the container.

Scheduler Decision Flowchart — easypj Pod Placement
  NEW POD: easypj (requests: 256Mi memory, 250m CPU)
       │
       ▼
  ════════════════ PHASE 1: FILTERING ════════════════
  "Which nodes CAN run this pod?"

  Node 1 (512Mi free, 500m CPU free)   → ✅ PASSES — has enough resources
  Node 2 (128Mi free, 100m CPU free)   → ❌ FAILS  — insufficient memory
  Node 3 (1Gi free, 1000m CPU free)    → ✅ PASSES — has enough resources
  Node 4 (taint: gpu=true:NoSchedule)  → ❌ FAILS  — no matching toleration
       │
       ▼ (only passing nodes continue)
  ════════════════ PHASE 2: SCORING ═════════════════
  "Which passing node is the BEST fit?"

  Node 1: Score 65  — good fit, resources balanced
  Node 3: Score 82  — better fit, more headroom,
                      topology spread bonus, affinity match
       │
       ▼
  ════════════════ PHASE 3: BINDING ═════════════════

  🏆 Winner: Node 3 (highest score: 82)
  → pod.spec.nodeName = "node-3"
  → kubelet on Node 3 pulls image → starts container
  → Pod status: Running ✅
🎯
Resource Fit

Does the node have enough CPU & memory to satisfy the pod's requests?

🏷️
Label Match

Does the node have the labels required by nodeSelector or nodeAffinity?

🚫
Taint Check

Does the pod tolerate the node's taints? No toleration = rejected.

📊
Spread Score

How well does this placement spread pods across nodes/zones?

Static Pods — Bypass the Scheduler

Static pods are managed directly by the kubelet on a specific node, not by the API server. They're used for control plane components (etcd, apiserver, scheduler itself). The CKA may ask you to create one.

Creating a Static Pod 
# Static pods live in the kubelet's manifest directory
# Default: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/

# Find the staticPodPath on any node
ssh worker-1 "cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep staticPodPath"
# staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests

# Create a static pod (just place a YAML file there)
ssh worker-1 "cat > /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-nginx.yaml" <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: static-nginx
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:1.25
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
EOF

# kubelet auto-starts it! Check from control plane:
kubectl get pods
# NAME                       READY   STATUS    AGE
# static-nginx-worker-1      1/1     Running   10s
#                  ^^^^^^^^^ node name appended!

# Delete: remove the file from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# kubectl delete won't work — kubelet will recreate it!
⚠️ CKA Exam: Static Pod Key Facts
  • Static pod names always end with -<nodename>
  • They can only be created/deleted by adding/removing YAML from the manifest directory
  • kubectl delete on a static pod will NOT permanently remove it — kubelet recreates it
  • Control plane components (apiserver, etcd, scheduler) are static pods on the control plane node

14.2 Node Selectors — Simple Placement

The simplest way to constrain a pod to specific nodes. Label a node, then reference that label in the pod spec. It's a hard requirement — the pod won't schedule if no node matches.

Label a Node, Then Select It 
# Step 1: Label the node
kubectl label node worker-1 disk=ssd

# Verify label was applied
kubectl get node worker-1 --show-labels | grep disk

# Step 2: Create pod with nodeSelector (see YAML below)
kubectl apply -f easypj-ssd-pod.yaml

# Verify pod landed on the right node
kubectl get pod easypj-ssd -o wide
# NAME         READY   STATUS    NODE
# easypj-ssd   1/1     Running   worker-1   ← correct!

# Clean up: remove label
kubectl label node worker-1 disk-
easypj-ssd-pod.yaml 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-ssd
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    disk: ssd                    # Only schedule on nodes with disk=ssd
  containers:
  - name: django
    image: easypj:v1
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
💡 nodeSelector vs nodeAffinity

nodeSelector is simple but limited — it only supports exact equality matching. For "prefer but don't require" or "match any of these values" logic, use Node Affinity (see 14.3).

14.3 Node Affinity — Advanced Placement

Node affinity is the more powerful version of nodeSelector. It supports operators (In, NotIn, Exists, Gt, Lt) and offers two types: hard rules (required) and soft rules (preferred).

Type Behavior When Pod Can't Match Use Case
requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution Hard rule — MUST match Pod stays Pending forever GPU workloads, compliance zones
preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution Soft rule — TRY to match Scheduled anywhere available Prefer SSD, prefer same zone
easypj-node-affinity.yaml 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj
    spec:
      affinity:
        nodeAffinity:
          # HARD: Must be on an SSD node
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
            - matchExpressions:
              - key: disk
                operator: In
                values:
                - ssd
                - nvme
          # SOFT: Prefer us-east zone (but ok if not available)
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - weight: 80           # 1-100, higher = stronger preference
            preference:
              matchExpressions:
              - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                operator: In
                values:
                - us-east-1a
                - us-east-1b
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: easypj:v1
Node Affinity Decision Matrix
  Pod: easypj (requires: disk ∈ {ssd, nvme}, prefers: zone ∈ {us-east-1a})

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Node          disk    zone          Required  Preferred   │
  │  ──────────    ────    ──────────    ────────  ─────────   │
  │  worker-1      ssd     us-east-1a   ✅ PASS   ✅ Match    │ ← Best (score 82)
  │  worker-2      ssd     us-west-1a   ✅ PASS   ❌ No match │ ← OK (score 65)
  │  worker-3      hdd     us-east-1a   ❌ FAIL   —           │ ← Rejected
  │  worker-4      nvme    us-east-1b   ✅ PASS   ✅ Match    │ ← Good (score 78)
  │  worker-5      —       us-east-1a   ❌ FAIL   —           │ ← Rejected
  │                                                             │
  │  Result: Pod scheduled on worker-1 (highest combined score)│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ "IgnoredDuringExecution" — What It Means

If you remove a node's label after a pod is already scheduled there, the pod keeps running. The affinity rule is only checked at scheduling time, not continuously. A future Kubernetes version may add RequiredDuringExecution to also evict running pods.

14.4 Pod Affinity and Anti-Affinity

While Node Affinity places pods relative to nodes, Pod Affinity/Anti-Affinity places pods relative to other pods. This is essential for performance (co-locate) and high availability (spread out).

🤝
Pod Affinity

"Place me near this pod." Put easypj Django on the same node/zone as its Redis cache for low latency.

↔️
Pod Anti-Affinity

"Keep me away from that pod." Spread easypj replicas across different nodes so one node failure doesn't take all of them down.

easypj-pod-antiaffinity.yaml — HA Deployment 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj
    spec:
      affinity:
        # Anti-Affinity: Spread replicas across nodes
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - labelSelector:
              matchExpressions:
              - key: app
                operator: In
                values:
                - easypj
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname  # "different nodes"

        # Affinity: Place near Redis cache
        podAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - weight: 100
            podAffinityTerm:
              labelSelector:
                matchExpressions:
                - key: app
                  operator: In
                  values:
                  - easypj-redis
              topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone  # "same zone"
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: easypj:v1
Pod Anti-Affinity — easypj Replicas Spread Across Nodes
  Deployment: easypj (replicas: 3)
  podAntiAffinity: kubernetes.io/hostname (no 2 on same node)

  ┌────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐
  │   worker-1     │  │   worker-2     │  │   worker-3     │
  │ ┌────────────┐ │  │ ┌────────────┐ │  │ ┌────────────┐ │
  │ │ easypj-abc │ │  │ │ easypj-def │ │  │ │ easypj-ghi │ │
  │ │   📦 v1    │ │  │ │   📦 v1    │ │  │ │   📦 v1    │ │
  │ └────────────┘ │  │ └────────────┘ │  │ └────────────┘ │
  │                │  │                │  │                │
  │ ┌────────────┐ │  │                │  │                │
  │ │ redis-xyz  │ │  │                │  │                │
  │ │   🔴 cache │ │  │                │  │                │
  │ └────────────┘ │  │                │  │                │
  └────────────────┘  └────────────────┘  └────────────────┘

  ✅ Each node has exactly 1 easypj pod — survives any single node failure!
  ✅ easypj-abc co-located with redis (podAffinity) for low latency

14.5 Taints and Tolerations

Taints are the opposite of affinity — taints repel pods from a node, while tolerations let specific pods override that repulsion. This is a CKA must-know concept and appears on almost every exam.

📖 The Analogy

Think of a node's taint as a "No Entry" sign. A toleration is the "VIP pass" that lets a pod in despite the sign. Without the pass, the pod is rejected.

Effect Behavior Running Pods Use Case
NoSchedule New pods WITHOUT tolerance are rejected Existing pods stay Dedicated GPU nodes, team isolation
PreferNoSchedule Try NOT to schedule here, but allow if no other option Existing pods stay Soft preference — avoid but don't block
NoExecute Reject new pods AND evict running pods without tolerance Evicted! Node going into maintenance, toxic node
Taint & Toleration Commands 
# Add a taint to a node
kubectl taint node worker-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule

# Verify taint
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A5 Taints
# Taints:  gpu=true:NoSchedule

# Remove a taint (add dash at the end)
kubectl taint node worker-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule-

# See control plane taints (this is why your pods don't run on master!)
kubectl describe node control-plane | grep Taints
# Taints:  node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule
pod-with-toleration.yaml 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ml-training-job
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: "gpu"
    operator: "Equal"        # Match exact value
    value: "true"
    effect: "NoSchedule"
  # Alternative: tolerate ANY value for the key
  # - key: "gpu"
  #   operator: "Exists"    # Don't care about value
  #   effect: "NoSchedule"
  containers:
  - name: trainer
    image: ml-trainer:v1
    resources:
      limits:
        nvidia.com/gpu: 1
Taints & Tolerations — Access Control
  ┌────────────────── Node: gpu-node ──────────────────┐
  │ Taint: gpu=true:NoSchedule   🚫                    │
  │                                                     │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  easypj pod (no toleration)                  │   │
  │  │  → ❌ REJECTED — "You don't have a VIP pass" │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                     │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  ml-job pod (toleration: gpu=true)           │   │
  │  │  → ✅ SCHEDULED — "VIP pass accepted!"      │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌────────────── Control Plane Node ──────────────────┐
  │ Taint: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:      │
  │        NoSchedule                                   │
  │                                                     │
  │  That's why your pods DON'T run on control plane!  │
  │  Only system pods (with tolerations) run here:     │
  │  ├── kube-apiserver                                 │
  │  ├── kube-scheduler                                 │
  │  ├── kube-controller-manager                        │
  │  └── etcd                                           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ CKA Trap: Taint Removal Syntax

To remove a taint, append a - (minus sign) at the end. Many candidates forget this on the exam:

  • Add: kubectl taint node worker-1 key=value:NoSchedule
  • Remove: kubectl taint node worker-1 key=value:NoSchedule-

14.6 Node Management for Admins

Cluster administrators regularly need to perform node maintenance — OS upgrades, kernel patches, hardware replacement. Kubernetes provides three commands for safe node management. This is a very common CKA exam scenario.

1
Cordon

Mark node as unschedulable. Existing pods stay, but no new pods can be scheduled here.

2
Drain

Safely evict all pods to other nodes. Respects PDB, grace periods, and pod lifecycle.

3
Maintenance

Perform the actual work — OS upgrade, kernel patch, reboot, hardware swap.

4
Uncordon

Mark node as schedulable again. New pods can now be placed here.

Node Maintenance Workflow 
# Step 1: Cordon — stop new pods from scheduling
kubectl cordon worker-1
# node/worker-1 cordoned

# Verify: node shows SchedulingDisabled
kubectl get nodes
# NAME        STATUS                     ROLES    AGE
# worker-1    Ready,SchedulingDisabled   worker   30d

# Step 2: Drain — safely evict all pods
kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
# evicting pod default/easypj-7d9f8b6c5d-abc12
# evicting pod default/easypj-7d9f8b6c5d-def34
# node/worker-1 drained

# Step 3: Perform maintenance (OS upgrade, reboot, etc.)
# ... work happens here ...

# Step 4: Uncordon — allow pods again
kubectl uncordon worker-1
# node/worker-1 uncordoned

# Verify: node is Ready again (no SchedulingDisabled)
kubectl get nodes
# NAME        STATUS   ROLES    AGE
# worker-1    Ready    worker   30d
Node Maintenance Flow — Safe Pod Migration
  ┌─────── worker-1 (BEFORE) ───────┐     ┌─────── worker-2 ────────┐
  │                                  │     │                          │
  │  📦 easypj-abc    📦 redis-xyz  │     │  📦 easypj-ghi          │
  │  📦 easypj-def                  │     │                          │
  │                                  │     │                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘     └──────────────────────────┘

  Step 1: kubectl cordon worker-1
  ┌─── worker-1 (🚫 SchedulingDisabled) ──┐
  │  📦 easypj-abc  📦 redis-xyz  (stay)  │  ← existing pods remain
  │  📦 easypj-def                (stay)  │  ← new pods blocked
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Step 2: kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets
  ┌─── worker-1 (EMPTY) ────┐     ┌─────── worker-2 ────────────┐
  │                          │     │  📦 easypj-ghi (existing)   │
  │  (all pods evicted)      │     │  📦 easypj-abc (migrated)   │
  │                          │     │  📦 easypj-def (migrated)   │
  │  🔧 Maintenance time!   │     │  📦 redis-xyz  (migrated)   │
  └──────────────────────────┘     └──────────────────────────────┘

  Step 3-4: Maintenance → uncordon
  ┌─── worker-1 (✅ Ready) ──┐
  │  Now accepts new pods!    │
  └───────────────────────────┘
🚨 Drain Gotchas
  • --ignore-daemonsets is required if DaemonSet pods exist (they can't be evicted)
  • --delete-emptydir-data is needed if pods use emptyDir volumes
  • --force only if there are standalone pods (not managed by RS/Deployment) — data will be lost!
  • Without these flags, drain will refuse and show an error — know which flag to add!

14.7 Topology Spread Constraints

Topology spread constraints give you fine-grained control over how pods are distributed across topology domains (zones, nodes, regions). Unlike pod anti-affinity which is "avoid same node", topology spread says "distribute evenly".

easypj-topology-spread.yaml 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1                           # Max diff in pod count between zones
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone  # Spread across zones
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule     # Hard constraint
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: easypj
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname   # Also spread across nodes
        whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway    # Soft constraint
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: easypj
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: easypj:v1
Topology Spread — Even Distribution Across Zones
  6 replicas, maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: zone

  ┌───── us-east-1a ──────┐  ┌───── us-east-1b ──────┐  ┌───── us-east-1c ──────┐
  │  📦 easypj-1           │  │  📦 easypj-3           │  │  📦 easypj-5           │
  │  📦 easypj-2           │  │  📦 easypj-4           │  │  📦 easypj-6           │
  │  Count: 2              │  │  Count: 2              │  │  Count: 2              │
  └────────────────────────┘  └────────────────────────┘  └────────────────────────┘

  maxSkew = max(count) - min(count) = 2 - 2 = 0  ✅ (within maxSkew of 1)

  ❌ Without topology spread (all could land on one zone):
  ┌───── us-east-1a ──────┐  ┌───── us-east-1b ──────┐  ┌───── us-east-1c ──────┐
  │  📦📦📦📦📦📦           │  │  (empty)               │  │  (empty)               │
  │  Count: 6   ← BAD!    │  │  Count: 0              │  │  Count: 0              │
  └────────────────────────┘  └────────────────────────┘  └────────────────────────┘
  Zone failure = total outage! 💀

Topology Spread Parameters

📏 maxSkew
Maximum allowed difference in pod counts between topology domains. Lower = more even.
🗺️ topologyKey
Node label to group by: kubernetes.io/hostname (node), topology.kubernetes.io/zone (zone)
🚫 whenUnsatisfiable
DoNotSchedule (hard — pod stays Pending) or ScheduleAnyway (soft — best effort)

14.8 Priority and Preemption

PriorityClasses let you assign importance levels to pods. When the cluster is full, a high-priority pod can preempt (evict) a lower-priority pod to make room.

priority-classes.yaml 
# High priority — critical production workloads
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: high-priority
value: 1000000
globalDefault: false
preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority
description: "Critical production workloads like easypj"
---
# Low priority — batch jobs, can be evicted
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: low-priority
value: 100
globalDefault: false
preemptionPolicy: Never          # Don't preempt others
description: "Batch jobs and background tasks"
---
# Usage in Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj
    spec:
      priorityClassName: high-priority   # ← assign priority
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: easypj:v1
Preemption — High Priority Pod Evicts Low Priority
  Cluster is FULL — no free capacity

  ┌──── worker-1 ─────┐  ┌──── worker-2 ─────┐
  │ 📦 batch-job-1     │  │ 📦 batch-job-3     │
  │ (low-priority:100) │  │ (low-priority:100) │
  │ 📦 batch-job-2     │  │ 📦 batch-job-4     │
  │ (low-priority:100) │  │ (low-priority:100) │
  └────────────────────┘  └────────────────────┘

  NEW POD: easypj (high-priority: 1000000) needs scheduling!

  Scheduler: "No room, but easypj has higher priority..."
  → PREEMPTS batch-job-1 on worker-1

  ┌──── worker-1 ─────┐  ┌──── worker-2 ─────┐
  │ 🌟 easypj          │  │ 📦 batch-job-3     │
  │ (high-priority!)   │  │ (low-priority:100) │
  │ 📦 batch-job-2     │  │ 📦 batch-job-4     │
  │ (low-priority:100) │  │ (low-priority:100) │
  └────────────────────┘  └────────────────────┘

  batch-job-1 was evicted to make room for easypj  ⚡
💡 When to Use PriorityClasses

Use high priority for production-critical workloads (web servers, APIs). Use low priority for batch jobs, CI/CD runners, dev environments. This ensures production always gets resources first.

🧩 Scheduling Mechanisms Comparison — When to Use What
Mechanism Controls Direction Best For
nodeSelector Pod → Node 🟢 Attract (hard) Simple label matching
Node Affinity Pod → Node 🟢 Attract (hard/soft) Complex rules, preferred placement
Pod Affinity Pod → Pod 🟢 Attract (co-locate) Low latency (app near cache)
Pod Anti-Affinity Pod → Pod 🔴 Repel (spread) HA (replicas on different nodes)
Taints/Tolerations Node → Pod 🔴 Repel + allow Dedicated nodes, maintenance
Topology Spread Pod distribution ⚖️ Even spread Balance across zones/nodes
Static Pods Fixed to node 📌 Pinned Control plane components
PriorityClass Pod importance ⬆️ Preempt lower Critical vs batch workloads

14.9 Practice Exercises

These exercises mirror actual CKA exam questions. Practice each one until you can complete it in under 5 minutes.

🏋️
Exercise 14.1: Taints & Tolerations

1. Taint node01 with env=prod:NoSchedule
2. Create an nginx pod — verify it does NOT schedule on node01
3. Add a toleration — verify it now schedules there
4. Remove the taint

🏋️
Exercise 14.2: Node Affinity

1. Label node01 with disktype=ssd
2. Create pod with required nodeAffinity for ssd nodes
3. Create pod with preferred nodeAffinity for ssd
4. Verify with kubectl get pods -o wide

🏋️
Exercise 14.3: Pod Anti-Affinity

1. Create easypj deployment (replicas: 3)
2. Add podAntiAffinity — no 2 pods on same node
3. Verify: kubectl get pods -o wide (all on different nodes)
4. Scale to 4 — what happens if only 3 nodes?

🏋️
Exercise 14.4: Node Maintenance

1. Cordon worker-1
2. Deploy nginx (replicas: 3) — verify none land on worker-1
3. Drain worker-1 safely
4. Uncordon and verify

Exercise 14.1 — Solution (try it yourself first!) 
# 1. Taint the node
kubectl taint node node01 env=prod:NoSchedule

# 2. Create nginx pod (no toleration)
kubectl run nginx-test --image=nginx
kubectl get pod nginx-test -o wide
# → Should be on a different node (not node01)

# 3. Create pod WITH toleration
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx-tolerant
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: "env"
    operator: "Equal"
    value: "prod"
    effect: "NoSchedule"
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx
EOF
kubectl get pod nginx-tolerant -o wide
# → Can schedule on node01

# 4. Remove taint
kubectl taint node node01 env=prod:NoSchedule-

# Clean up
kubectl delete pod nginx-test nginx-tolerant
Under the Hood — How the Scheduler Filters and Scores Nodes: Filtering Plugins, Scoring Algorithms, Taints/Tolerations, and Node Affinity Resolution
🗺️ The Scheduling Pipeline — Two-Phase Decision Making

The kube-scheduler doesn't randomly assign pods. It runs a sophisticated two-phase algorithm: FILTERING (eliminate infeasible nodes) → SCORING (rank remaining nodes). Understanding this helps you debug "0/3 nodes are available" errors.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SCHEDULING PIPELINE — Full Algorithm                                        │
│                                                                              │
│  Pod to schedule: easypj-web (requests: cpu=500m, memory=512Mi)             │
│  Cluster: 5 worker nodes                                                      │
│                                                                              │
│  ═══════════════════ PHASE 1: FILTERING (5 nodes → ?) ═══════════════════    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │ FILTER PLUGIN          CHECK                   N1  N2  N3  N4  N5   │    │
│  │ ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │    │
│  │ NodeUnschedulable      node.spec.unschedulable?  ✅  ✅  ✅  ✅  ✅   │    │
│  │ NodeResourcesFit       enough cpu/memory?       ✅  ✅  ❌  ✅  ✅   │    │
│  │                         (N3: only 200m cpu free)                      │    │
│  │ NodeSelector           node labels match?        ✅  ✅  -   ✅  ✅   │    │
│  │ NodeAffinity           affinity rules match?     ✅  ✅  -   ✅  ✅   │    │
│  │ TaintToleration        pod tolerates taints?    ✅  ❌  -   ✅  ✅   │    │
│  │                         (N2: taint gpu=true:NoSchedule)               │    │
│  │ NodePorts              hostPort conflicts?       ✅  -   -   ✅  ✅   │    │
│  │ VolumeLimits           can attach more volumes?  ✅  -   -   ✅  ✅   │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │ FILTERED: 3 nodes survive (N1, N4, N5)                               │    │
│  │ ELIMINATED: N2 (taint), N3 (insufficient resources)                  │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
│  ═══════════════════ PHASE 2: SCORING (3 nodes → ranking) ═══════════════    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │ SCORING PLUGIN          WEIGHT     N1     N4     N5    DESCRIPTION   │    │
│  │ ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │    │
│  │ NodeResourcesFit        1.0        85     72     90    Least loaded  │    │
│  │   (LeastAllocated)                                   wins (N5)      │    │
│  │ NodeResourcesBalanced   1.0        78     88     65    Balanced CPU  │    │
│  │   (BalancedAllocation)                               /memory (N4)   │    │
│  │ ImageLocality           1.0        90     50     50    Image cached  │    │
│  │   (image already on node)                             on N1?         │    │
│  │ NodeAffinityPriority    1.0        100    50     50    Preferred     │    │
│  │   (preferredDuringScheduling)                        affinity (N1)  │    │
│  │ InterPodAffinity        2.0        50     100    50    Pods with     │    │
│  │   (preferredDuringScheduling)                        same affinity  │    │
│  │                                                      on N4          │    │
│  │ TaintTolerationPriority 1.0        80     80     100   Prefer no     │    │
│  │   (PreferNoSchedule taint)                           taint nodes    │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │ FINAL SCORES (weighted sum):                                         │    │
│  │   N1: (85+78+90+100+50+80)/6 = 80.5                                 │    │
│  │   N4: (72+88+50+50+100+80)/6 = 73.3                                 │    │
│  │   N5: (90+65+50+50+50+100)/6 = 67.5  ← LOWEST score                 │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │ 🏆 WINNER: N1 (score 80.5) → Pod bound to N1                       │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  TAINTS & TOLERATIONS — Like a "No Entry" Sign with VIP Passes:             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  TAINT (on node):          TOLERATION (on pod):                      │    │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────┐            │    │
│  │  │ key=value:Effect     │   │ key: "gpu"               │            │    │
│  │  │                     │   │ operator: "Equal"         │            │    │
│  │  │ Effect types:       │   │ value: "nvidia"           │            │    │
│  │  │  NoSchedule  (hard) │   │ effect: "NoSchedule"      │            │    │
│  │  │  PreferNoSchedule   │   └──────────────────────────┘            │    │
│  │  │    (soft, preferred)│                                            │    │
│  │  │  NoExecute (hard,   │   TOLERATION MATCHES IF:                   │    │
│  │  │    evict existing)  │   1. Same key                              │    │
│  │  └─────────────────────┘   2. Same effect                            │    │
│  │                             3. Either: operator=Exists (any value)   │    │
│  │                                OR: operator=Equal AND same value     │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  NODE DRAIN MECHANISM:                                               │    │
│  │  kubectl drain node01 --ignore-daemonsets                            │    │
│  │  1. Cordon node (mark unschedulable)                                 │    │
│  │  2. Evict all pods (respects PDBs, graceful termination)            │    │
│  │  3. DaemonSet pods ignored (recreated automatically)                 │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CKA Insight: On the CKA, when a pod is stuck in Pending with "0/3 nodes are available," use kubectl describe pod and look at the Events section. The scheduler explains WHY each node was rejected: "1 node(s) had taint {gpu: true}," "2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity," "3 Insufficient cpu." Also check: kubectl top nodes (resource usage) and kubectl describe node | grep -A5 Taints.

🔑 Key Takeaways

Bulleted key takeaways go here.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • nodeSelector vs nodeAffinity — nodeSelector is simple key=value matching. nodeAffinity supports In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist. The exam tests both
  • Taint effect matters — NoSchedule = new pods blocked. NoExecute = existing pods EVICTED. PreferNoSchedule = soft preference. Mixing them up = wrong answer
  • kubectl drain flags — Without --ignore-daemonsets it fails on DaemonSet pods. Without --delete-emptydir-data it fails on emptyDir volumes. Always use both
  • Cordon ≠ Drain — cordon only prevents NEW pods. drain evicts existing pods AND cordons. After maintenance: uncordon
  • Toleration must EXACTLY match taint — key, value, AND effect must match. A toleration with the wrong effect won't work
⚡ Speed Tips

CKA Speed Tip — Node maintenance in 30 seconds:
kubectl drain node01 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
… perform maintenance (upgrade, reboot) …
kubectl uncordon node01
Done. Pods will be rescheduled back automatically.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 14)

Action Command
Label a nodekubectl label node NAME key=value
Remove labelkubectl label node NAME key-
Add taintkubectl taint node NAME key=val:Effect
Remove taintkubectl taint node NAME key=val:Effect-
Cordon nodekubectl cordon NAME
Drain nodekubectl drain NAME --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
Uncordon nodekubectl uncordon NAME
Check node taintskubectl describe node NAME | grep Taints
Show node labelskubectl get nodes --show-labels
Check pod placementkubectl get pods -o wide
🧪 Drill

Timed challenge (target: 6 minutes):

  • 1. Label node node01 with disk=ssd
  • 2. Create a pod with nodeSelector: disk: ssd — verify it lands on node01
  • 3. Taint node01: kubectl taint node node01 maintenance=true:NoSchedule
  • 4. Create another pod WITHOUT toleration — it should go to a different node
  • 5. Drain node01, uncordon, verify pods reschedule

⚙️ Chapter 14 — Scenario & Command Drills (12)

Quick recall of scheduling & node-placement rules — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Schedule a pod named gpu-pod to run ONLY on nodes labeled hardware=gpu. Show the imperative generation and the relevant YAML fields.
Show Answer
Answer
first, label the target node
# First, label the target node
kubectl label node worker-1 hardware=gpu

# Generate pod YAML (add nodeSelector manually)
kubectl run gpu-pod --image=nvidia/cuda:12.0-base \
--dry-run=client -o yaml > gpu-pod.yaml

# Add nodeSelector to spec:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: gpu-pod
spec:
nodeSelector:         # ← Simple key-value matching
hardware: gpu
containers:
- name: gpu-pod
image: nvidia/cuda:12.0-base

kubectl apply -f gpu-pod.yaml

# Verify placement
kubectl get pod gpu-pod -o wide
# NAME      READY  STATUS   NODE
# gpu-pod   1/1    Running  worker-1
Explanation

nodeSelector is the simplest way to constrain pods to specific nodes. It uses exact label matching — the node MUST have all specified labels. If no node matches, the pod stays Pending. On the CKA, nodeSelector is the most commonly tested scheduling mechanism because it's fast to configure. Remember: the label must exist on the node BEFORE the pod is created (or the pod stays Pending). Use kubectl get nodes --show-labels to verify.

Q2
A node named node01 has a taint env=production:NoSchedule. Write a pod YAML that can be scheduled on this node. What happens if you use NoExecute instead?
Show Answer
Answer
apply the taint
# Apply the taint
kubectl taint node node01 env=production:NoSchedule

# Pod YAML with matching toleration:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: prod-pod
spec:
tolerations:
- key: "env"
operator: "Equal"
value: "production"
effect: "NoSchedule"
containers:
- name: app
image: nginx

# Taint effects comparison:
# NoSchedule:    Won't schedule new pods without toleration
#                Existing pods stay
# PreferNoSchedule: Try to avoid, but allow if no other option
# NoExecute:     Won't schedule new pods AND evicts existing
#                pods without toleration

# NoExecute with tolerationSeconds:
tolerations:
- key: "env"
operator: "Equal"
value: "production"
effect: "NoExecute"
tolerationSeconds: 3600   # Stay for 1 hour, then evicted
Explanation

NoSchedule only prevents NEW pods from being scheduled. NoExecute is more aggressive — it also EVICTS pods that are already running on the node unless they have a matching toleration. tolerationSeconds allows a pod to remain for a limited time before eviction. On the CKA, the taint effect is critical: NoSchedule for maintenance windows (existing pods stay), NoExecute for draining workloads. The operator: "Equal" requires exact key+value match; operator: "Exists" matches any value for that key.

Q3
You need to drain a node for maintenance. What sequence of commands should you use, and what safety flags are important?
Show Answer
Answer
cordon the node (mark unschedulable)
# Step 1: Cordon the node (mark unschedulable)
kubectl cordon node01
# node/node01 cordoned

# Step 2: Drain the node (evict all pods)
kubectl drain node01 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
# Evicts all pods, ignoring DaemonSet-managed pods

# Important flags:
# --ignore-daemonsets    Required! DaemonSet pods can't be evicted
# --delete-emptydir-data  Required if pods use emptyDir volumes
# --force                 Required for pods not managed by a controller
#                         (standalone pods will be LOST forever!)
# --grace-period=30       Override default termination grace period

# Verify node is drained
kubectl get nodes
# NAME     STATUS                     ROLES
# node01   Ready,SchedulingDisabled   worker

kubectl get pods -o wide | grep node01
# (no pods, except DaemonSet ones)

# Step 3: Perform maintenance...

# Step 4: Uncordon when done
kubectl uncordon node01
# node/node01 uncordoned (scheduling re-enabled)
Explanation

kubectl drain = cordon + evict all pods. Without --ignore-daemonsets, it fails because DaemonSet pods are supposed to run on every node. Without --delete-emptydir-data, it fails for pods using emptyDir (data will be lost). --force deletes standalone pods (not managed by a controller) — these pods are gone permanently since no controller recreates them. On the CKA, always include --ignore-daemonsets. If the drain refuses, read the error — it tells you exactly which flag to add.

Q4
What is the difference between nodeSelector and nodeAffinity? When must you use nodeAffinity instead?
Show Answer
Answer
Feature nodeSelector nodeAffinity
Operators Exact match only In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist, Gt, Lt
Required vs Preferred Always required Both options available
Complexity Simple key:value Complex expressions
nodeaffinity — required (hard rule)
# nodeAffinity — required (hard rule)
spec:
affinity:
nodeAffinity:
  requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
    nodeSelectorTerms:
    - matchExpressions:
      - key: disktype
        operator: In
        values: ["ssd", "nvme"]    # Match either value

# nodeAffinity — preferred (soft rule)
  preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
  - weight: 80
    preference:
      matchExpressions:
      - key: zone
        operator: In
        values: ["us-east-1a"]
Explanation

Use nodeAffinity when you need: (1) multiple possible values (operator: In), (2) negation (NotIn), (3) soft preferences (preferred vs required), or (4) complex expressions. nodeSelector only supports exact single-value matching. On the CKA, nodeAffinity is harder to type from memory — bookmark the docs page. requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution means "enforce at schedule time, don't evict if label changes later." The word required = hard constraint; preferred = best-effort.

Q5
Schedule a pod on a specific node named controlplane without using labels or taints. What mechanism allows this?
Show Answer
Answer
use nodename to bypass the scheduler entirely
# Use nodeName to bypass the scheduler entirely
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: debug-pod
spec:
nodeName: controlplane    # ← Direct node assignment
containers:
- name: debug
image: busybox
command: ["sleep", "3600"]

# This pod is NOT scheduled by kube-scheduler
# It's bound directly to the named node
# If controlplane doesn't exist → pod stays Pending forever

# Verify:
kubectl get pod debug-pod -o wide
# NAME       READY  STATUS   NODE
# debug-pod  1/1    Running  controlplane
Explanation

nodeName bypasses the scheduler completely — the pod is directly assigned to the specified node. This ignores all taints, tolerations, nodeSelector, and affinity rules. It's useful for debugging or when the scheduler is down. On the CKA, nodeName appears in questions about "static scheduling" or "scheduling without the scheduler." Drawbacks: if the node goes down, the pod is NOT rescheduled (no controller watching). Use only for temporary debugging, not production workloads.

Q6
A pod is stuck in Pending state. kubectl describe pod shows: "0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had taint {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:}, 2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector." Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
diagnosis
# Diagnosis:
# - 1 node: tainted as control-plane (expected)
# - 2 nodes: don't match the pod's nodeSelector or affinity

# Step 1: Check what the pod requires
kubectl get pod pending-pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeSelector}'
# {"gpu":"true"}

# Step 2: Check available node labels
kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep gpu
# (no output — no node has gpu=true label!)

# Fix Option 1: Label a worker node
kubectl label node worker-1 gpu=true

# Fix Option 2: Remove the nodeSelector from the pod
# (Delete and recreate without nodeSelector)
kubectl get pod pending-pod -o yaml > pod.yaml
# Edit pod.yaml: remove nodeSelector section
kubectl delete pod pending-pod
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml

# Verify
kubectl get pod pending-pod
# STATUS: Running
Explanation

The scheduler message tells you exactly why no node is suitable. On the CKA, this is a common troubleshooting scenario. The diagnostic flow: (1) Check Events in kubectl describe pod for the scheduler message, (2) Extract the pod's scheduling constraints (nodeSelector, affinity, tolerations), (3) Compare against available nodes and their labels/taints. Remember: control-plane nodes have a default taint — pods won't schedule there unless they have the matching toleration.

Q7
How do you remove a taint from a node? Show the command for removing env=production:NoSchedule from node01.
Show Answer
Answer
remove a specific taint (note the trailing minus -)
# Remove a specific taint (note the trailing minus -)
kubectl taint node node01 env=production:NoSchedule-
# node/node01 untainted

# Remove taint by key only (removes all effects for that key)
kubectl taint node node01 env-
# Removes env:NoSchedule, env:NoExecute, etc.

# Verify taint is removed
kubectl describe node node01 | grep -i taint
# Taints: <none>

# Common mistake — forgetting the minus sign:
kubectl taint node node01 env=production:NoSchedule
# This ADDS the taint instead of removing it!
Explanation

The trailing - (minus sign) at the end of the taint specification removes it. This is the same pattern as kubectl label node node01 key- for removing labels. On the CKA, forgetting the - is a common time-wasting error that ADDS the taint instead. If you specify key=value:effect, it removes that exact taint. If you specify just key-, it removes all taints with that key regardless of value or effect.

Q8
What is podAffinity vs podAntiAffinity? Give a scenario where you'd use each on the CKA exam.
Show Answer
Answer
podaffinity: schedule near pods with specific labels
# podAffinity: Schedule NEAR pods with specific labels
# Use case: web pod should be on same node as cache pod
spec:
affinity:
podAffinity:
  requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
  - labelSelector:
      matchExpressions:
      - key: app
        operator: In
        values: ["redis-cache"]
    topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname

# podAntiAffinity: Schedule AWAY from pods with specific labels
# Use case: spread replicas across different nodes
spec:
affinity:
podAntiAffinity:
  requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
  - labelSelector:
      matchExpressions:
      - key: app
        operator: In
        values: ["webapp"]
    topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
# Each webapp replica lands on a different node
Explanation

podAffinity = co-locate pods (low latency between services). podAntiAffinity = spread pods apart (high availability). topologyKey defines the "zone" — kubernetes.io/hostname means per-node, topology.kubernetes.io/zone means per-AZ. On the CKA, anti-affinity is more commonly tested — especially "ensure no two replicas of the same app run on the same node." If you have 3 replicas and only 2 nodes with required anti-affinity, the 3rd pod stays Pending.

Q9
How do you check which taints are applied to all nodes in the cluster? And how do you find which pods have tolerations?
Show Answer
Answer
view taints on all nodes
# View taints on all nodes
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=\
NAME:.metadata.name,\
TAINTS:.spec.taints

# Or with describe
kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 "Taints:"
# Taints: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule
# Taints: env=production:NoSchedule

# JSON path for specific node
kubectl get node node01 -o jsonpath='{.spec.taints[*]}'

# Find pods with tolerations
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.tolerations}{"\n"}{end}'

# Or describe a specific pod
kubectl describe pod my-pod | grep -A10 "Tolerations:"
# Tolerations: node.kubernetes.io/not-ready:NoExecute op=Exists for 300s
#              node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute op=Exists for 300s
Explanation

Every pod automatically gets two default tolerations: node.kubernetes.io/not-ready:NoExecute and node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute with 300s tolerance — this is why pods stay for 5 minutes after a node becomes unreachable. On the CKA, quickly checking taints with custom-columns is efficient. The control-plane taint node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule prevents workload pods from scheduling on the control plane — this is normal and expected. DaemonSet pods (like kube-proxy) tolerate this automatically.

Q10
A DaemonSet pod is not running on node02 but runs on all other nodes. What are the possible causes and how do you investigate?
Show Answer
Answer
check if node02 is cordoned
# Step 1: Check if node02 is cordoned
kubectl get node node02
# STATUS: Ready,SchedulingDisabled ← cordoned!

# Step 2: Check taints on node02
kubectl describe node node02 | grep Taints
# Taints: special=true:NoSchedule

# Step 3: Check DaemonSet tolerations
kubectl get ds monitoring-agent -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.tolerations}'
# Missing toleration for special=true:NoSchedule!

# Fix Option 1: Add toleration to DaemonSet
kubectl edit ds monitoring-agent
# Add toleration for the taint

# Fix Option 2: Remove the taint
kubectl taint node node02 special-

# Step 4: Check node conditions
kubectl describe node node02 | grep -A5 Conditions
# MemoryPressure: True ← node under memory pressure
# DiskPressure: True   ← node under disk pressure
# These auto-add taints that evict pods!

# Step 5: Check DaemonSet's nodeSelector
kubectl get ds monitoring-agent -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.nodeSelector}'
# {"os":"linux"} — does node02 have this label?
Explanation

DaemonSets are designed to run on every node, but they still respect taints and nodeSelectors. Common causes for missing DaemonSet pods: (1) node is cordoned (scheduling disabled), (2) taint without matching toleration, (3) nodeSelector mismatch, (4) node conditions like MemoryPressure auto-add taints. On the CKA, DaemonSet scheduling issues are a classic troubleshooting question. Note: DaemonSets automatically tolerate node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable:NoSchedule (cordon), but if you manually add a custom taint, the DaemonSet must explicitly tolerate it.

Q11
Create a Deployment with topologySpreadConstraints that spreads pods evenly across nodes with a maximum skew of 1. What happens when the constraint can't be satisfied?
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
name: easypj-web
spec:
replicas: 6
selector:
matchLabels:
  app: easypj
template:
metadata:
  labels:
    app: easypj
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1                           # Max difference between zones
    topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname   # Spread across nodes
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule      # Block if can't spread
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: easypj
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: easypj:v1

# With 3 nodes and 6 replicas:
#   node1: 2 pods, node2: 2 pods, node3: 2 pods ✅
#   node1: 3 pods, node2: 2 pods, node3: 1 pod  ❌ skew=2

# whenUnsatisfiable options:
# DoNotSchedule  → Pod stays Pending (strict)
# ScheduleAnyway → Schedule anyway, best-effort (soft)

# Check distribution:
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj -o wide \
--sort-by='.spec.nodeName'
# Shows which pod is on which node
Explanation

topologySpreadConstraints provide fine-grained control over pod distribution across failure domains (nodes, zones, regions). maxSkew defines the maximum allowed difference in pod count between topology domains. topologyKey determines what defines a domain — kubernetes.io/hostname for nodes, topology.kubernetes.io/zone for zones. whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule makes pods Pending if they'd violate the constraint — like a hard anti-affinity but more flexible. On the CKA, topology spread is the modern replacement for podAntiAffinity when you need even distribution with more control.

Q12
What is a PriorityClass? Create a high-priority class and show how a high-priority pod can preempt a lower-priority one.
Show Answer
Answer
create priorityclasses
# Step 1: Create PriorityClasses
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
name: high-priority
value: 1000000
globalDefault: false
preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority
description: "Critical production workloads"
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
name: low-priority
value: 100
globalDefault: false
preemptionPolicy: Never     # ← Won't evict others
description: "Background batch jobs"

# Step 2: Use in a Pod spec
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: critical-app
spec:
priorityClassName: high-priority   # ← Reference by name
containers:
- name: app
image: easypj:v1
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "2"
    memory: "4Gi"

# What happens during preemption:
# 1. Cluster is full — no node has space for critical-app
# 2. Scheduler finds low-priority pods on a node
# 3. Scheduler evicts low-priority pods to make room
# 4. critical-app gets scheduled

# Check PriorityClasses:
kubectl get priorityclasses
# NAME            VALUE      GLOBAL-DEFAULT
# high-priority   1000000    false
# low-priority    100        false
# system-*        very high  (built-in for kube-system)
Explanation

PriorityClasses assign scheduling priority to pods. When the cluster is full, the scheduler evicts lower-priority pods to make room for higher-priority ones. value is an integer (higher = more important). preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority (default) allows evicting others; Never means the pod waits without evicting. Kubernetes has built-in system priority classes (e.g., system-cluster-critical value 2000000000) for control plane components. On the CKA, you may need to create a PriorityClass and assign it to a pod. Remember: PriorityClass is cluster-scoped (no namespace), and the API group is scheduling.k8s.io/v1.

Chapter 15 · Resource Management

Every container in Kubernetes can request a minimum amount of CPU and memory, and be limited to a maximum. Understanding requests, limits, QoS classes, LimitRanges, and ResourceQuotas is critical for cluster stability — and prominently tested on the CKA exam. A misconfigured resource setting can crash an entire node.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 📊 Resources 📝 CKA EXAM

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Set CPU and memory requests (scheduling guarantee) and limits (hard ceiling)
  • ✅ Understand QoS classes — Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort
  • ✅ Configure LimitRange for namespace-wide default limits
  • ✅ Configure ResourceQuota to cap total namespace consumption
  • ✅ Know what happens when CPU is exceeded (throttle) vs memory (OOMKilled)
🎓 CKA Relevance
Workloads & Scheduling 15% Cluster Architecture 25%
Resource Questions on the CKA

You'll likely be asked to:

  • Create pods with specific resource requests and limits
  • Create LimitRange or ResourceQuota for a namespace
  • Identify why a pod is OOMKilled or stuck in Pending
  • Know: kubectl top pods and kubectl top nodes

15.1 Resource Requests and Limits

Every container can specify requests (minimum guaranteed) and limits (maximum allowed). The scheduler uses requests to decide where to place pods. The kubelet enforces limits at runtime.

📋
Requests

"I need at least this much." Used by the scheduler for placement. The node must have this amount free or the pod won't be scheduled.

🚧
Limits

"Don't use more than this." Enforced by the kubelet. CPU exceeds limit → throttled. Memory exceeds limit → OOMKilled.

easypj-resources.yaml 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj
spec:
  containers:
  - name: django
    image: easypj:v1
    resources:
      requests:                  # Scheduling guarantee
        cpu: "250m"              # 0.25 CPU cores (250 millicores)
        memory: "256Mi"          # 256 MiB RAM
      limits:                    # Hard ceiling
        cpu: "500m"              # 0.5 CPU cores max
        memory: "512Mi"          # 512 MiB RAM max

CPU & Memory Units

⚙️ CPU: 1000m = 1 core
100m = 0.1 core, 250m = 0.25 core, 1 = 1 full core, 2 = 2 cores
💾 Memory: Mi, Gi
128Mi = 128 MiB, 1Gi = 1 GiB. Use Mi/Gi (binary) not MB/GB (decimal).
⏳ CPU exceeded
Throttled — process slows down but keeps running. Not killed.
💀 Memory exceeded
OOMKilled — container is killed immediately. Restarts per restartPolicy.
⏳ CPU Exceeded → Throttled
  • Container is NOT killed
  • Process slows down, capped at the limit
  • No restarts, no OOM events
  • Hard to detect — app just becomes slow
  • Diagnose: kubectl top pod shows CPU pinned at limit
  • Fix: Increase limits.cpu or optimize app
💀 Memory Exceeded → OOMKilled
  • Container is killed immediately (SIGKILL)
  • Exit code 137 in pod description
  • Pod restarts → often leads to CrashLoopBackOff
  • Easy to detect: status shows OOMKilled
  • Diagnose: kubectl describe pod → Last State → OOMKilled
  • Fix: Increase limits.memory or fix memory leak
  Node Capacity: 4 CPU, 8Gi Memory
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────── easypj container ─────────────┐                  │
  │  │                                            │                  │
  │  │  CPU:    [====request 250m====|...limit 500m....]             │
  │  │          ├─── guaranteed ────┤├── can burst ──┤               │
  │  │                                            │                  │
  │  │  Memory: [====request 256Mi===|...limit 512Mi...]             │
  │  │          ├─── guaranteed ────┤├── can use ───┤                │
  │  │                                   ↑ exceed = OOMKill 💀      │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘                  │
  │                                                                  │
  │  What happens:                                                   │
  │  ├── Actual CPU  = 300m  → ✅ Within limit, no throttle         │
  │  ├── Actual CPU  = 600m  → ⏳ Throttled to 500m                 │
  │  ├── Actual Mem  = 400Mi → ✅ Within limit, fine                │
  │  └── Actual Mem  = 600Mi → 💀 OOMKilled! Container restarts    │
  │                                                                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🚨 Never Skip Resource Settings in Production
  • No requests: Scheduler doesn't know what the pod needs → random placement → resource contention
  • No limits: Pod can consume ALL available node memory → OOMs other pods → cascading failure
  • Always set both on every production container!
Monitoring Resource Usage 
# Check actual usage vs requests/limits
kubectl top pods
# NAME      CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
# easypj   120m         180Mi

kubectl top nodes
# NAME       CPU(cores)   CPU%   MEMORY(bytes)   MEMORY%
# worker-1   850m         42%    3200Mi           40%

# Find pods with no resource limits (dangerous!)
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | 
  select(.spec.containers[].resources.limits == null) | 
  .metadata.name'

Troubleshooting OOMKilled Pods

One of the most common issues on the CKA and in production. Here's a systematic approach:

1
Find OOMKilled Pods

kubectl get pods -A | grep OOMKilled or grep CrashLoopBackOff (often caused by repeated OOM)

2
Confirm OOM Reason

kubectl describe pod NAME → look for Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137

3
Check Current Limits

kubectl get pod NAME -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}' → see current memory limit

4
Check Actual Usage

kubectl top pod NAME → if usage is close to limit, the limit is too low

5
Fix & Verify

Increase memory limit: kubectl set resources deployment/NAME --limits=memory=512Mi. Watch pod restart successfully.

OOMKilled Diagnosis Steps 
# Step 1: Find OOMKilled pods
kubectl get pods -A | grep OOMKilled
kubectl get pods -A | grep CrashLoopBackOff   # often caused by OOM

# Step 2: Check the pod's last state
kubectl describe pod easypj-abc12 | grep -A5 "Last State"
#   Last State:  Terminated
#     Reason:    OOMKilled
#     Exit Code: 137       ← 137 = SIGKILL (memory limit hit)

# Step 3: Check current resource config
kubectl get pod easypj-abc12 -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'
# {"limits":{"memory":"256Mi"},"requests":{"memory":"128Mi"}}

# Step 4: Check actual usage (if pod is running)
kubectl top pod easypj-abc12
# CPU: 100m    MEMORY: 245Mi   ← close to 256Mi limit!

# Step 5: Fix — increase memory limit
kubectl set resources deployment/easypj -c django \
  --limits=memory=512Mi --requests=memory=256Mi
OOMKill Decision Tree — Is It the Container or the Node?
  Pod terminated with Exit Code 137?
       │
       ├── YES → OOMKilled!
       │        │
       │   Was the pod using more memory
       │   than its spec.resources.limits.memory?
       │        │
       │   ┌────┴────┐
       │   YES        NO
       │   │          │
       │   Container  Node-level OOM
       │   limit hit  (node ran out of memory)
       │   │          │
       │   Fix:       Fix: add more nodes,
       │   Increase   reduce other workloads,
       │   memory     or fix memory leaks
       │   limits
       │
       └── Exit Code 1 = app error (not OOM)

15.2 QoS Classes — Quality of Service

Kubernetes automatically assigns a QoS class to every pod based on its resource configuration. This determines the eviction priority when a node runs out of resources.

QoS Class Criteria Eviction Priority easypj Use Case
Guaranteed Every container has requests == limits (both CPU & memory set and equal) Last to be evicted (safest) 🛡️ ✅ Production easypj
Burstable At least one container has requests < limits (or only requests set) Evicted after BestEffort ⚠️ ⚠️ Dev/staging easypj
BestEffort No requests or limits set on any container First to be evicted (riskiest) 💀 ❌ Never in production
QoS Eviction Order — Node Under Memory Pressure
  Node memory: 95% used — kubelet starts evicting pods!

  Eviction Order:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                   │
  │  💀 FIRST: BestEffort pods                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Pod: test-pod (no requests, no limits)      │ │
  │  │ → EVICTED immediately                       │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │          │                                        │
  │          ▼ (still need more memory?)              │
  │  ⚠️ SECOND: Burstable pods                      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Pod: dev-easypj (requests < limits)         │ │
  │  │ → EVICTED if using more than requests       │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │          │                                        │
  │          ▼ (extreme pressure only)                │
  │  🛡️ LAST: Guaranteed pods                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Pod: prod-easypj (requests == limits)       │ │
  │  │ → Only evicted as absolute last resort      │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
QoS Examples 
# Guaranteed QoS — requests EQUAL limits
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "512Mi"
  limits:
    cpu: "500m"          # same as request
    memory: "512Mi"      # same as request
# → QoS: Guaranteed ✅

---
# Burstable QoS — requests LESS THAN limits
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: "256Mi"
  limits:
    cpu: "500m"          # more than request
    memory: "512Mi"      # more than request
# → QoS: Burstable ⚠️

---
# BestEffort QoS — NO resources at all
# (just don't include the resources section)
# → QoS: BestEffort 💀
Check Pod QoS Class 
# Check QoS class of a pod
kubectl get pod easypj -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
# Guaranteed

# Check QoS of all pods
kubectl get pods -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,QOS:.status.qosClass'
# NAME              QOS
# easypj-abc12      Guaranteed
# dev-app-xyz       Burstable
# test-pod          BestEffort
💡 Production QoS Strategy for easypj

For your production stack, aim for these QoS classes:

  • Guaranteed: easypj Django (production), PostgreSQL — set requests == limits
  • Burstable: easypj staging, Redis cache — allow bursting for efficiency
  • BestEffort: Only for throwaway test pods in dev. Never in production!

Pro tip: Use Guaranteed for anything facing users. Use Burstable for internal services that benefit from occasional burst capacity.

15.3 LimitRange — Namespace Default Limits

A LimitRange sets default resource requests and limits for containers in a namespace. It also enforces min/max boundaries. This prevents pods from running without any resource configuration.

limitrange.yaml 
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: easypj-limits
  namespace: easypj-dev
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:                     # Default LIMITS (if not specified)
      cpu: "500m"
      memory: "512Mi"
    defaultRequest:              # Default REQUESTS (if not specified)
      cpu: "250m"
      memory: "256Mi"
    max:                         # Maximum allowed
      cpu: "2"
      memory: "2Gi"
    min:                         # Minimum allowed
      cpu: "50m"
      memory: "32Mi"
  - type: Pod
    max:
      cpu: "4"
      memory: "4Gi"
LimitRange in Action 
# Create namespace and LimitRange
kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
kubectl apply -f limitrange.yaml

# Create pod WITHOUT specifying resources
kubectl run test-pod --image=nginx -n easypj-dev

# Check — LimitRange injected default values!
kubectl get pod test-pod -n easypj-dev -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'
# {"limits":{"cpu":"500m","memory":"512Mi"},"requests":{"cpu":"250m","memory":"256Mi"}}

# Try to create pod exceeding max
# → Error: maximum cpu usage per Container is 2, but limit is 4
LimitRange — Automatic Defaults
  Namespace: easypj-dev (with LimitRange)

  Pod created WITHOUT resources:        Pod received DEFAULTS:
  ┌──────────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ spec:                    │   →     │ spec:                        │
  │   containers:            │   →     │   containers:                │
  │   - name: nginx          │   →     │   - name: nginx              │
  │     image: nginx         │   →     │     image: nginx             │
  │     # no resources!      │   →     │     resources:               │
  │                          │   →     │       requests:              │
  │                          │   →     │         cpu: "250m"    ← injected! │
  │                          │   →     │         memory: "256Mi" ← injected!│
  │                          │   →     │       limits:               │
  │                          │   →     │         cpu: "500m"    ← injected! │
  │                          │   →     │         memory: "512Mi" ← injected!│
  └──────────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────────────┘

15.4 ResourceQuota — Namespace Capacity Control

A ResourceQuota limits the total resources consumed across all pods in a namespace. This prevents one team from using all cluster resources and is a key tool for multi-tenant clusters.

resourcequota.yaml 
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: easypj-quota
  namespace: easypj-dev
spec:
  hard:
    # Compute resources
    requests.cpu: "4"            # Total CPU requests across all pods
    requests.memory: "8Gi"       # Total memory requests
    limits.cpu: "8"              # Total CPU limits
    limits.memory: "16Gi"        # Total memory limits

    # Object count limits
    pods: "10"                   # Max 10 pods in this namespace
    services: "5"                # Max 5 services
    persistentvolumeclaims: "5"  # Max 5 PVCs
    configmaps: "20"
    secrets: "20"
ResourceQuota Commands 
# Apply quota
kubectl apply -f resourcequota.yaml

# Check quota usage
kubectl get resourcequota -n easypj-dev
# NAME           AGE   REQUEST                                              LIMIT
# easypj-quota   5m    requests.cpu: 750m/4, requests.memory: 768Mi/8Gi    limits.cpu: 1500m/8, limits.memory: 1536Mi/16Gi

# Detailed view
kubectl describe resourcequota easypj-quota -n easypj-dev
# Name:                   easypj-quota
# Namespace:              easypj-dev
# Resource                Used    Hard
# --------                ----    ----
# limits.cpu              1500m   8
# limits.memory           1536Mi  16Gi
# pods                    3       10
# requests.cpu            750m    4
# requests.memory         768Mi   8Gi
Resource Control Hierarchy — 3 Levels
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LEVEL 1: ResourceQuota (namespace total budget)               │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ "easypj-dev can use max 4 CPUs, 8Gi memory total"       │  │
  │  │  Used: 750m / 4 CPU    Used: 768Mi / 8Gi memory         │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │       │                                                        │
  │       ▼                                                        │
  │  LEVEL 2: LimitRange (per-container defaults & bounds)       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ "Each container: default 250m req, 500m limit"           │  │
  │  │ "Min: 50m CPU, Max: 2 CPU per container"                 │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │       │                                                        │
  │       ▼                                                        │
  │  LEVEL 3: Pod spec (individual container settings)            │
  │  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐              │
  │  │ easypj-1   │  │ easypj-2   │  │ easypj-3   │              │
  │  │ req: 250m  │  │ req: 250m  │  │ req: 250m  │              │
  │  │ lim: 500m  │  │ lim: 500m  │  │ lim: 500m  │              │
  │  └────────────┘  └────────────┘  └────────────┘              │
  │  Total: 750m request, 1500m limit (within quota ✅)           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ ResourceQuota Requires Resource Specs

When a ResourceQuota is active in a namespace, every pod must specify resource requests and limits. Without them, the pod creation will be rejected. Use a LimitRange to auto-inject defaults so developers don't have to specify them manually.

🔥

Scenario: "Pod Creation Rejected — Forbidden"

CKA EXAM

Symptom: kubectl run test --image=nginx -n dev → Error: forbidden: failed quota: dev-quota: must specify limits.cpu,limits.memory

Step 1 — Check quota

kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev → quota exists and enforces limits. No LimitRange present to auto-inject defaults.

Step 2 — Two fixes

Option A: Add resources to pod spec. Option B: Create a LimitRange with default and defaultRequest so future pods get automatic defaults.

Step 3 — Verify

Re-run kubectl run test --image=nginx -n dev → pod created. kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev → Used values increased.

Lesson: When ResourceQuota exists, always pair it with a LimitRange. This is a classic CKA trap — the exam expects you to know both work together.
Under the Hood — How CPU and Memory Limits Are Actually Enforced by the Linux Kernel: CFS Quotas, Cgroups v2, OOM Scoring, and QoS Classes
🗺️ Resource Enforcement — From Kubernetes YAML to Kernel Mechanisms

Kubernetes resource limits aren't just suggestions — they're enforced by the Linux kernel through cgroups. Understanding the exact mechanism helps you set correct limits and debug OOMKilled pods.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  KUBERNETES RESOURCES → LINUX CGROUPS MAPPING                                 │
│                                                                              │
│  Pod YAML:                           Kernel Cgroup (cgroups v2):             │
│  ┌────────────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ resources:                 │      │ /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods/         │   │
│  │   requests:                │      │   burstable/                     │   │
│  │     cpu: 250m              │─────▶│   pod<uid>/                      │   │
│  │     memory: 256Mi          │      │     cpu.weight: ~25              │   │
│  │                            │      │     memory.min: 256Mi             │   │
│  │   limits:                  │      │                                   │   │
│  │     cpu: 500m              │─────▶│     cpu.max: 50000 100000        │   │
│  │     memory: 512Mi          │      │     memory.max: 512Mi             │   │
│  └────────────────────────────┘      └──────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  CPU LIMIT ENFORCEMENT (CFS — Completely Fair Scheduler):                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Linux CFS uses QUOTA and PERIOD:                                    │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │   limits.cpu: 500m → 0.5 CPU cores                                  │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │   CFS settings (kernel):                                             │    │
│  │     cpu.cfs_period_us  = 100000  (100ms — the accounting period)    │    │
│  │     cpu.cfs_quota_us   = 50000   (50ms — max CPU time per period)   │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │   RESULT: Container gets at MOST 50ms of CPU every 100ms.            │    │
│  │           This equals 0.5 cores = 500 millicores.                     │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  WHAT HAPPENS WHEN CPU LIMIT IS HIT:                                 │    │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │    │
│  │  │ CPU is THROTTLED (not killed):                               │    │    │
│  │  │ • Process is paused by CFS scheduler                         │    │    │
│  │  │ • Resumes in next accounting period                          │    │    │
│  │  │ • Observable as: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total   │    │    │
│  │  │ • Effect: increased latency, NOT pod termination             │    │    │
│  │  │                                                               │    │    │
│  │  │ $ kubectl top pod easypj-web-xxx                              │    │    │
│  │  │ NAME               CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)                 │    │    │
│  │  │ easypj-web-xxx     498m          489Mi  ← Near limit!        │    │    │
│  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  MEMORY LIMIT ENFORCEMENT (OOM Killer):                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  limits.memory: 512Mi                                                │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  Cgroup setting: memory.max = 536870912 bytes (512Mi)                │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  WHAT HAPPENS WHEN MEMORY LIMIT IS EXCEEDED:                        │    │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │    │
│  │  │ 1. Container tries to allocate more than 512Mi               │    │    │
│  │  │ 2. Kernel memory allocator returns -ENOMEM                   │    │    │
│  │  │ 3. OOM Killer invoked (cgroup-level, not host-level)         │    │    │
│  │  │ 4. Process with highest oom_score in cgroup is KILLED        │    │    │
│  │  │ 5. Container exits with code 137 (128 + SIGKILL)             │    │    │
│  │  │ 6. kubelet detects container death → restarts (if RestartPolicy allows)│    │    │
│  │  │                                                               │    │    │
│  │  │ $ kubectl describe pod easypj-web-xxx                         │    │    │
│  │  │ Last State:   Terminated                                      │    │    │
│  │  │   Reason:     OOMKilled                                        │    │    │
│  │  │   Exit Code:  137                                              │    │    │
│  │  │   Started:    Mon, 02 Jun 2026 10:00:00 +0000                 │    │    │
│  │  │   Finished:   Mon, 02 Jun 2026 10:05:23 +0000                 │    │    │
│  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  QOS CLASSES — How Kubernetes Prioritizes Which Pod to Kill First:          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  ┌──────────────────┬─────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐ │    │
│  │  │ QoS CLASS        │ CONDITION        │ OOM KILL ORDER           │ │    │
│  │  ├──────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤ │    │
│  │  │ Guaranteed       │ requests ==       │ KILLED LAST (safest)     │ │    │
│  │  │                  │ limits for BOTH   │                          │ │    │
│  │  │                  │ cpu AND memory    │                          │ │    │
│  │  ├──────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤ │    │
│  │  │ Burstable        │ At least one      │ KILLED MIDDLE            │ │    │
│  │  │                  │ container has      │                          │ │    │
│  │  │                  │ request < limit   │                          │ │    │
│  │  ├──────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤ │    │
│  │  │ BestEffort       │ No requests or    │ KILLED FIRST (riskiest)  │ │    │
│  │  │                  │ limits set        │                          │ │    │
│  │  └──────────────────┴─────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘ │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  CKA RULE: On the exam, always set requests=limits for critical      │    │
│  │  pods (Guaranteed QoS). On a resource-starved node, BestEffort pods  │    │
│  │  die first when the OOM killer runs.                                 │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CKA Insight: The CKA frequently tests finding and fixing OOMKilled pods. The diagnostic flow: (1) kubectl get pods → look for RESTARTS column > 0, (2) kubectl describe pod → check Last State for OOMKilled, (3) kubectl top pod → check actual memory usage, (4) Fix: increase resources.limits.memory or reduce app memory usage. Exit code 137 ALWAYS means OOMKilled (128 + 9 SIGKILL).

🔑 Key Takeaways

Bulleted key takeaways go here.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Requests vs Limits — requests = guaranteed minimum (used for scheduling). limits = maximum allowed (enforced at runtime). Scheduler uses requests, NOT limits
  • CPU units — 1 = 1 vCPU. 500m = 0.5 CPU. 100m = 0.1 CPU. The exam loves asking you to convert between these
  • Memory units — Mi (mebibytes) ≠ M (megabytes). Use Mi for consistency. 128Mi = 134MB
  • QoS classes — Guaranteed (requests=limits for all containers), Burstable (some requests set), BestEffort (no requests/limits). OOM killer targets BestEffort first
  • LimitRange applies to NEW pods only — Existing pods aren't affected. ResourceQuota blocks creation when the namespace total is exceeded
⚡ Speed Tips

CKA Speed Tip: Find which pods are hogging resources:
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu — highest CPU consumers
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory — highest memory consumers
kubectl describe node <name> | grep -A5 "Allocated resources" — node-level usage summary

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 15)

Action Command
Check pod resource usagekubectl top pods
Check node resource usagekubectl top nodes
View pod QoS classkubectl get pod NAME -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
View LimitRangekubectl describe limitrange -n NAMESPACE
View ResourceQuotakubectl describe resourcequota -n NAMESPACE
Check OOMKilled podskubectl get pods | grep OOMKilled
View container resourceskubectl get pod NAME -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].resources}'
Set container resource requests/limitskubectl set resources deployment/web -c=nginx --requests=cpu=100m,memory=128Mi --limits=cpu=500m,memory=256Mi
Create a ResourceQuotakubectl create quota my-quota --hard=pods=10,requests.cpu=4,requests.memory=8Gi -n dev
see used vs hard limitskubectl describe resourcequota -n dev
