Under the Hood — How NetworkPolicy Is Enforced at the Kernel Level: From YAML Rules to iptables/eBPF Filters, and How Ingress Controllers Route External Traffic
🗺️ NetworkPolicy — From YAML to Kernel Rules

NetworkPolicy YAML looks simple, but it translates into complex iptables rules (or eBPF programs with Cilium). Understanding the translation helps you debug "why isn't my policy working" scenarios.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NETWORKPOLICY → IPTABLES TRANSLATION (Calico example)                       │
│                                                                              │
│  YAML:                                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1                                      │   │
│  │ kind: NetworkPolicy                                                    │   │
│  │   podSelector:                                                        │   │
│  │     matchLabels: {app: easypj, tier: backend}                        │   │
│  │   ingress:                                                             │   │
│  │   - from:                                                              │   │
│  │     - podSelector: {role: frontend}                                   │   │
│  │     ports:                                                             │   │
│  │     - port: 8000                                                       │   │
│  │       protocol: TCP                                                    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  GENERATED IPTABLES RULES (on every node where matching pods run):          │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ # 1. Mark packets from frontend pods as ALLOWED                       │   │
│  │ -A cali-fw-cali12345 -m comment --comment "allow frontend→backend" \ │   │
│  │   -m set --match-set cali40-frontend-src src \                       │   │
│  │   -p tcp --dport 8000 -j MARK --set-mark 0x10000                     │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ # 2. Allow MARKED packets (matching policy)                           │   │
│  │ -A cali-fw-cali12345 -m mark --mark 0x10000 -j ACCEPT                │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ # 3. DEFAULT DENY (no matching mark → DROP)                           │   │
│  │ -A cali-fw-cali12345 -j DROP                                          │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  NETWORKPOLICY RULES (memorize for CKA):                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. Policies are ADDITIVE — multiple policies UNION their rules       │   │
│  │ 2. Empty podSelector = ALL pods in namespace                         │   │
│  │ 3. Empty ingress = ALLOW ALL traffic (not useful alone)              │   │
│  │ 4. Empty from = ALL sources (any pod, any namespace, any IP)         │   │
│  │ 5. namespaceSelector + podSelector in same rule = AND (both must     │   │
│  │    match: pods from namespace X AND with label Y)                    │   │
│  │ 6. namespaceSelector OR podSelector in DIFFERENT rules = OR          │   │
│  │                                                                       │   │
│  │ DEFAULT DENY ALL ingress:                                             │   │
│  │   podSelector: {}          # selects all pods                        │   │
│  │   ingress: []              # empty list = deny all                   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 Ingress Controller — External Traffic Routing

Ingress is NOT a built-in controller — you must install one (nginx, traefik, etc.). It runs as a pod and watches Ingress resources to configure itself:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  INGRESS CONTROLLER — How External Traffic Reaches Your Pod                  │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  INTERNET                                                              │   │
│  │    │                                                                   │   │
│  │    │  https://easypj.com/api/users                                    │   │
│  │    ▼                                                                   │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────────┐                                                  │   │
│  │  │ Cloud LB / MetalLB│  (External IP: 203.0.113.5)                     │   │
│  │  └────────┬─────────┘                                                  │   │
│  │           │ NodePort 30080-30081 OR LoadBalancer                        │   │
│  │           ▼                                                              │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │   │
│  │  │  INGRESS CONTROLLER POD (nginx-ingress)                        │     │   │
│  │  │                                                                │     │   │
│  │  │  1. Watches Ingress resources via K8s API                      │     │   │
│  │  │  2. Generates nginx.conf from Ingress rules:                   │     │   │
│  │  │                                                                │     │   │
│  │  │     server {                                                   │     │   │
│  │  │       listen 443 ssl;                                          │     │   │
│  │  │       server_name easypj.com;                                   │     │   │
│  │  │                                                                │     │   │
│  │  │       location /api {                                          │     │   │
│  │  │         proxy_pass http://backend-svc:8080;                    │     │   │
│  │  │       }                                                        │     │   │
│  │  │                                                                │     │   │
│  │  │       location / {                                             │     │   │
│  │  │         proxy_pass http://frontend-svc:80;                     │     │   │
│  │  │       }                                                        │     │   │
│  │  │     }                                                          │     │   │
│  │  │                                                                │     │   │
│  │  │  3. Reloads nginx on Ingress changes                           │     │   │
│  │  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘     │   │
│  │                             │ proxy_pass                               │   │
│  │                             ▼                                          │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐                           │   │
│  │  │ backend-svc:8080 │  │ frontend-svc:80  │  (ClusterIP Services)     │   │
│  │  │ → backend pods   │  │ → frontend pods  │                           │   │
│  │  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘                           │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  INGRESS RESOURCE (routes — NOT the controller!):                            │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1                                      │   │
│  │ kind: Ingress                                                          │   │
│  │ spec:                                                                   │   │
│  │   rules:                                                                │   │
│  │   - host: easypj.com                                                    │   │
│  │     http:                                                                │   │
│  │       paths:                                                             │   │
│  │       - path: /api                                                       │   │
│  │         pathType: Prefix                                                  │   │
│  │         backend:                                                          │   │
│  │           service:                                                        │   │
│  │             name: backend-svc                                             │   │
│  │             port: {number: 8080}                                          │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CKA Insight: NetworkPolicy requires a CNI that supports it (Calico, Cilium, Weave). Flannel does NOT support NetworkPolicy by default. On the CKA, if you create a NetworkPolicy and it doesn't work, verify: (1) kubectl get networkpolicy — does the policy exist in the right namespace? (2) Does your CNI support NetworkPolicy? (3) Policies are namespace-scoped — a policy in namespace A cannot affect pods in namespace B (except via namespaceSelector).

🔑 Key Takeaways

Bulleted key takeaways go here.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Ingress requires a controller — Creating an Ingress resource does nothing without an Ingress Controller (nginx, traefik). The exam cluster has one pre-installed — check with kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx
  • Ingress pathType is REQUIRED — Must be Prefix, Exact, or ImplementationSpecific. Missing it = validation error. Prefix matches /app AND /app/sub
  • NetworkPolicy default behavior — By default, ALL traffic is allowed. Once you apply ANY NetworkPolicy that selects a pod, all non-matching traffic to that pod is DENIED. This catches people off guard
  • NetworkPolicy is namespace-scoped — A policy in prod doesn't affect dev. To allow cross-namespace traffic, use namespaceSelector in the ingress/egress rules
  • Egress policies block DNS too — If you create an egress policy, you must explicitly allow DNS (port 53 UDP to kube-system) or all name resolution breaks
⚡ Speed Tips

CKA Speed Tip — NetworkPolicy deny-all then allow pattern:
Step 1: Create a deny-all ingress policy for the namespace
Step 2: Create specific allow policies for needed traffic
This is the most common exam pattern. Memorize the deny-all YAML:

🧪 Drill

Timed challenge (target: 8 minutes):

  • 1. Create a deny-all NetworkPolicy for namespace secure
  • 2. Create an allow policy: only pods with label role=frontend can reach role=backend on port 8080
  • 3. Verify: exec into a frontend pod and curl backend-svc:8080 — should work
  • 4. Exec into an unlabeled pod and curl — should be blocked
  • 5. Create an Ingress routing /api to backend-svc:8080 and / to frontend-svc:80

Key insight: NetworkPolicy + Ingress = 20% of CKA networking domain.

│  │                             ▼                                          │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐                           │   │
│  │  │ backend-svc:8080 │  │ frontend-svc:80  │  (ClusterIP Services)     │   │
│  │  │ → backend pods   │  │ → frontend pods  │                           │   │
│  │  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘                           │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  INGRESS RESOURCE (routes — NOT the controller!):                            │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1                                      │   │
│  │ kind: Ingress                                                          │   │
│  │ spec:                                                                   │   │
│  │   rules:                                                                │   │
│  │   - host: easypj.com                                                    │   │
│  │     http:                                                                │   │
│  │       paths:                                                             │   │
│  │       - path: /api                                                       │   │
│  │         pathType: Prefix                                                  │   │
│  │         backend:                                                          │   │
│  │           service:                                                        │   │
│  │             name: backend-svc                                             │   │
│  │             port: {number: 8080}                                          │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CKA Insight: NetworkPolicy requires a CNI that supports it (Calico, Cilium, Weave). Flannel does NOT support NetworkPolicy by default. On the CKA, if you create a NetworkPolicy and it doesn't work, verify: (1) kubectl get networkpolicy — does the policy exist in the right namespace? (2) Does your CNI support NetworkPolicy? (3) Policies are namespace-scoped — a policy in namespace A cannot affect pods in namespace B (except via namespaceSelector).

⚙️ Chapter 20 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Quick recall of Ingress routing & NetworkPolicy rules — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Create a deny-all NetworkPolicy that blocks ALL ingress traffic to pods in namespace secure.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
name: deny-all-ingress
namespace: secure
spec:
podSelector: {}        # ← Empty = ALL pods in namespace
policyTypes:
- Ingress              # ← Only block ingress (not egress)
# No ingress rules → all ingress denied!

# Apply:
kubectl apply -f deny-all.yaml

# Verify — nothing can reach pods in "secure" ns:
kubectl exec -n default test-pod -- curl -s --max-time 3 \
http://web-svc.secure:80
# curl: (28) Connection timed out ← Blocked!
Explanation

podSelector: {} selects ALL pods in the namespace. Listing Ingress in policyTypes without any ingress: rules means zero ingress is allowed — effectively a deny-all. This is the most common CKA NetworkPolicy question. Without this policy, all pods accept traffic from anywhere (Kubernetes is open by default). Once ANY NetworkPolicy selects a pod, that pod switches to "default deny" for the listed policyTypes.

Q2
Allow pods with label role=frontend to access pods with label role=backend on port 8080 in the same namespace. Write the NetworkPolicy.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
name: allow-frontend-to-backend
namespace: production
spec:
podSelector:
matchLabels:
role: backend          # ← Applies to backend pods
policyTypes:
- Ingress
ingress:
- from:
- podSelector:
matchLabels:
  role: frontend     # ← Allow from frontend pods
ports:
- protocol: TCP
port: 8080             # ← Only on port 8080

# Test:
# From frontend pod → backend: ALLOWED
kubectl exec frontend-pod -- curl -s backend-svc:8080 ✓

# From random pod → backend: DENIED
kubectl exec other-pod -- curl -s backend-svc:8080 ✗
Explanation

The podSelector (target) defines WHICH pods the policy applies to (backend). The ingress.from.podSelector (source) defines WHO can send traffic (frontend). The ports restrict to specific ports. On the CKA, pay attention to: (1) which pods the policy selects (target), (2) which pods are allowed (source), (3) the port. A common mistake is confusing target vs source selectors.

Q3
Create an Ingress resource that routes /api to api-svc on port 8080 and / to web-svc on port 80. Use pathType Prefix.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
name: app-ingress
namespace: default
annotations:
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
ingressClassName: nginx      # ← Required since K8s 1.18+
rules:
- http:
paths:
- path: /api
pathType: Prefix       # ← Matches /api, /api/v1, /api/users
backend:
  service:
    name: api-svc
    port:
      number: 8080
- path: /
pathType: Prefix       # ← Matches everything else
backend:
  service:
    name: web-svc
    port:
      number: 80

# Apply and verify:
kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml
kubectl get ingress app-ingress
# NAME          CLASS   HOSTS  ADDRESS        PORTS  AGE
# app-ingress   nginx   *      192.168.1.50   80     10s
Explanation

Ingress provides HTTP/HTTPS routing to Services. Key fields: ingressClassName selects which controller handles it, pathType defines matching (Prefix = prefix match, Exact = exact match, ImplementationSpecific = controller decides). Order matters — more specific paths should come first (/api before /). On the CKA, always include ingressClassName — it's required. An Ingress without a deployed Ingress Controller does nothing.

Q4
How do you verify that an Ingress Controller is installed and running? What happens if you create an Ingress without a controller?
Show Answer
Answer
check for ingress controller pods
# Check for Ingress Controller pods:
kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx
# NAME                                       READY  STATUS   AGE
# ingress-nginx-controller-6b94c75599-abc    1/1    Running  5d

# Check IngressClass:
kubectl get ingressclass
# NAME    CONTROLLER                           PARAMETERS  AGE
# nginx   k8s.io/ingress-nginx                 <none>      5d

# Check if Ingress has an ADDRESS:
kubectl get ingress
# NAME      CLASS   HOSTS  ADDRESS         PORTS  AGE
# my-ing    nginx   *      192.168.1.50    80     1h  ← Controller assigned
# bad-ing   nginx   *      <none>          80     1h  ← No controller!

# Without a controller:
# - Ingress resource is created (kubectl get ingress works)
# - ADDRESS remains <none> forever
# - No traffic routing occurs
# - No errors — it just silently does nothing!
Explanation

An Ingress resource is just a config object — it needs an Ingress Controller (like NGINX) to actually route traffic. On the CKA, the controller is usually pre-installed. Check with kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx and kubectl get ingressclass. If the Ingress shows no ADDRESS, the controller isn't processing it (wrong ingressClassName or no controller). Common CKA trap: creating a valid Ingress but routing doesn't work because the Service name or port is wrong.

Q5
Write a NetworkPolicy that allows pods in namespace web to access pods in namespace db on port 5432. Use namespaceSelector.
Show Answer
Answer
first, label the source namespace
# First, label the source namespace:
kubectl label namespace web purpose=web-tier

# NetworkPolicy in the db namespace:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
name: allow-web-to-db
namespace: db              # ← Applied in TARGET namespace
spec:
podSelector:
matchLabels:
app: postgres          # ← Protect postgres pods
policyTypes:
- Ingress
ingress:
- from:
- namespaceSelector:
matchLabels:
  purpose: web-tier  # ← Allow from "web" namespace
ports:
- protocol: TCP
port: 5432

# Important: namespaceSelector uses NAMESPACE labels
# You must label the namespace first!
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels | grep web
Explanation

Cross-namespace NetworkPolicies use namespaceSelector which matches on namespace labels (not names). You must label the source namespace first (kubectl label ns web purpose=web-tier). The policy goes in the TARGET namespace (where the pods being protected live). On the CKA, forgetting to label the namespace is a very common mistake. A namespaceSelector without a podSelector allows ALL pods from that namespace. Combine both to restrict to specific pods in specific namespaces.

Q6
What is the difference between pathType: Prefix, pathType: Exact, and pathType: ImplementationSpecific in an Ingress?
Show Answer
Answer
pathType Matches Example
Prefix URL prefix (path segment level) /api → matches /api, /api/, /api/v1
Exact Exact URL match (case-sensitive) /api → only /api (NOT /api/)
ImplementationSpecific Depends on IngressClass Controller-specific behavior
prefix matching rules
# Prefix matching rules:
# path: /api
# /api     → MATCH ✓
# /api/    → MATCH ✓
# /api/v1  → MATCH ✓
# /apis    → NO MATCH ✗ (not a segment boundary)

# Exam tip: pathType is REQUIRED since K8s 1.22
# Omitting it causes validation error
Explanation

Prefix matching works on path segments — /api matches /api/v1 but NOT /apis. Exact matches the exact path only. ImplementationSpecific defers to the controller. On the CKA, almost always use Prefix. Know that pathType is mandatory (since v1.22) — omitting it fails validation. A trailing slash matters for Exact but not for Prefix.

Q7
Write a NetworkPolicy that allows egress ONLY to DNS (port 53) and blocks all other outgoing traffic.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
name: allow-dns-only
namespace: restricted
spec:
podSelector:
matchLabels:
app: locked-down
policyTypes:
- Egress                  # ← Control outgoing traffic
egress:
- ports:
- protocol: UDP
port: 53              # ← DNS UDP
- protocol: TCP
port: 53              # ← DNS TCP (for large responses)
# No "to:" selector = allow DNS to ANY destination
# (CoreDNS, external DNS servers, etc.)

# Result:
# ✓ DNS queries work (nslookup succeeds)
# ✗ curl google.com → blocked (port 80/443 not allowed)
# ✗ Any non-DNS traffic → blocked

# Common mistake: forgetting TCP/53
# Some DNS queries use TCP (large responses, zone transfers)
Explanation

Egress NetworkPolicies control outgoing traffic. Blocking all egress except DNS (port 53) is a common CKA scenario. Without the DNS exception, pods can't resolve ANY names (even internal Service names). Always include both UDP/53 and TCP/53. On the CKA, if a question says "block all egress but allow the pod to resolve DNS," this is the answer. Omitting the to: field means DNS is allowed to any destination (needed because CoreDNS pod IPs change).

Q8
An Ingress is created but traffic returns 404. The Service and pods are running. How do you troubleshoot?
Show Answer
Answer
check ingress resource
# Step 1: Check Ingress resource
kubectl describe ingress my-ingress
# Look for:
#   Default backend: <default>
#   Rules:
#     Host  Path  Backend
#     *     /app  app-svc:8080 (10.244.1.5:8080, 10.244.2.8:8080)
#                              ↑ Endpoints listed = good
#                 app-svc:8080 ()  ← Empty = broken!

# Step 2: Verify Service has endpoints
kubectl get endpoints app-svc
# NAME      ENDPOINTS
# app-svc   10.244.1.5:8080,10.244.2.8:8080  ← Good
# app-svc   <none>  ← Labels don't match!

# Step 3: Check Service selector matches pod labels
kubectl get svc app-svc -o yaml | grep -A2 selector
kubectl get pods --show-labels | grep app

# Step 4: Check Service port matches Ingress backend port
kubectl get svc app-svc
# PORT(S): 80/TCP  ← Ingress says 8080, Service is 80!

# Step 5: Check Ingress Controller logs
kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx

# Common causes:
# 1. Service port mismatch (Ingress port ≠ Service port)
# 2. Service selector doesn't match pod labels
# 3. Wrong namespace
# 4. Wrong pathType causing no match
Explanation

The 404 on Ingress troubleshooting flow: (1) kubectl describe ingress to check rules and endpoints, (2) verify Service has endpoints, (3) match Service selector to pod labels, (4) verify port numbers match across Ingress → Service → Pod. On the CKA, the most common issues are: port mismatch (Ingress backend port must match Service port, not container port), wrong Service name, or labels not matching. Always use describe first — it shows the endpoint IPs right in the Ingress output.

Q9
How do you combine podSelector AND namespaceSelector in the same NetworkPolicy rule? What's the difference between putting them in the same item vs separate items?
Show Answer
Answer
same item = and (both must match)
# SAME item = AND (both must match):
ingress:
- from:
- namespaceSelector:        # ← Single rule
matchLabels:
env: production
podSelector:              # ← AND condition
matchLabels:
role: frontend
# Allows: frontend pods IN production namespace

# SEPARATE items = OR (either matches):
ingress:
- from:
- namespaceSelector:        # ← Rule 1
matchLabels:
env: production
- podSelector:              # ← Rule 2 (separate item)
matchLabels:
role: frontend
# Allows: ANY pod from production namespace
#     OR: frontend pods from ANY namespace
# ⚠️ Much more permissive!

# The difference is the YAML array dash "-":
# No dash before podSelector = AND (combined)
# Dash before podSelector = OR (separate rule)

# CKA TRAP: One small dash changes everything!
Explanation

This is the #1 CKA NetworkPolicy trap. A single from: item with both selectors means AND (namespace AND pod labels). Two separate from: items means OR (either namespace OR pod labels). The difference is a single YAML dash (-). The OR version is MUCH more permissive — it allows any pod from the namespace, plus any matching pod from any namespace. On the CKA, read the YAML carefully: are the selectors in the same array item (AND) or different items (OR)?

Q10
How do you add TLS termination to an Ingress? Show the complete steps from creating the TLS secret to the Ingress spec.
Show Answer
Answer
create tls secret from cert files
# Step 1: Create TLS secret from cert files:
kubectl create secret tls my-tls-secret \
--cert=tls.crt \
--key=tls.key \
-n default

# Step 2: Create Ingress with TLS:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
name: secure-ingress
spec:
ingressClassName: nginx
tls:
- hosts:
- myapp.example.com      # ← Must match rules host
secretName: my-tls-secret # ← TLS secret name
rules:
- host: myapp.example.com  # ← Must match tls host
http:
paths:
- path: /
pathType: Prefix
backend:
  service:
    name: web-svc
    port:
      number: 80

# Verify:
kubectl describe ingress secure-ingress
# TLS:
#   my-tls-secret terminates myapp.example.com

# Test:
curl -k https://myapp.example.com
# -k to skip cert verification in testing
Explanation

TLS in Ingress has 3 components: (1) a TLS Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt and tls.key, (2) the spec.tls section listing hosts and the secret name, (3) the rules.host must match the TLS host. On the CKA, use kubectl create secret tls (not generic!) — it validates the cert format. The Ingress Controller handles TLS termination: HTTPS outside, HTTP between controller and backend Service. Common mistake: host in tls doesn't match host in rules.

🟡 Part 5 · Recap · Complete

Services & Networking — What You Now Know

You can now move a packet end to end: from the flat pod network and its CNI, through the Service that gives pods a stable virtual IP, to CoreDNS that resolves names, to the Ingress and NetworkPolicies that route and firewall HTTP into easypj. This is the CKA’s 20% Services & Networking domain.

🔑 🟡 Part 5 — Key Takeaways

  • Network model (Ch 17): every pod gets a routable IP on a flat network; the CNI plugin implements it and kube-proxy programs Service routing (iptables/IPVS).
  • Services (Ch 18): ClusterIP (internal) · NodePort (node:port) · LoadBalancer (cloud LB) · headless (per-pod DNS). A Service selects pods → Endpoints; no ready endpoints = no traffic.
  • DNS (Ch 19): CoreDNS resolves svc.ns.svc.cluster.local; search domains + ndots explain short-name lookups; broken DNS is a top exam failure.
  • Ingress & NetworkPolicy (Ch 20): Ingress = L7 HTTP routing via a controller; NetworkPolicy = default-deny + allow rules to isolate tiers (e.g. only easypj-web → easypj-db).
  • 🎯 Exam: 20% here — expose a Deployment, fix a Service with no endpoints, debug CoreDNS, and write a NetworkPolicy are recurring tasks.
📌 Part 5 Visual Summary — browser → Ingress → Service → pod, with DNS & policy
   🌐 browser ──▶ 🚪 Ingress (L7 host/path) ──▶ 🔀 Service (ClusterIP)
                                                   │ selector → Endpoints
                                                   ▼
                              📦 easypj pod  ◀── 🔎 CoreDNS resolves the name
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   🛡️ NetworkPolicy fences who may talk to whom (default-deny + allow).

In words: Part 5 connected the fleet. A pod gets a flat, routable IP (CNI); a Service gives a stable virtual IP and load-balances across the pods its selector matches (Endpoints); CoreDNS turns Service names into those IPs; and Ingress routes external HTTP in while NetworkPolicies decide which pods may talk.

The takeaway: master the chain browser → Ingress → Service → Endpoints → pod, plus CoreDNS resolution and default-deny NetworkPolicies, and you own the 20% Services & Networking domain — second only to Troubleshooting. Next: Part 6 keeps easypj’s data alive with persistent storage.

🟡 Part 6 · Storage

Don’t Lose the Data

Chapters 21–23 · CKA 10% · "State that survives a pod"

Pods are ephemeral; data must not be. Part 6 covers the volume model and its lifecycle, the PV/PVC binding that decouples storage requests from storage supply, StorageClasses for dynamic provisioning, and how ConfigMaps & Secrets inject configuration and credentials into easypj.

🎯 What you’ll be able to do by the end: attach emptyDir/hostPath volumes; statically and dynamically provision PVs via PVCs and StorageClasses; resize and reclaim volumes; and mount ConfigMaps/Secrets as env vars and files for easypj.

Chapter 21 · Volumes & Persistent Storage

Containers are ephemeral by design — when a container dies, everything inside it vanishes. For our easypj/jobpost Django app, that means uploaded resumes, profile photos, and the entire SQLite database would be wiped on every restart. Volumes solve this problem by providing storage that outlives containers. In this chapter you'll understand why volumes exist, explore the different volume types Kubernetes offers, and master emptyDir and hostPath — the two simplest volume types that form the foundation for everything in Chapters 22 and 23.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 💾 Volumes 📝 CKA EXAM

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why container storage is ephemeral and the real-world problems this causes
  • ✅ The 7 most important volume types in Kubernetes and when to use each
  • ✅ How emptyDir enables sidecar container patterns with shared temp storage
  • ✅ How hostPath maps node directories into pods — and why it's dangerous in production
  • ✅ Volume lifecycle — what survives container restarts vs pod deletions
🎓 CKA Relevance
Storage 10% Workloads & Scheduling 15%
Storage Is 10% of the CKA Exam

CKA storage questions typically ask you to create PVs, PVCs, and mount them into pods. But understanding basic volume types is the prerequisite. Key skills for this chapter:

  • Know the difference between emptyDir (pod-scoped) and hostPath (node-scoped)
  • Understand volume lifecycle: emptyDir survives container restarts but NOT pod deletions
  • Be able to write a pod spec with volumes: and volumeMounts: from scratch
  • Know why hostPath is NOT recommended in production (node affinity, security)

Pod with Volume — Exam Skeleton

Memorize this structure — you'll write it from scratch on the CKA exam.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts:                    # ◀── WHERE to mount
    - name: my-vol
      mountPath: /data               # ◀── path inside container
      readOnly: false                 # ◀── optional
  volumes:                           # ◀── WHAT to mount
  - name: my-vol                     # ◀── must match volumeMounts.name
    emptyDir: {}                     # ◀── volume type
    # OR: hostPath: { path: /host/path, type: Directory }
    # OR: persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: my-pvc }
    # OR: configMap: { name: my-cm }
    # OR: secret: { secretName: my-secret }

Find Volume Fields Fast

kubectl explain pod.spec.volumes              # all volume types
kubectl explain pod.spec.volumes.emptyDir      # emptyDir options
kubectl explain pod.spec.volumes.hostPath      # hostPath options
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.volumeMounts  # mount options
  • pod.spec.volumes[].emptyDir.medium — "" (disk) or "Memory" (tmpfs)
  • pod.spec.volumes[].emptyDir.sizeLimit — max size before eviction
  • pod.spec.volumes[].hostPath.path — required, path on node
  • pod.spec.volumes[].hostPath.type — validation type (Directory, File, etc.)
  • pod.spec.containers[].volumeMounts[].subPath — mount single file without hiding dir
7 Key Volume Types
2 CKA Must-Know (emptyDir, hostPath)
Pod emptyDir Lifecycle
⚠️ hostPath — Security Risk

🗺️ Volume Types — When to Use What

Pod Storage Need
📂 emptyDir Temp scratch space, sidecar sharing
🖥️ hostPath Node logs, etcd certs, dev/testing
💾 PVC Databases, uploads, persistent data
⚙️ configMap Config files mounted into containers
🔐 secret TLS certs, passwords as files

21.1 The Problem: Container Storage is Ephemeral

Every container starts with a fresh, writable filesystem layer provided by its image. When the container stops or crashes, that layer is destroyed. Any files created, modified, or downloaded during runtime are gone forever. This is by design — containers are disposable — but it creates a massive problem for stateful applications.

The Data Loss Problem — Without Volumes
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WITHOUT VOLUMES — DATA IS LOST ON EVERY POD RESTART                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Timeline:  t=0              t=5min             t=5min+1sec              │
  │             Pod starts       Pod crashes         New pod starts          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌────────────────┐    ┌────────────────┐    ┌────────────────┐         │
  │  │ 📦 easypj Pod  │    │ 📦 easypj Pod  │    │ 📦 easypj Pod  │         │
  │  │                │    │                │    │   (new)         │         │
  │  │ 📄 db.sqlite3  │    │ 📄 db.sqlite3  │    │                │         │
  │  │ 📄 resume.pdf  │    │ 📄 resume.pdf  │    │ 📄 (empty!)    │  💀     │
  │  │ 📄 photo.jpg   │    │ 📄 photo.jpg   │    │                │         │
  │  │                │    │    💥 CRASH!    │    │ ALL DATA LOST! │         │
  │  └────────────────┘    └────────────────┘    └────────────────┘         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  50 job posts created    Everything inside     New container starts      │
  │  3 resumes uploaded      the container dies    with BLANK filesystem     │
  │  User profiles saved     with the container    Users see: "No jobs"     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WITH VOLUMES — DATA SURVIVES POD RESTARTS                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌────────────────┐    ┌────────────────┐    ┌────────────────┐         │
  │  │ 📦 easypj Pod  │    │ 📦 easypj Pod  │    │ 📦 easypj Pod  │         │
  │  │                │    │                │    │   (new)         │         │
  │  │ 📄 db.sqlite3 ─┼─┐  │    💥 CRASH!   │    │ 📄 db.sqlite3 ─┼─┐      │
  │  │ 📄 resume.pdf ─┼─┤  │                │    │ 📄 resume.pdf ─┼─┤      │
  │  └────────────────┘ │  └────────────────┘    └────────────────┘ │      │
  │                     │                                            │      │
  │                     │    ┌──────────────────┐                    │      │
  │                     └───▶│    💾 VOLUME      │◀───────────────────┘      │
  │                          │  db.sqlite3  ✅  │                           │
  │                          │  resume.pdf  ✅  │  Data survives!           │
  │                          │  photo.jpg   ✅  │  New pod reads same files │
  │                          └──────────────────┘                           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ This Happens More Often Than You Think

Pods restart frequently in Kubernetes: OOMKilled (out of memory), node failures, rolling updates, scaling down. If your application stores ANY data inside the container filesystem, you will lose it. This includes:

  • Database files (SQLite, PostgreSQL data dir)
  • User uploads (resumes, images, documents)
  • Application logs written to local files
  • Cache files and session data
📦
Container Writable Layer

Each container gets a thin writable layer on top of its read-only image layers. Writes go here. When the container stops, this layer is deleted. It's fast but temporary — perfect for stateless apps, fatal for stateful ones.

💾
Kubernetes Volumes

A Volume is storage that lives outside the container but is mounted inside it at a specific path. The container reads and writes normally, but the data is stored externally. When the container restarts, the Volume is re-mounted with all data intact.

🔑 Key Concept: volumes vs volumeMounts

Every pod spec has two related fields. spec.volumes[] defines the storage (what type, where it comes from). spec.containers[].volumeMounts[] mounts that storage into a specific path inside the container. You always need both — a volume definition AND a mount point.

volumes-vs-volumemounts.yaml 
# The two parts of Kubernetes volume configuration
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: django
    image: easypj:latest
    volumeMounts:                    # ◀── WHERE to mount (inside container)
    - name: app-data                 #     references volumes[] by name
      mountPath: /app/data           #     path inside the container
    - name: static-files
      mountPath: /app/static
      readOnly: true                 #     container can only READ
  volumes:                           # ◀── WHAT to mount (storage source)
  - name: app-data                   #     name must match volumeMounts
    emptyDir: {}                     #     type: temporary pod-scoped storage
  - name: static-files
    configMap:                       #     type: files from a ConfigMap
      name: easypj-static-config
📖 Volume Lifecycle Rule

A volume's lifetime depends on its type. An emptyDir lives as long as the pod — it survives container crashes but is deleted when the pod is removed. A PersistentVolume lives as long as the cluster — it survives pod deletions entirely. Understanding this lifecycle is critical for choosing the right volume type.

21.2 Volume Types Overview

Kubernetes supports over 20 volume types, but for the CKA exam and daily work, you need to know 7 key types. Each serves a different purpose, has a different lifecycle, and is suited to specific use cases.

Volume Type Persists? Scope Use Case CKA Exam?
emptyDir ❌ Pod lifetime only Pod Temp files, cache, sidecar sharing ✅ Yes
hostPath ⚠️ Node lifetime Node Dev/testing, node logs access ✅ Yes
persistentVolumeClaim ✅ Cluster lifetime Cluster Databases, user uploads, any persistent data ✅ Heavily tested
configMap N/A (config data) Cluster Config files mounted as volumes ✅ Yes
secret N/A (sensitive data) Cluster TLS certs, passwords as files ✅ Yes
nfs ✅ Network storage Network Shared storage across pods/nodes ⚠️ Sometimes
csi ✅ Provider-managed Provider Cloud storage (AWS EBS, GCE PD, Azure Disk) ⚠️ Conceptual
Volume Types by Lifecycle and Scope
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  VOLUME LIFECYCLE SPECTRUM                                               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Shortest ◀──────────────────────────────────────────▶ Longest          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  emptyDir    │   │  hostPath   │   │  persistentVolumeClaim (PVC) │  │
  │  │             │   │             │   │                              │  │
  │  │  Lives with  │   │  Lives on   │   │  Lives in cluster           │  │
  │  │  the POD     │   │  the NODE   │   │  Independent of pods        │  │
  │  │             │   │             │   │                              │  │
  │  │  Pod dies →  │   │  Node dies →│   │  Pod dies → data SAFE ✅   │  │
  │  │  data GONE 💀│   │  data GONE 💀│   │  Node dies → data SAFE ✅  │  │
  │  └─────────────┘   └─────────────┘   └──────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  configMap / secret          │  nfs / csi                       │    │
  │  │                              │                                   │    │
  │  │  NOT storage — these inject  │  Network/cloud storage            │    │
  │  │  configuration and secrets   │  Fully independent of cluster     │    │
  │  │  as files into containers    │  Survives cluster deletion        │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🎯
CKA Exam Focus

The exam heavily tests persistentVolumeClaim (creating PVs, PVCs, binding). You'll also see emptyDir in multi-container pod questions and hostPath for etcd backup paths. configMap and secret volumes appear in configuration questions.

🏗️
easypj Storage Plan

Our Django app needs: PVC for PostgreSQL data (10Gi), PVC for user uploads (resumes, photos), ConfigMap volume for Django settings, Secret volume for database credentials, emptyDir for nginx ↔ Django static file sharing.

💡 Quick Decision Guide

Need temp scratch space shared between containers? → emptyDir. Need data to survive pod deletion? → PVC. Need to inject config files? → configMap. Need to inject secrets as files? → secret. Need shared storage across multiple nodes? → nfs or CSI with ReadWriteMany.

21.3 emptyDir — Temporary Shared Storage

An emptyDir volume is the simplest volume type. It's created as an empty directory when a pod starts and is deleted when the pod is removed. It's perfect for sharing data between containers in the same pod — the classic sidecar pattern.

✅
When to Use emptyDir

Sidecar containers sharing data (nginx + Django), temporary scratch space for computation, cache that can be regenerated, checkpoint data during multi-step processing.

❌
When NOT to Use emptyDir

Database storage, user uploads, anything that must survive a pod restart. If the data matters, use a PersistentVolumeClaim instead.

emptyDir — Sidecar Pattern: Django + Nginx Sharing Static Files
  ┌──────────────────────── Pod: easypj-web ─────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                    │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────┐         │
  │  │  Container 1:      │         │  Container 2:        │         │
  │  │  django            │         │  nginx               │         │
  │  │                    │         │                      │         │
  │  │  1. collectstatic  │         │  3. Serves static    │         │
  │  │     writes CSS/JS  │         │     files from       │         │
  │  │     to /static/    │         │     /usr/share/nginx │         │
  │  │                    │         │                      │         │
  │  │  volumeMount:      │         │  volumeMount:        │         │
  │  │    /app/static     │         │    /usr/share/nginx  │         │
  │  └─────────┬──────────┘         └──────────┬───────────┘         │
  │            │                               │                      │
  │            │   2. SHARED emptyDir volume    │                      │
  │            └──────────┐  ┌─────────────────┘                      │
  │                       ▼  ▼                                         │
  │              ┌──────────────────┐                                  │
  │              │  emptyDir: {}    │                                  │
  │              │  /static-files   │                                  │
  │              │                  │                                  │
  │              │  style.css  ✅   │                                  │
  │              │  app.js     ✅   │                                  │
  │              │  logo.png   ✅   │                                  │
  │              └──────────────────┘                                  │
  │                                                                    │
  │  Both containers see the SAME files — writes by Django are        │
  │  immediately visible to Nginx. No network calls needed!           │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
easypj-emptydir-sidecar.yaml 
# easypj Django + Nginx sidecar sharing static files via emptyDir
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  labels:
    app: easypj
    component: web
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: collect-static
    image: easypj:latest
    command: ["python", "manage.py", "collectstatic", "--noinput"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: static-files              # ◀── writes static files here
      mountPath: /app/staticfiles
  containers:
  - name: django
    image: easypj:latest
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
    command: ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: static-files              # ◀── Django can still access them
      mountPath: /app/staticfiles
    - name: tmp-scratch               # ◀── scratch space for processing
      mountPath: /tmp/processing
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
    volumeMounts:
    - name: static-files              # ◀── Nginx serves the same files
      mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html/static
      readOnly: true                  #     Nginx only READS, never writes
  volumes:
  - name: static-files               # ◀── Shared between all containers
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: tmp-scratch                 # ◀── Only used by Django
    emptyDir:
      sizeLimit: 100Mi               #     Optional: limit disk usage
📖 emptyDir Medium Options

By default, emptyDir uses the node's disk. You can also use RAM-backed storage with emptyDir: { medium: Memory }. This is faster but counts against the container's memory limit. Useful for high-speed temp files, but remember: RAM is more expensive than disk and the data is still lost when the pod dies.

emptydir-memory-backed.yaml 
# RAM-backed emptyDir — fast but size-limited
volumes:
- name: cache-volume
  emptyDir:
    medium: Memory          # ◀── Uses RAM instead of disk (tmpfs)
    sizeLimit: 256Mi        #     Pod evicted if exceeds this limit

🔬 emptyDir Lifecycle — What Survives What?

🔄 Container restart
Data SURVIVES ✅ — emptyDir lives at the pod level, not the container level. If Django crashes and kubelet restarts it, the static files are still there.
💀 Pod deletion
Data LOST ❌ — When the pod is deleted (scaling down, rescheduling, node failure), the emptyDir is permanently deleted. Cannot be recovered.
🔄 Rolling update
Data LOST ❌ — A rolling update creates a NEW pod. The old pod (and its emptyDir) is deleted. The new pod gets a fresh empty emptyDir.
📍 Node failure
Data LOST ❌ — Pod is rescheduled to a different node. The emptyDir was on the old node's disk. New pod starts fresh.

21.4 hostPath — Node-Level Storage

A hostPath volume mounts a file or directory from the node's filesystem directly into the pod. Unlike emptyDir, the data exists on the node's disk and persists even after the pod is deleted — but only on that specific node.

⚠️ hostPath Is Dangerous in Production

hostPath gives the container direct access to the node's filesystem. This is a security risk (containers can read/write sensitive host files) and a portability problem (pod must always run on the same node). Use it only for development, testing, or accessing node-level system files like logs.

hostPath — Pod Reads Node's Log Directory
  ┌──────── Node: worker-1 ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                    │
  │  Node Filesystem:                                                  │
  │  /var/log/                                                         │
  │  ├── syslog                                                        │
  │  ├── kern.log                                                      │
  │  ├── containers/                                                   │
  │  │   ├── easypj-abc.log                                            │
  │  │   └── postgres-0.log                                            │
  │  └── pods/                                                         │
  │                                                                    │
  │  ┌────────────────────── Pod: log-collector ──────────────────┐   │
  │  │                                                              │   │
  │  │  Container: fluentd                                         │   │
  │  │  mountPath: /var/log/host  ◀──── hostPath: /var/log/        │   │
  │  │                                                              │   │
  │  │  $ ls /var/log/host/                                        │   │
  │  │  syslog  kern.log  containers/  pods/                       │   │
  │  │                                                              │   │
  │  │  ✅ Can read all node logs!                                 │   │
  │  │  ⚠️ Only works on THIS node                                │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                    │
  │  If pod moves to worker-2 → different /var/log/ directory!        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
hostpath-log-collector.yaml 
# Log collector pod using hostPath to access node logs
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: log-collector
spec:
  containers:
  - name: fluentd
    image: fluent/fluentd:latest
    volumeMounts:
    - name: node-logs
      mountPath: /var/log/host        # ◀── appears here inside container
      readOnly: true                  #     ALWAYS use readOnly for safety
    - name: container-logs
      mountPath: /var/lib/docker/containers
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: node-logs
    hostPath:
      path: /var/log                  # ◀── actual path on the NODE
      type: Directory                 #     must exist, must be a directory
  - name: container-logs
    hostPath:
      path: /var/lib/docker/containers
      type: DirectoryOrCreate        #     creates if doesn't exist
hostPath Type Behavior Fails If...
"" (empty) No checks before mounting Never (unsafe)
DirectoryOrCreate Creates directory if missing Never (auto-creates)
Directory Must exist as a directory Path doesn't exist or isn't a dir
FileOrCreate Creates file if missing Never (auto-creates)
File Must exist as a file Path doesn't exist or isn't a file
Socket Must exist as a UNIX socket Not a socket file
✅
Legitimate hostPath Uses

Accessing node logs (/var/log), Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock), etcd data dir for backups, /etc/kubernetes for kubelet config. Always with readOnly: true when possible.

⛔
Never Use hostPath For

Application databases, user uploads, any data that needs to move between nodes. If the pod gets rescheduled to a different node, it will see a different (or empty) directory. Use PVC instead.

CKA Exam: etcd backup using hostPath 
# CKA Exam Classic: etcd backup pod needs hostPath for certificates
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: etcd-backup
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  containers:
  - name: etcd-backup
    image: registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.5.12-0
    command:
    - /bin/sh
    - -c
    - |
      etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db \
        --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
        --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
        --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
        --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
    volumeMounts:
    - name: etcd-certs                # ◀── CKA: etcd certs on control plane
      mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd
      readOnly: true
    - name: backup-dir                # ◀── where snapshot is saved
      mountPath: /backup
  volumes:
  - name: etcd-certs
    hostPath:
      path: /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd  # ◀── actual certs on the node
      type: Directory
  - name: backup-dir
    hostPath:
      path: /opt/etcd-backup          # ◀── backup saved on node filesystem
      type: DirectoryOrCreate
  hostNetwork: true
  nodeName: controlplane              # ◀── must run on control plane node
🏋️ CKA Practice Scenario: Volume Troubleshooting

Scenario: A developer reports that their easypj pod keeps losing uploaded resumes every time it restarts. They've configured the pod as shown:

broken-pod.yaml (spot the problem) 
# What's wrong with this pod?
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: django
    image: easypj:latest
    volumeMounts:
    - name: uploads
      mountPath: /app/media/uploads
  volumes:
  - name: uploads
    emptyDir: {}        # ◀── 🤔 Is this the right volume type?

Diagnosis: emptyDir data is deleted when the pod is deleted. Every restart creates a new, empty directory. For data that must persist, they need a PersistentVolumeClaim.

Fix: Replace emptyDir: {} with a PVC reference:

fixed-pod.yaml 
# Fixed: Use PVC instead of emptyDir for persistent data
  volumes:
  - name: uploads
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: easypj-uploads-pvc   # ◀── data survives pod restarts!

🔧 Volume Troubleshooting Quick Reference

Symptom Likely Cause Fix
Pod won't start — MountVolume.SetUp failed hostPath directory doesn't exist on node Use type: DirectoryOrCreate or pre-create the directory
Data disappears after pod restart Using emptyDir for persistent data Switch to persistentVolumeClaim
Container can't write to volume readOnly: true set on volumeMount Remove readOnly or set to false
Permission denied inside container Container runs as non-root but volume owned by root Add fsGroup in securityContext to change group ownership
emptyDir exceeds size — pod evicted sizeLimit exceeded (or node disk pressure) Increase sizeLimit or clean up data inside the volume
Volume shows different data after reschedule hostPath is node-specific — different node = different data Use PVC with network storage (NFS, cloud) for multi-node access

⌨️ Chapter 21 — Essential kubectl Commands

🔍 Inspect pod volumes
kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A10 "Volumes:"
📂 List files in mounted volume
kubectl exec <pod> -- ls -la /path/to/mount
💾 Check disk usage in volume
kubectl exec <pod> -- df -h /path/to/mount
📋 View pod events (mount errors)
kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A5 "Events:"
🔄 Watch pod status during restart
kubectl get pod <name> -w
Under the Hood — How Volume Mounts Are Actually Implemented: Bind Mounts, tmpfs, and the Container Filesystem Stack
🗺️ The Container Filesystem Stack — Where Volumes Fit

When a container mounts a volume, the kubelet instructs the container runtime to create an additional mount point that overlays the container's root filesystem. Understanding where volumes sit in the filesystem stack helps you debug mount failures and data persistence issues.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CONTAINER FILESYSTEM STACK — Layers from Top to Bottom                      │
│                                                                              │
│  Container's view of /:                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  /app/                                                               │    │
│  │  ├── media/          ← VOLUME MOUNT (emptyDir/hostPath/PVC)          │    │
│  │  │   └── uploads/    ← Survives container restart                   │    │
│  │  ├── manage.py       ← From image layer 3 (COPY . .)               │    │
│  │  ├── requirements/   ← From image layer 2 (pip install)            │    │
│  │  └── usr/bin/python  ← From image layer 1 (FROM python:3.12)       │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
│  UNDERLYING IMPLEMENTATION (overlay2 + volume mounts):                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐  ← VOLUME MOUNT (separate mount)      │    │
│  │  │ /var/lib/kubelet/pods/   │    This sits ON TOP of the image       │    │
│  │  │   <uid>/volumes/kuber-   │    layers. Everything written here     │    │
│  │  │   netes.io~empty-dir/    │    stays on the node until pod is      │    │
│  │  │   media/                 │    deleted.                             │    │
│  │  └──────────────────────────┘                                         │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐  ← WRITABLE LAYER (ephemeral)         │    │
│  │  │ /var/lib/containerd/...  │    All writes NOT in volume mounts     │    │
│  │  │   <container-id>/upper   │    go here. DELETED on container stop. │    │
│  │  └──────────────────────────┘                                         │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐  ← IMAGE LAYERS (read-only)           │    │
│  │  │ easypj code (sha:jkl012) │    Never modified. Shared across      │    │
│  │  │ pip packages (sha:ghi789)│    all containers using same layers.  │    │
│  │  │ python:3.12 (sha:def456) │                                        │    │
│  │  └──────────────────────────┘                                         │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  VOLUME TYPE IMPLEMENTATIONS:                                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  emptyDir:                                                           │    │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │    │
│  │  │ • Created as a DIRECTORY on the node's filesystem           │     │    │
│  │  │ • Default: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<uid>/volumes/...         │     │    │
│  │  │ • medium: "" → node's default disk (ext4/xfs)               │     │    │
│  │  │ • medium: "Memory" → tmpfs (RAM-backed, faster, ephemeral) │     │    │
│  │  │ • LIFETIME: Tied to POD. Survives container restarts.       │     │    │
│  │  │   DELETED when pod is deleted from the node.                │     │    │
│  │  │ • Use case: scratch space, cache, inter-container sharing   │     │    │
│  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  hostPath:                                                           │    │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │    │
│  │  │ • Direct bind-mount from NODE filesystem → container        │     │    │
│  │  │ • /var/log on node → /host-logs in container                │     │    │
│  │  │ • LIFETIME: Survives pod deletion (data stays on node)      │     │    │
│  │  │ • DANGER: Pod scheduled to different node → DIFFERENT data  │     │    │
│  │  │ • Use case: accessing node logs, Docker socket, /sys        │     │    │
│  │  │ • CKA: hostPath is the simplest PV type for testing         │     │    │
│  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │    │
│  │                                                                      │    │
│  │  PVC (PersistentVolumeClaim):                                        │    │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │    │
│  │  │ • kubelet ATTACHES the PV's storage to the node             │     │    │
│  │  │ • For cloud: AWS EBS → AttachVolume → mount to container    │     │    │
│  │  │ • For NFS: mount -t nfs <server>:<path> <mountpoint>        │     │    │
│  │  │ • LIFETIME: Survives pod deletion (PV must be manually       │     │    │
│  │  │   deleted or reclaimed per reclaimPolicy)                   │     │    │
│  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CKA Insight: On the CKA, emptyDir is your go-to for sharing data between containers in a pod. hostPath is for accessing node filesystem directly (but avoid in production except for specific use cases like log collectors). PVC is for persistent data across pod restarts. Remember: emptyDir lasts as long as the POD exists; hostPath lasts as long as the NODE exists; PVC lasts as long as the PV exists.

🔑 Key Takeaways

Bulleted key takeaways go here.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • ❌ emptyDir persists across pod restarts — it persists across container restarts, NOT pod deletions
  • ✅ emptyDir survives container crashes but dies with the pod
  • ❌ hostPath works the same on any node — it reads that specific node's filesystem. Different node = different data
  • ✅ hostPath is node-specific — pod rescheduling changes the data
  • volumes[] and volumeMounts[] names must match exactly — typo = mount failure
  • emptyDir: {medium: Memory} counts against the container's memory limit, not disk
  • Forgetting readOnly: true on hostPath mounts is a security risk
  • emptyDir is NOT persistent — It survives container restarts but is deleted when the pod is removed. Never use it for database files. The exam may present a scenario where data disappears after pod rescheduling — emptyDir is the culprit
  • hostPath pins pods to specific nodes — Data only exists on that one node. If the pod reschedules to another node, the data is gone. CKA traps: "Why can't my pod find its data after rescheduling?"
  • volumeMounts vs volumes — volumes: declares the volume at pod level. volumeMounts: mounts it into a specific container. Forgetting either causes the pod to fail or the mount to not appear
  • subPath prevents directory overwrite — Without subPath, mounting a volume at /etc/nginx replaces ALL existing files in that directory. With subPath: nginx.conf, only that one file is mounted
  • readOnly: true — Add this to volumeMounts for security when the container should only read data. The exam may ask you to mount a config volume as read-only
⚡ Speed Tips

CKA Speed Tip — Volume type decision tree:
Need temp scratch space between containers? → emptyDir
Need to access node files (logs, sockets)? → hostPath (use sparingly)
Need data to survive pod deletion? → PV/PVC (Chapter 22)
Need to inject config files? → ConfigMap volume (Chapter 23)
Need to inject credentials? → Secret volume (Chapter 23)

⚙️ Chapter 21 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Quick recall of volume types & mount behavior — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Create a pod with two containers that share an emptyDir volume. Container writer writes to /data/output.log and container reader reads from the same path.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: shared-volume-pod
spec:
volumes:                         # ← Pod-level: DECLARE the volume
- name: shared-data
emptyDir: {}                   # ← Ephemeral, deleted with pod

containers:
- name: writer
image: busybox
command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
args: ["while true; do echo $(date) >> /data/output.log; sleep 5; done"]
volumeMounts:                  # ← Container-level: MOUNT the volume
- name: shared-data
  mountPath: /data

- name: reader
image: busybox
command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
args: ["tail -f /data/output.log"]
volumeMounts:
- name: shared-data
  mountPath: /data             # ← Same volume, same path

# Verify:
kubectl exec shared-volume-pod -c reader -- cat /data/output.log
Explanation

emptyDir creates an empty directory on the node when a pod is assigned to it. Both containers see the same files because they mount the same volume. Key facts: (1) volumes: is pod-level, volumeMounts: is container-level, (2) the name: in volumeMount must match the volume name, (3) emptyDir data survives container restarts but NOT pod deletion. On the CKA, sidecar patterns (log collector + app) almost always use emptyDir.

Q2
What happens to data in an emptyDir volume when: (a) the container crashes, (b) the pod is deleted, (c) the pod is rescheduled to another node?
Show Answer
Answer
Scenario Data Preserved? Why?
Container crashes/restarts ✅ YES emptyDir is tied to the pod, not the container
Pod is deleted ❌ NO emptyDir lifecycle = pod lifecycle
Pod rescheduled to new node ❌ NO emptyDir is node-local storage
common cka trap scenario
# Common CKA trap scenario:
# "My database pod restarted and data is still there" → emptyDir, container restart
# "My database pod was rescheduled and data is GONE" → emptyDir, pod recreation
# Solution: Use PV/PVC for data that must survive pod deletion
Explanation

emptyDir is ephemeral — its lifetime matches the pod's. Container restarts don't affect it because the pod still exists on the same node. But pod deletion (or rescheduling by a Deployment) destroys the emptyDir. On the CKA, if you see a scenario where "data disappears after pod restart" — check if it's an emptyDir and the pod was DELETED (not just the container restarted). Use PersistentVolumes for durable storage.

Q3
Create a pod that mounts the host's /var/log directory as read-only. What are the security concerns?
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: log-reader
spec:
volumes:
- name: host-logs
hostPath:
  path: /var/log
  type: Directory          # ← Must already exist
containers:
- name: reader
image: busybox
command: ["sleep", "3600"]
volumeMounts:
- name: host-logs
  mountPath: /host-logs
  readOnly: true           # ← Security: read-only access

# hostPath type options:
# ""                    - no checks (default)
# DirectoryOrCreate     - creates dir if missing
# Directory             - must exist, must be dir
# FileOrCreate          - creates file if missing
# File                  - must exist, must be file
# Socket                - must be Unix socket
# CharDevice            - must be char device
# BlockDevice           - must be block device

# Security concerns:
# 1. Access to host filesystem = container escape risk
# 2. Pod pinned to specific node (data not portable)
# 3. PodSecurityAdmission may block hostPath mounts
# 4. ALWAYS use readOnly: true when possible
Explanation

hostPath mounts a file or directory from the host node's filesystem. It's useful for DaemonSets that need node-level access (like log collectors or monitoring agents). On the CKA: (1) always specify the type field for validation, (2) use readOnly: true unless writing is required, (3) remember that hostPath ties pods to specific nodes. The CKA may ask you to mount logs for troubleshooting — know this pattern.

Q4
What is subPath in a volume mount and when do you use it? Show an example.
Show Answer
Answer
problem: mounting a configmap at /etc/nginx…
# Problem: mounting a ConfigMap at /etc/nginx overwrites ALL files
# Solution: subPath mounts only ONE file

# Without subPath (BAD — replaces entire /etc/nginx):
volumeMounts:
- name: config-vol
mountPath: /etc/nginx          # ← Entire dir replaced!

# With subPath (GOOD — only replaces nginx.conf):
volumeMounts:
- name: config-vol
mountPath: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
subPath: nginx.conf            # ← Only this file!

# Full example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: nginx-custom
spec:
volumes:
- name: config
configMap:
  name: nginx-config         # ← ConfigMap with key "nginx.conf"
containers:
- name: nginx
image: nginx
volumeMounts:
- name: config
  mountPath: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf  # ← Target file
  subPath: nginx.conf               # ← Key from ConfigMap

# ⚠️ subPath limitation: NO auto-update!
# ConfigMap volume without subPath → updates automatically
# ConfigMap with subPath → does NOT auto-update
Explanation

subPath mounts a single file from a volume instead of the entire volume. Without it, mounting at a directory path replaces everything in that directory. On the CKA, use subPath when mounting a ConfigMap key as a specific file without overwriting other files in the same directory. Critical caveat: subPath prevents auto-update — if you change the ConfigMap, the mounted file won't change until the pod restarts. This is a known CKA trick question.

Q5
How do you inspect volumes and volume mounts of an existing pod using kubectl?
Show Answer
Answer
describe (human-readable)
# Method 1: describe (human-readable)
kubectl describe pod my-pod
# Look for:
#   Volumes:
#     data-vol:
#       Type: PersistentVolumeClaim
#       ClaimName: my-pvc
#   Containers:
#     app:
#       Mounts:
#         /data from data-vol (rw)

# Method 2: JSONPath (machine-parseable)
# List all volumes:
kubectl get pod my-pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumes[*].name}'
# data-vol config-vol

# List volume mounts for first container:
kubectl get pod my-pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].volumeMounts}'

# Pretty-print volumes:
kubectl get pod my-pod -o jsonpath='{range .spec.volumes[*]}{.name}{"\t"}{end}'

# Method 3: From inside the container
kubectl exec my-pod -- mount | grep /data
# /dev/sda1 on /data type ext4 (rw,relatime)

kubectl exec my-pod -- df -h /data
# Filesystem  Size  Used  Avail  Use%  Mounted on
# /dev/sda1   5.0G  42M   4.9G   1%    /data
Explanation

Three approaches for volume inspection: describe for quick overview, jsonpath for scripting, and exec + mount/df for verifying from inside the pod. On the CKA, kubectl describe pod is fastest — it shows volumes, mounts, and whether they're read-only. The Mounts section in describe output shows (rw) or (ro) — useful for debugging permission issues.

Q6
How do you use emptyDir with medium: Memory? When would you use it?
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: tmpfs-pod
spec:
volumes:
- name: cache
emptyDir:
  medium: Memory          # ← Backed by tmpfs (RAM)
  sizeLimit: 256Mi        # ← Optional: cap memory usage
containers:
- name: app
image: nginx
volumeMounts:
- name: cache
  mountPath: /cache

# Verify it's tmpfs:
kubectl exec tmpfs-pod -- mount | grep cache
# tmpfs on /cache type tmpfs (rw,relatime,size=262144k)

kubectl exec tmpfs-pod -- df -h /cache
# Filesystem  Size  Used  Avail  Use%  Mounted on
# tmpfs       256M  0     256M   0%    /cache

# Use cases:
# - High-speed temporary cache
# - Sensitive data that should never touch disk
# - Performance-critical scratch space
# ⚠️ Counts against container's memory limit!
Explanation

emptyDir with medium: Memory creates a tmpfs (RAM-backed) volume. It's extremely fast but: (1) data is lost on pod deletion (like normal emptyDir), (2) uses node memory (counts against cgroup limits), (3) if no sizeLimit is set, can consume all memory and cause OOM. On the CKA, this is tested in scenarios like "store temporary encryption keys in memory only" or "high-performance cache." Always set sizeLimit to prevent memory exhaustion.

Q7
A pod spec has volumeMounts but is missing the volumes section. What happens?
Show Answer
Answer
broken spec (volumes missing)
# Broken spec (volumes missing):
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: broken-pod
spec:
containers:
- name: app
image: nginx
volumeMounts:
- name: data-vol            # ← References "data-vol"
  mountPath: /data
# volumes: ← MISSING!

# Error when applying:
kubectl apply -f broken.yaml
# Error: pod "broken-pod" spec.containers[0].volumeMounts[0].name:
# Not found: "data-vol"
# Pod won't be created!

# Fix — add the volumes section:
spec:
volumes:                       # ← Pod level
- name: data-vol               # ← Must match volumeMount name
emptyDir: {}
containers:
- name: app
image: nginx
volumeMounts:
- name: data-vol             # ← References volumes[].name
  mountPath: /data
Explanation

The pod will fail validation — the API server rejects it because the volumeMount references a volume name that doesn't exist. This is a syntax error, not a runtime error. On the CKA, always verify both parts: (1) spec.volumes[] at the pod level to DECLARE the volume, (2) spec.containers[].volumeMounts[] at the container level to MOUNT it. The name field links the two. Forgetting either side is one of the most common YAML mistakes.

Q8
List ALL volume types available in Kubernetes with their primary use cases.
Show Answer
Answer
Volume Type Use Case CKA Relevance
emptyDir Temp scratch space, sidecar sharing ⭐⭐⭐
hostPath Node files, DaemonSet logs ⭐⭐⭐
persistentVolumeClaim Durable storage via PVC ⭐⭐⭐
configMap Config files as volumes ⭐⭐⭐
secret Sensitive data as files ⭐⭐⭐
downwardAPI Pod metadata as files ⭐⭐
projected Combine multiple sources ⭐⭐
nfs, csi, iscsi Network/cloud storage ⭐
Explanation

On the CKA, focus on the 5 most common: emptyDir, hostPath, persistentVolumeClaim, configMap, and secret. Know when to use each. projected volumes combine multiple sources (secrets + configmaps + downwardAPI) into a single mount. CSI volume types are the modern standard for cloud storage but are rarely tested deeply on the CKA — you just need to know they exist.

Q9
How do you mount a single key from a ConfigMap as a specific file without using subPath?
Show Answer
Answer
method: use the configmap volume's items field
# Method: Use the ConfigMap volume's items field
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: selective-mount
spec:
volumes:
- name: config-vol
configMap:
  name: app-settings
  items:                      # ← Select specific keys
  - key: database.properties  # ← ConfigMap key
    path: db.conf             # ← Filename in the mount
  - key: app.properties
    path: app.conf
containers:
- name: app
image: nginx
volumeMounts:
- name: config-vol
  mountPath: /etc/config

# Result:
# /etc/config/db.conf   ← content of database.properties
# /etc/config/app.conf  ← content of app.properties
# Other ConfigMap keys are NOT mounted

# vs subPath approach:
# items → selective keys, still replaces dir, auto-updates ✓
# subPath → single file, preserves other files, no auto-update ✗
Explanation

The items field in a ConfigMap volume selects specific keys and maps them to custom filenames. Unlike subPath, this approach still auto-updates when the ConfigMap changes. The tradeoff: items replaces the entire mountPath directory (only selected keys appear). On the CKA, items is preferred when you need selective keys with auto-update. Use subPath only when you need to preserve existing files in the directory.

Q10
Create a pod that uses a downwardAPI volume to expose its own labels and annotations as files.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: downward-pod
labels:
app: web
version: v2
annotations:
owner: team-alpha
spec:
volumes:
- name: pod-info
downwardAPI:
  items:
  - path: "labels"             # ← File name
    fieldRef:
      fieldPath: metadata.labels
  - path: "annotations"
    fieldRef:
      fieldPath: metadata.annotations
  - path: "name"
    fieldRef:
      fieldPath: metadata.name
  - path: "namespace"
    fieldRef:
      fieldPath: metadata.namespace
containers:
- name: app
image: busybox
command: ["sleep", "3600"]
volumeMounts:
- name: pod-info
  mountPath: /etc/podinfo

# Verify:
kubectl exec downward-pod -- cat /etc/podinfo/labels
# app="web"
# version="v2"

kubectl exec downward-pod -- cat /etc/podinfo/name
# downward-pod
Explanation

The Downward API exposes pod metadata to containers via volumes or environment variables. As a volume, each field becomes a file. Available fields: metadata.labels, metadata.annotations, metadata.name, metadata.namespace, metadata.uid, and resource limits/requests via resourceFieldRef. On the CKA, this is less common than ConfigMap/Secret volumes, but knowing it exists helps for debugging scenarios where pods need self-awareness (e.g., registering themselves in a service discovery system).

Chapter 22 · PersistentVolumes, PVCs & StorageClasses

This is the most heavily tested storage topic on the CKA exam. The PV/PVC model separates storage provisioning (admin responsibility) from storage consumption (developer responsibility). You'll create PersistentVolumes, bind them with PersistentVolumeClaims, mount them into pods, and set up StorageClasses for automatic dynamic provisioning — all demonstrated with our easypj/jobpost PostgreSQL database setup.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 💾 PV/PVC 📝 CKA EXAM

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The PV/PVC model — how admin provisioning and developer consumption are separated
  • ✅ How to create PersistentVolumes with correct access modes and reclaim policies
  • ✅ How to create PersistentVolumeClaims and understand binding rules
  • ✅ How to mount PVCs into Pods and Deployments for persistent storage
  • ✅ StorageClasses for dynamic provisioning — eliminate manual PV creation
  • ✅ Complete PostgreSQL + easypj storage setup using volumeClaimTemplates
🎓 CKA Relevance
Storage 10%
PV/PVC Is the #1 Storage Topic on the CKA

Expect at least 1-2 questions on PV/PVC creation and binding. Master these commands:

  • kubectl get pv,pvc — check PV and PVC status
  • kubectl describe pvc <name> — debug why a PVC is Pending
  • Know all three access modes: ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany
  • Know reclaim policies: Retain (keep data), Delete (destroy data)
  • Write PV + PVC YAML from scratch — the exam doesn't always have templates
