32.1 Node Not Ready — Diagnosis

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

A node in NotReady state means the kubelet has stopped reporting to the API server. Your job is to find out why and fix it.

Common NotReady Causes

🛑
kubelet Stopped

The most common cause. kubelet crashed or was stopped. Fix: systemctl start kubelet and systemctl enable kubelet.

🔌
CNI Plugin Missing

No network plugin installed or CNI binary missing. Pods can't get IPs. Fix: Install/reinstall the CNI plugin (Calico, Flannel, etc.).

💾
Swap Enabled

kubelet refuses to start if swap is on (default). Fix: swapoff -a and remove swap entry from /etc/fstab.

📦
containerd Down

Container runtime crashed. No containers can be created. Fix: systemctl restart containerd.

Systematic Node NotReady Fix

1
SSH to Node

ssh worker01 — You can't fix node issues remotely via kubectl. You must be on the node.

2
Check kubelet

systemctl status kubelet — Is it active? If dead: systemctl start kubelet.

3
Read Logs

journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -50 — Error messages reveal the root cause.

4
Fix & Restart

Fix the underlying issue (config, certs, swap, containerd) then systemctl restart kubelet.

5
Verify

kubectl get nodes — Wait for node to transition from NotReady to Ready (may take 30-60s).

🔍 Node Troubleshooting Flowchart

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  $ kubectl get nodes                                                         │
│  NAME           STATUS     ROLES           AGE   VERSION                     │
│  controlplane   Ready      control-plane   30d   v1.31.0                    │
│  worker01       NotReady   <none>          30d   v1.31.0  ◄── PROBLEM      │
│       │                                                                      │
│       ▼                                                                      │
│  $ kubectl describe node worker01                                            │
│       │                                                                      │
│       ├── Conditions Section:                                                │
│       │   ┌──────────────────┬────────┬──────────────────────────────┐       │
│       │   │ Condition        │ Status │ What It Means                │       │
│       │   ├──────────────────┼────────┼──────────────────────────────┤       │
│       │   │ Ready            │ False  │ kubelet not reporting        │       │
│       │   │ MemoryPressure   │ True   │ Node running out of RAM     │       │
│       │   │ DiskPressure     │ True   │ Node running out of disk    │       │
│       │   │ PIDPressure      │ True   │ Too many processes          │       │
│       │   │ NetworkUnavail.  │ True   │ CNI plugin not working      │       │
│       │   └──────────────────┴────────┴──────────────────────────────┘       │
│       │                                                                      │
│       ▼                                                                      │
│  SSH into the node: $ ssh worker01                                           │
│       │                                                                      │
│       ├── $ systemctl status kubelet                                         │
│       │    ├── active (running) → kubelet is up, check network              │
│       │    └── inactive (dead)  → kubelet crashed or was stopped            │
│       │                                                                      │
│       ├── $ journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -50                      │
│       │    └── Look for error messages about certificates, config, etc.     │
│       │                                                                      │
│       └── Common Fixes:                                                      │
│            ├── Kubelet stopped   → systemctl start kubelet                   │
│            ├── Kubelet disabled  → systemctl enable --now kubelet            │
│            ├── Container runtime → systemctl restart containerd              │
│            ├── Swap enabled      → swapoff -a                                │
│            └── Wrong config      → check /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml       │
│                                                                              │
│  VERIFY: $ kubectl get nodes   → worker01 should show Ready                 │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Node Conditions vs Node Status

Status (Ready/NotReady) is the overall health. Conditions (MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, etc.) tell you why a node is unhealthy. A node is Ready only when ALL pressure conditions are False and kubelet is communicating with the API server.

Node Diagnosis Commands 
# Step 1: Get node status overview
kubectl get nodes -o wide

# Step 2: Describe the problematic node
kubectl describe node worker01

# Key areas to check in the output:
# - Conditions     → Ready, MemoryPressure, DiskPressure
# - Capacity       → Total CPU, memory, pods
# - Allocatable    → Available for pods
# - Allocated      → Currently used by pods
# - Events         → Recent node events

# Step 3: SSH to node and check kubelet
ssh worker01
systemctl status kubelet
journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager -l | tail -50

# Step 4: Check container runtime
systemctl status containerd
crictl ps -a                    # List all containers on the node

# Step 5: Check disk and memory
df -h                           # Disk usage
free -m                         # Memory usage
top                             # Process and CPU overview

32.2 Troubleshooting kubelet

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

kubelet is the only component that runs as a systemd service (not a static pod). It's the node agent — if kubelet is down, the node goes NotReady.

kubelet — The Node Agent Architecture

┌──────────────────────────── Worker Node ─────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐        │
│  │                    kubelet (systemd service)                 │        │
│  │                                                             │        │
│  │  📡 Reports to API Server every 10s (node heartbeat)        │        │
│  │  📋 Watches for pod assignments from Scheduler              │        │
│  │  🔄 Manages pod lifecycle via Container Runtime             │        │
│  │  💉 Runs health probes (liveness, readiness, startup)       │        │
│  │  📊 Collects metrics for Metrics Server                     │        │
│  │                                                             │        │
│  │  Config: /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml                       │        │
│  │  Certs:  /var/lib/kubelet/pki/                              │        │
│  │  Logs:   journalctl -u kubelet                              │        │
│  └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘        │
│                           │                                              │
│                           ▼                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐                       │
│  │         Container Runtime (containerd)        │                       │
│  │                                              │                       │
│  │  ┌─────┐  ┌─────┐  ┌─────┐  ┌─────┐        │                       │
│  │  │Pod A│  │Pod B│  │Pod C│  │Pod D│        │                       │
│  │  └─────┘  └─────┘  └─────┘  └─────┘        │                       │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘                       │
│                                                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Common kubelet Issues and Fixes

Problem Symptom Diagnosis Fix
kubelet stopped Node goes NotReady systemctl status kubelet → inactive systemctl start kubelet
kubelet disabled Doesn't start after reboot systemctl is-enabled kubelet → disabled systemctl enable kubelet
Wrong config kubelet crashes repeatedly journalctl -u kubelet → config errors Fix /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
Certificate expired "x509: certificate has expired" openssl x509 -in cert -noout -dates kubeadm certs renew all
Cannot reach API server "connection refused" in kubelet logs Check network, firewall, API server IP Fix network/firewall or API server address in kubelet config
Swap enabled kubelet refuses to start free -m shows swap swapoff -a and remove from /etc/fstab
kubelet Troubleshooting — Step by Step 
# ═══ On the problematic node (SSH in first) ═══

# 1. Check kubelet status
systemctl status kubelet
# Look for: active (running) vs inactive (dead) vs failed

# 2. Check kubelet logs for errors
journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -50
journalctl -u kubelet -f                    # Follow live

# 3. If kubelet is stopped, start it
systemctl start kubelet
systemctl enable kubelet                    # Persist across reboots

# 4. Check kubelet configuration
cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# Verify: clusterDNS, clusterDomain, authentication/authorization

# 5. Check kubelet certificate
openssl x509 -in /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem \
  -noout -text | grep -A2 "Validity"

# 6. Restart kubelet after any config change
systemctl daemon-reload                     # If service file changed
systemctl restart kubelet

# 7. Verify from control plane
kubectl get nodes                           # Should show Ready

⚠️ kubelet Gotchas on the CKA Exam

  • ✗ Wrong Looking for kubelet in kubectl get pods -n kube-system — kubelet is NOT a pod
  • ✓ Right Check kubelet via systemctl status kubelet on the node itself
  • ✗ Wrong Forgetting systemctl daemon-reload after editing service files
  • ✓ Right Always run daemon-reload before restart if you modified a systemd unit
  • ✗ Wrong Restarting kubelet without checking WHY it crashed
  • ✓ Right Read journalctl -u kubelet first to understand the root cause

32.3 Troubleshooting Control Plane Components

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

Control plane components run as static pods managed by kubelet. Their manifests live in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. If a component is broken, check its manifest and logs.

Control Plane Components — Where They Live

┌──────────────────────── Control Plane Node ──────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                          │
│  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/           ← kubelet watches this directory   │
│  ├── kube-apiserver.yaml              ← API Server static pod           │
│  ├── kube-controller-manager.yaml     ← Controller Manager static pod   │
│  ├── kube-scheduler.yaml              ← Scheduler static pod            │
│  └── etcd.yaml                        ← etcd static pod                 │
│                                                                          │
│  How static pods work:                                                   │
│  ┌──────────┐    watches    ┌────────────────────┐                      │
│  │ kubelet  │ ──────────▶  │ /etc/kubernetes/   │                      │
│  │          │    dir for    │    manifests/      │                      │
│  │          │    changes    │                    │                      │
│  └────┬─────┘               └────────────────────┘                      │
│       │ creates/restarts                                                 │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐                   │
│  │API Server│ │Controller│ │Scheduler │ │  etcd   │                   │
│  │   Pod    │ │Mgr Pod   │ │   Pod    │ │   Pod   │                   │
│  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘                   │
│                                                                          │
│  ⚠️ If kubelet is down, static pods don't restart!                      │
│  ⚠️ If manifest has syntax error, static pod won't start!              │
│                                                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Control Plane Troubleshooting Commands 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# 1. CHECK — Are control plane pods running?
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
# Expected: kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, etcd

# 2. CHECK — Control plane pod logs
kubectl logs kube-apiserver-controlplane -n kube-system
kubectl logs kube-scheduler-controlplane -n kube-system
kubectl logs kube-controller-manager-controlplane -n kube-system
kubectl logs etcd-controlplane -n kube-system

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# 3. IF API SERVER IS DOWN — kubectl won't work!
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Use container runtime directly:
crictl ps -a                               # List all containers
crictl ps -a | grep kube-apiserver         # Find API server container
crictl logs <container-id>                 # Read its logs

# 4. CHECK — Static pod manifests
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml

# 5. FIX — Edit manifest, kubelet auto-restarts the pod
vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
# kubelet detects change → restarts the static pod automatically

# 6. VERIFY
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
kubectl get componentstatuses             # Quick cluster health check
💡 CKA Pro Tip: When API Server Is Down

If the API server won't start, kubectl doesn't work at all. You must use crictl (the container runtime CLI) to check container status and logs directly. This is a common CKA exam scenario — they break the API server manifest and you need to fix it.

✅ When kubectl Works
  • kubectl get pods -n kube-system
  • kubectl logs <pod> -n kube-system
  • kubectl describe node <name>
  • kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'
🚨 When kubectl Is Dead
  • crictl ps -a | grep kube
  • crictl logs <container-id>
  • journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager
  • cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/*.yaml

🏋️ Practice: Break and Fix the Control Plane

1
Break the scheduler: sudo sed -i 's/--leader-elect=true/--leader-elect=BROKEN/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml

Watch: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -w — scheduler pod will restart/crash

2
Diagnose: kubectl logs kube-scheduler-controlplane -n kube-system

Find the error message pointing to the invalid flag

3
Fix: Edit the manifest back to --leader-elect=true

kubelet detects the change and restarts the scheduler automatically

32.4 Troubleshooting Networking

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

Network problems manifest as pods that can't reach services, DNS failures, or external traffic not arriving. Systematic diagnosis is key.

Network Troubleshooting — Layer by Layer

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NETWORKING TROUBLESHOOTING LAYERS                                           │
│                                                                              │
│  Layer 1: POD-TO-POD                                                         │
│  ┌──────────┐              ┌──────────┐                                     │
│  │  Pod A   │──── CNI ────▶│  Pod B   │                                     │
│  │ 10.244.1 │   network    │ 10.244.2 │                                     │
│  └──────────┘              └──────────┘                                     │
│  Debug: kubectl exec podA -- ping <podB-IP>                                 │
│  Fix:   Check CNI plugin pods (Calico/Weave/Flannel) running in kube-system │
│                                                                              │
│  Layer 2: POD-TO-SERVICE                                                     │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌───────────────┐  ┌──────────┐                             │
│  │  Pod A   │─▶│  Service      │─▶│  Pod B   │                             │
│  │          │  │  (ClusterIP)  │  │(endpoint)│                             │
│  └──────────┘  └───────────────┘  └──────────┘                             │
│  Debug: kubectl get endpoints <svc>   ← Are there endpoints?               │
│  Fix:   Service selector must match pod labels                               │
│                                                                              │
│  Layer 3: DNS RESOLUTION                                                     │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────────┐                              │
│  │  Pod A   │─▶│ CoreDNS  │─▶│ Service IP   │                              │
│  │nslookup  │  │(kube-dns)│  │  resolved    │                              │
│  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────────┘                              │
│  Debug: kubectl exec pod -- nslookup <svc-name>                             │
│  Fix:   Check CoreDNS pods, ConfigMap, and kube-dns Service                  │
│                                                                              │
│  Layer 4: EXTERNAL ACCESS                                                    │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐                   │
│  │ External │─▶│ NodePort │─▶│ Service  │─▶│  Pod     │                   │
│  │  Client  │  │  :30080  │  │ ClusterIP│  │(backend) │                   │
│  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘                   │
│  Debug: curl http://<node-ip>:<nodeport>                                    │
│  Fix:   Check firewall rules, kube-proxy, service type                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Network Debugging Commands 
# ═══ SERVICE NOT RESPONDING ═══
# Step 1: Check endpoints — are pods registered?
kubectl get endpoints <service-name>
# If <none>: service selector doesn't match any pod labels!

# Step 2: Compare service selector with pod labels
kubectl get svc <service-name> -o yaml | grep -A5 selector
kubectl get pods --show-labels

# ═══ DNS NOT WORKING ═══
# Step 1: Test DNS from inside a pod
kubectl run dnstest --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never -- \
  nslookup kubernetes.default

# Step 2: Check CoreDNS pods
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns

# Step 3: Check CoreDNS ConfigMap for typos
kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml

# Step 4: Check kube-dns Service ClusterIP
kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system
# This IP should match /etc/resolv.conf inside pods

# ═══ CNI PLUGIN ISSUES ═══
# Check CNI plugin pods (Calico, Weave, Flannel, etc.)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -i "calico\|weave\|flannel\|cilium"
kubectl get ds -n kube-system            # CNI typically runs as DaemonSet

# ═══ KUBE-PROXY ISSUES ═══
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-proxy
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
# kube-proxy manages iptables rules for Service → Pod routing

✅ Verify Your Node & Cluster Troubleshooting Skills

  • Can you check a node's kubelet status? → ssh node; systemctl status kubelet
  • Can you view static pod manifests? → ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
  • Can you debug when API server is down? → crictl ps -a; crictl logs <id>
  • Can you test DNS from a pod? → kubectl exec pod -- nslookup svc-name
  • Can you check if service has endpoints? → kubectl get endpoints svc-name

kube-proxy Modes — How Service Routing Works

Mode How It Works Performance Check Command
iptables (default) Creates iptables rules for each Service → Pod mapping. Kernel-level packet routing. Good — random pod selection. Scales to ~5K services. iptables -t nat -L -n | grep <service-clusterip>
ipvs Uses IPVS kernel module with hash tables. More efficient routing algorithms. Better — supports round-robin, least-conn, etc. Scales to 10K+ services. ipvsadm -Ln
nftables (v1.31+) Successor to iptables using nftables kernel subsystem. More efficient rule processing. Best — modern kernel-level routing with better rule optimization. nft list ruleset
💡 Diagnosing kube-proxy Issues

If services exist but traffic doesn't reach pods (and endpoints ARE populated), the problem may be kube-proxy. Check: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy. If kube-proxy is down, iptables rules become stale and services stop routing to new pods.

Under the Hood — How Node and Control Plane Troubleshooting Works: NotReady Diagnosis, Component Health Checks, and the Systemd/CRI Debug Chain
🗺️ Node NotReady — Systematic Diagnosis Flow

A node going NotReady is one of the most common CKA scenarios. The kubelet stops reporting heartbeats, and the node controller marks it NotReady after ~40 seconds.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  NODE NOTREADY — Root Cause Diagnosis Tree                                    │
│                                                                              │
│  $ kubectl get nodes → worker-1   NotReady                                   │
│                                                                              │
│  LEVEL 1: Check kubelet (most common cause)                                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ $ ssh worker-1                                                        │   │
│  │ $ sudo systemctl status kubelet   ← Is kubelet running?               │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  ┌───────────────────┐                                                │   │
│  │  │ kubelet STOPPED    │ → sudo systemctl start kubelet                │   │
│  │  │ (inactive/dead)   │    Check why: journalctl -u kubelet -n 50     │   │
│  │  └───────────────────┘                                                │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  ┌───────────────────┐                                                │   │
│  │  │ kubelet RUNNING    │ → Check kubelet logs for errors:              │   │
│  │  │ but node NotReady │    sudo journalctl -u kubelet -f               │   │
│  │  └───────────────────┘                                                │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  Common kubelet issues:                                               │   │
│  │  • Container runtime (containerd) stopped                              │   │
│  │    → sudo systemctl status containerd                                  │   │
│  │  • Kubelet cert expired                                                │   │
│  │    → Look for "certificate expired" in journalctl                     │   │
│  │  • API Server unreachable                                              │   │
│  │    → Check: curl -k https://<api-server>:6443/healthz                │   │
│  │  • Node disk full                                                      │   │
│  │    → df -h (check /var, /var/lib/kubelet)                             │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  LEVEL 2: Check control plane components                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -v Running                   │   │
│  │ → Any control plane pods crashing?                                     │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ $ kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20          │   │
│  │ → Recent cluster-wide issues                                           │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ NODE CONTROLLER:                                                       │   │
│  │ 1. kubelet sends heartbeat to API Server every node-status-update-    │   │
│  │    frequency (default 10s)                                             │   │
│  │ 2. Node controller checks: last heartbeat < node-monitor-grace-period │   │
│  │    (default 40s)                                                       │   │
│  │ 3. If grace period exceeded → marks node NotReady                     │   │
│  │ 4. After pod-eviction-timeout (default 5m) → evicts pods              │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  CONTROL PLANE COMPONENT FAILURE DIAGNOSIS:                                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ SYMPTOM                      LIKELY CAUSE         CHECK              │   │
│  │ ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │   │
│  │ kubectl: connection refused  API Server down       crictl ps | grep  │   │
│  │                                                     kube-apiserver    │   │
│  │ kubectl: etcd errors         etcd unavailable       crictl ps | grep  │   │
│  │                                                     etcd              │   │
│  │ Controller manager logs      kubeconfig invalid    Check mount paths  │   │
│  │ "0/3 nodes available"        Scheduler down        Get scheduler pod  │   │
│  │ All pods pending              Scheduler down        Check scheduler    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CKA Insight: Node troubleshooting is CKA core. Diagnostic sequence: kubectl describe node <name> (check Conditions section) → ssh node → systemctl status kubelet → journalctl -u kubelet → systemctl status containerd. If kubelet is running but node NotReady: check kubelet logs for certificate/API server errors. The `Conditions` section in `describe node` shows exactly why the node is NotReady (MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure, NetworkUnavailable).

🔑 Key Takeaways

Bulleted key takeaways go here.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • ✗ Wrong Looking for kubelet in kubectl get pods -n kube-system — kubelet is NOT a pod
  • ✓ Right Check kubelet via systemctl status kubelet on the node itself
  • ✗ Wrong Forgetting systemctl daemon-reload after editing service files
  • ✓ Right Always run daemon-reload before restart if you modified a systemd unit
  • ✗ Wrong Restarting kubelet without checking WHY it crashed
  • ✓ Right Read journalctl -u kubelet first to understand the root cause
  • Node NotReady top causes — (1) kubelet not running: systemctl status kubelet. (2) kubelet config error: journalctl -u kubelet -f. (3) CNI plugin missing: ls /etc/cni/net.d/. (4) Container runtime down: systemctl status containerd
  • Static pod manifests location — /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. If kube-apiserver.yaml has a typo, the API server crashes. Fix the YAML, kubelet auto-restarts the pod. The exam loves this pattern
  • crictl not docker — Modern clusters use containerd. Debug with crictl ps, crictl logs, crictl inspect. On the CKA exam, docker CLI is NOT available
  • kubelet runs as systemd service — systemctl restart kubelet to restart. journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager -l for full logs. Config file at /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
  • Control plane component logs — kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-<node> for API server. Same pattern for controller-manager, scheduler. If API server is down, use crictl logs <container-id>
⚡ Speed Tips

CKA Speed Tip — Node NotReady systematic fix:
1. SSH into the node
2. systemctl status kubelet — is it running?
3. journalctl -u kubelet -f — what's the error?
4. Common fixes: systemctl enable --now kubelet, fix /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, reinstall CNI
5. systemctl restart kubelet after any fix

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 32)

ActionCommand
node status + versions + IPskubectl get nodes -o wide
conditions, capacity, taints, eventskubectl describe node <name>
recent kubelet logsssh <node> journalctl -u kubelet --since "5 min ago"
all containers including exited onesssh <node> crictl ps -a
(deprecated but still works) quick health checkkubectl get componentstatuses
🧪 Drill

Timed challenge (target: 6 minutes):

  • 1. SSH to a worker node and stop kubelet: systemctl stop kubelet
  • 2. From control plane: kubectl get nodes — observe NotReady status (may take ~40s)
  • 3. Diagnose: ssh worker journalctl -u kubelet
  • 4. Fix: ssh worker systemctl start kubelet
  • 5. Verify: kubectl get nodes — node returns to Ready

🧠 Chapter 32 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check

Concept-check questions go here.

⚙️ Chapter 32 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Fast node & control-plane troubleshooting recall — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
A node shows NotReady. Walk through the troubleshooting process.
Show Answer
Answer
identify which node is notready
# Step 1: Identify which node is NotReady
kubectl get nodes
# NAME       STATUS     ROLES    AGE  VERSION
# worker-2   NotReady   <none>   30d  v1.31.0

# Step 2: Describe the node for conditions
kubectl describe node worker-2 | grep -A20 Conditions
# MemoryPressure    False
# DiskPressure      False
# PIDPressure       False
# Ready             False  ← kubelet is NOT reporting
#   Last Heartbeat: 5 minutes ago

# Step 3: SSH to the node
ssh worker-2

# Step 4: Check kubelet status
systemctl status kubelet
# Active: inactive (dead)  ← Kubelet is stopped!

# Step 5: Check kubelet logs for errors
journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager
# "failed to load kubelet config file"
# OR "unable to connect to API server"

# Step 6: Common fixes:
# kubelet stopped → systemctl start kubelet
# kubelet crashing → check config: /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# cert expired → check /var/lib/kubelet/pki/
# wrong API server → check /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf

# Step 7: Start and enable kubelet
systemctl start kubelet
systemctl enable kubelet

# Step 8: Verify from control plane
kubectl get nodes
# worker-2   Ready   <none>   30d  v1.31.0 ✓
Explanation

NotReady = kubelet stopped sending heartbeats. On the CKA: SSH to the node, check systemctl status kubelet, check journalctl -u kubelet for errors, fix the issue, restart kubelet. The most common CKA scenario: kubelet is stopped or has a config error. Always check the config file path and API server address. After fixing, verify with kubectl get nodes.

Q2
The kubelet is running but keeps restarting. How do you diagnose the config issue?
Show Answer
Answer
check kubelet status
# Step 1: Check kubelet status
systemctl status kubelet
# Active: activating (auto-restart)
# ← kubelet keeps crashing and systemd restarts it

# Step 2: Check journal logs
journalctl -u kubelet -n 100 --no-pager
# Look for error messages:

# Error A: "failed to load kubelet config file"
cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# Check YAML syntax, missing fields

# Error B: "unable to load client CA file"
ls -la /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
# Check if cert file exists and is readable

# Error C: "server.key: no such file or directory"
# Wrong cert/key path in kubelet config

# Step 3: Check kubelet systemd unit
cat /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf
# Look for wrong flags or paths

# Step 4: Verify kubelet config
cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# Common issues:
# - Wrong clusterDNS IP
# - Wrong clusterDomain
# - Invalid YAML syntax

# Step 5: Fix and restart
vi /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml  # Fix the issue
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart kubelet

# Step 6: Verify
systemctl status kubelet  # Should show "active (running)"
kubectl get nodes          # Node should be Ready
Explanation

When kubelet keeps restarting (activating/auto-restart), it's usually a configuration problem. On the CKA, check journalctl -u kubelet for the specific error message. Common causes: broken kubelet config YAML, missing/wrong cert paths, wrong systemd flags. Fix the config file, daemon-reload, restart kubelet. Always do daemon-reload if you changed the systemd unit file.

Q3
A static pod isn't starting on a node. How do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer
find static pod manifest directory
# Step 1: Find static pod manifest directory
# Check kubelet config:
cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep staticPodPath
# staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests

# OR check kubelet flags:
ps aux | grep kubelet | grep -- --pod-manifest-path

# Step 2: Check the manifest exists
ls -la /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml
# kube-scheduler.yaml  my-static-pod.yaml

# Step 3: Validate the manifest YAML
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/my-static-pod.yaml

# Step 4: Check for syntax errors
# Common issues:
# - Wrong indentation
# - Missing required fields (apiVersion, kind, spec)
# - Wrong image name
# - Invalid port numbers

# Step 5: Check kubelet logs for static pod errors
journalctl -u kubelet | grep "my-static-pod"
# "failed to parse static pod manifest: ..."

# Step 6: Fix the manifest
vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/my-static-pod.yaml
# Kubelet auto-detects changes — no restart needed!

# Step 7: Verify
kubectl get pods -A | grep my-static-pod
# my-static-pod-worker-1   1/1  Running  0  10s

# Remember: Static pod names have node name appended
# Static pods are managed by kubelet, NOT the scheduler
Explanation

Static pods are managed directly by the kubelet (not the API server). They read manifests from staticPodPath (default: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/). On the CKA: if a static pod isn't working, check the YAML in the manifest directory. Kubelet watches the directory and auto-restarts when manifests change — no need to restart kubelet. Static pod names have the node name appended (e.g., etcd-master). Control plane components (etcd, apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager) are static pods.

Q4
How do you use crictl to troubleshoot container runtime issues on a node?
Show Answer
Answer
crictl = cri container runtime interface tool
# crictl = CRI Container Runtime Interface tool
# Works with containerd, CRI-O (not Docker)

# SSH to the node first
ssh worker-1

# List running containers (like docker ps)
crictl ps
# CONTAINER ID  IMAGE     CREATED    STATE    NAME     POD ID
# a1b2c3d4e5    nginx     5min ago   Running  nginx    f6g7h8

# List ALL containers (including stopped)
crictl ps -a

# Get container logs
crictl logs a1b2c3d4e5

# Inspect container details
crictl inspect a1b2c3d4e5

# List pods on this node
crictl pods
# POD ID    STATE  NAME         NAMESPACE  AGE
# f6g7h8    Ready  web-pod      default    30m

# List images
crictl images

# Check container runtime socket
crictl info
# If error: "connect: no such file or directory"
# → Container runtime is down!

# Fix container runtime:
systemctl status containerd  # check status
systemctl restart containerd  # restart if needed
systemctl restart kubelet     # restart kubelet after

# Pull an image manually (for debugging)
crictl pull nginx:1.25
Explanation

crictl interacts with the container runtime directly on the node. On the CKA, use it when kubectl commands timeout (API server issue) or to debug container-level problems. Key commands: crictl ps (list containers), crictl logs (container logs), crictl pods (list pods on node). If crictl info fails, the container runtime is down. Restart containerd first, then kubelet.

Q5
How do you check control plane component health?
Show Answer
Answer
check control plane pods in kube-system
# Method 1: Check control plane pods in kube-system
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
# NAME                              READY  STATUS   RESTARTS
# etcd-master                       1/1    Running  0
# kube-apiserver-master             1/1    Running  0
# kube-controller-manager-master    1/1    Running  0
# kube-scheduler-master             1/1    Running  0
# coredns-5d78c9869d-abcde          1/1    Running  0
# kube-proxy-12345                  1/1    Running  0

# Method 2: Component status (deprecated but still works)
kubectl get componentstatuses
# NAME                 STATUS    MESSAGE
# scheduler            Healthy   ok
# controller-manager   Healthy   ok
# etcd-0               Healthy   ok

# Method 3: Check API server directly
kubectl cluster-info
# Kubernetes control plane is running at https://10.0.0.1:6443
# CoreDNS is running at https://10.0.0.1:6443/api/v1/namespaces/...

# Method 4: Check logs of control plane components
kubectl logs kube-apiserver-master -n kube-system | tail -20
kubectl logs kube-scheduler-master -n kube-system | tail -20
kubectl logs kube-controller-manager-master -n kube-system | tail -20
kubectl logs etcd-master -n kube-system | tail -20

# Method 5: On the master node directly
crictl ps | grep kube
journalctl -u kubelet | grep -i error
Explanation

Control plane components run as static pods on the master node (in kube-system namespace). On the CKA: check if all 4 components are Running, check logs for errors, and use crictl on the master if kubectl doesn't work (API server down). Common issue: if API server is down, kubectl won't work — SSH to master and use crictl to check the container, then look at the static pod manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.

Q6
How do you troubleshoot CNI (Container Network Interface) issues?
Show Answer
Answer
symptom: pods stuck in containercreating
# Symptom: Pods stuck in ContainerCreating
kubectl describe pod stuck-pod
# Warning  FailedCreatePodSandBox
# "network plugin is not ready: cni config uninitialized"

# Step 1: Check CNI plugin is installed
ls /etc/cni/net.d/
# Should contain config files like:
# 10-calico.conflist  OR  10-weave.conflist

# If empty → CNI plugin not installed!

# Step 2: Check CNI plugin pods
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|weave|flannel"
# calico-node-abc12   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff  ← Problem!

# Step 3: Check CNI plugin logs
kubectl logs calico-node-abc12 -n kube-system

# Step 4: Check CNI binary
ls /opt/cni/bin/
# Should contain: calico, bandwidth, bridge, etc.

# Fix 1: Install CNI plugin (if missing)
kubectl apply -f https://docs.projectcalico.org/manifests/calico.yaml

# Fix 2: Restart CNI pods
kubectl delete pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=calico-node
# DaemonSet recreates them

# Fix 3: Check node network
ssh worker-1
ip link show  # Network interfaces
ip route     # Routing table

# Verify: Pods should move from ContainerCreating to Running
kubectl get pods -w
Explanation

CNI provides pod networking. Without CNI, pods can't get IP addresses and stay in ContainerCreating. On the CKA: check /etc/cni/net.d/ for config files and /opt/cni/bin/ for binaries. If no CNI is installed, you need to apply the CNI plugin manifest. CNI plugins run as DaemonSets in kube-system. Common exam question: "pods stuck in ContainerCreating on a new node" = CNI not configured.

Q7
A node shows MemoryPressure or DiskPressure. What happens and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer
check node conditions
# Check node conditions:
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A20 Conditions
# Type              Status
# MemoryPressure    True    ← Node running out of memory!
# DiskPressure      True    ← Node running out of disk!
# PIDPressure       False
# Ready             True    (can be True with pressure)

# What happens automatically:
# MemoryPressure → kubelet starts evicting pods (BestEffort first)
# DiskPressure   → kubelet reclaims dead containers, unused images
# Both           → Node gets tainted: node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure:NoSchedule

# Check memory on the node:
ssh worker-1
free -h
# total: 4Gi  used: 3.8Gi  available: 200Mi ← Very low!

# Check disk:
df -h /
# /dev/sda1  50G  48G  2G  96% /  ← 96% full!

# Fix MemoryPressure:
# 1. Find memory-hungry pods:
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory | head -10
# 2. Delete or reduce limits on heavy consumers
# 3. Add memory to the node (if possible)

# Fix DiskPressure:
ssh worker-1
# Clean up container logs:
journalctl --vacuum-size=100M
# Remove unused images:
crictl rmi --prune
# Clear unused containers:
crictl rm $(crictl ps -a -q --state exited)

# Eviction thresholds (defaults):
# memory.available < 100Mi
# nodefs.available < 10%
# imagefs.available < 15%
Explanation

Node pressure conditions trigger automatic eviction. The kubelet evicts pods in order: BestEffort (no limits) first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed last. Pressure also adds a NoSchedule taint so new pods won't be scheduled. On the CKA: check with describe node, SSH to the node to check free -h and df -h, fix by removing unused resources or moving pods. The kubelet's eviction thresholds are configurable in kubelet config.yaml.

Q8
The kube-proxy DaemonSet isn't running on a node. How do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer
symptom: services don't work on one specific node
# Symptom: Services don't work on one specific node
# Pods can ping other pods but Service ClusterIP fails

# Step 1: Check kube-proxy pods
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o wide
# NAME              READY  STATUS   NODE
# kube-proxy-abc12  1/1    Running  worker-1
# kube-proxy-def34  0/1    Error    worker-2  ← Problem!

# Step 2: Check logs
kubectl logs kube-proxy-def34 -n kube-system
# "failed to load config: couldn't read file"

# Step 3: Check kube-proxy ConfigMap
kubectl get configmap kube-proxy -n kube-system -o yaml | head -30

# Step 4: Check kube-proxy DaemonSet
kubectl get ds kube-proxy -n kube-system
kubectl describe ds kube-proxy -n kube-system

# Step 5: Check iptables/ipvs rules on the node
ssh worker-2
iptables -L -t nat | grep -i kube
# If empty → kube-proxy isn't creating rules

# Fix: Delete the erroring pod (DaemonSet recreates)
kubectl delete pod kube-proxy-def34 -n kube-system

# If still broken, check kube-proxy mode:
kubectl get configmap kube-proxy -n kube-system -o yaml | grep mode
# mode: "iptables" (default) or "ipvs"

# Restart ALL kube-proxy pods:
kubectl rollout restart ds kube-proxy -n kube-system
Explanation

kube-proxy runs as a DaemonSet (one pod per node) and maintains network rules (iptables/ipvs) for Service routing. If kube-proxy is broken on a node, Services won't work on that node. On the CKA: check the kube-proxy pod logs, delete the broken pod (DaemonSet auto-recreates), or rollout restart the DaemonSet. Config comes from the kube-proxy ConfigMap in kube-system.

Q9
How do you troubleshoot a kubelet that won't start after a cluster upgrade?
Show Answer
Answer
after kubeadm upgrade, kubelet won't start
# After kubeadm upgrade, kubelet won't start:
systemctl status kubelet
# Active: activating (auto-restart)

# Step 1: Check journal
journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager
# Error messages to look for:

# A: "mismatched kubelet version"
kubelet --version
# v1.30.0 ← Not upgraded to v1.31!
# Fix: Upgrade kubelet package
apt-get install kubelet=1.31.0-1.1

# B: "failed to read kubelet config"
cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# Config may need updating
kubeadm upgrade node  # Updates kubelet config

# C: "certificate has expired"
ls -la /var/lib/kubelet/pki/
openssl x509 -in /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem \
-noout -dates
# Fix: kubeadm certs renew all (on master)

# Step 2: Full fix sequence
apt-get update
apt-get install -y kubelet=1.31.0-1.1 kubectl=1.31.0-1.1
kubeadm upgrade node  # Only on worker nodes
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart kubelet

# Step 3: Verify
systemctl status kubelet  # active (running)
kubectl get nodes          # Node Ready, correct version
Explanation

Post-upgrade kubelet issues are common on the CKA. Key checks: (1) kubelet binary version matches the cluster version, (2) kubeadm upgrade node was run to update config, (3) daemon-reload was done before restart, (4) certificates are valid. The most common mistake is forgetting kubeadm upgrade node on workers or not doing daemon-reload. Always check journalctl first — the error message tells you exactly what's wrong.

Q10
How do you find which pods are running on a specific node and what resources they're using?
Show Answer
Answer
field selector (recommended)
# Method 1: Field selector (recommended)
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName=worker-1
# NAMESPACE     NAME              READY  STATUS
# default       web-abc12         1/1    Running
# kube-system   kube-proxy-xyz    1/1    Running
# kube-system   calico-node-123   1/1    Running

# Method 2: Using -o wide shows NODE column
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep worker-1

# Method 3: Resource usage on the node
kubectl top node worker-1
# NAME       CPU(cores)  CPU%  MEMORY(bytes)  MEMORY%
# worker-1   350m        17%   1200Mi         60%

# Method 4: Resource usage per pod on the node
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu --field-selector spec.nodeName=worker-1

# Method 5: Node capacity vs allocatable vs used
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A10 "Allocated resources"
# Allocated resources:
#   CPU Requests  CPU Limits  Memory Requests  Memory Limits
#   750m (37%)    2 (100%)    1Gi (50%)        2Gi (100%)

# Method 6: All resource details
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A5 "Capacity"
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A5 "Allocatable"

# CKA shortcut: See what's running and how much room is left
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A30 "Non-terminated"
Explanation

--field-selector spec.nodeName= filters pods by node. On the CKA, kubectl describe node shows Capacity, Allocatable, and Allocated Resources — this tells you total vs available vs used. kubectl top node shows real-time usage. Key CKA scenario: scheduling failure because node is at capacity — use describe node to see Allocated vs Allocatable resources to confirm.

33.1 Application Logging

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

Containers write to stdout/stderr, and the container runtime captures these streams as log files on the node. kubectl logs retrieves this output.

kubectl logs — Debugging Flow

1
Basic Logs

kubectl logs <pod> — Start with current container output. If pod is running, this shows real-time stdout/stderr.

2
Previous Crash

kubectl logs <pod> --previous — If CrashLoopBackOff, this shows output from the last crashed container instance.

3
Specific Container

kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> — Multi-container pods require specifying which container. Use --all-containers for everything.

4
Label Selector

kubectl logs -l app=name --tail=50 — Check logs across ALL replicas of a Deployment at once.

Application Logging Examples 
# Basic logs
kubectl logs easypj-web-xxxx -n easypj

# Previous crashed container ⭐ (CKA critical)
kubectl logs easypj-web-xxxx -n easypj --previous

# Follow live (useful during testing)
kubectl logs easypj-web-xxxx -n easypj -f

# Multi-container pod: specify the container
kubectl logs easypj-web-xxxx -n easypj -c django
kubectl logs easypj-web-xxxx -n easypj -c nginx-sidecar

# All containers at once
kubectl logs easypj-web-xxxx -n easypj --all-containers

# Logs from all pods with label app=easypj
kubectl logs -l app=easypj -n easypj --tail=50

# Combine flags: last 100 lines from last hour, follow live
kubectl logs easypj-web-xxxx --tail=100 --since=1h -f
📖 Where Do Container Logs Actually Live?

On the node, container logs are stored at:
/var/log/containers/<pod-name>_<namespace>_<container>-<id>.log
/var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod-name>_<uid>/<container>/
These are symlinks managed by the container runtime. kubectl logs reads these files via kubelet.

33.2 Cluster-Level Logging

Node-level logging only keeps logs on individual nodes. For production, you need a centralized logging architecture — a DaemonSet log agent that ships logs to a central store.

The 3 Logging Patterns

📋
Node-Level Agent (Recommended)

DaemonSet runs 1 log agent per node (fluentd, filebeat). Agent reads /var/log/containers/ and ships to central store. Lightweight, no pod modification needed.

🔀
Sidecar Streaming

Sidecar container reads app log files and streams to its own stdout. Node agent then picks up the sidecar's output. Use when app writes to files instead of stdout.

📡
Sidecar with Agent

Sidecar runs its own logging agent (fluentd) that ships directly to the backend. More flexible but resource-heavy — each pod gets its own agent.

💡
CKA Focus

Know the architecture concepts and kubectl logs flags. The exam won't ask you to deploy EFK/Loki stacks — but may ask you to create a sidecar logging container.

Kubernetes Logging Architecture — From Container to Central Store

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  KUBERNETES LOGGING ARCHITECTURE                             │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────── Worker Node 1 ─────────────────────────────┐                 │
│  │                                                         │                 │
│  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐             │                 │
│  │  │  Pod A   │  │  Pod B   │  │  Pod C   │             │                 │
│  │  │ stdout→  │  │ stdout→  │  │ stdout→  │             │                 │
│  │  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘             │                 │
│  │       │              │              │                   │                 │
│  │       ▼              ▼              ▼                   │                 │
│  │  /var/log/containers/*.log                              │                 │
│  │  /var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod>/                       │                 │
│  │       │                                                 │                 │
│  │       ▼                                                 │                 │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐                       │                 │
│  │  │ 📋 DaemonSet Log Agent     │   fluentd /            │                 │
│  │  │    (1 per node)             │   filebeat /           │                 │
│  │  │                             │   fluent-bit           │                 │
│  │  └──────────────┬──────────────┘                       │                 │
│  └─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┘                 │
│                    │                                                         │
│  ┌─────────────────┼── Worker Node 2 ──────────────────────┐                │
│  │  (same pattern) │                                        │                │
│  │  Pods → /var/log/ → DaemonSet Agent ───────────────┤    │                │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────┘                │
│                                                        │                     │
│              ┌─────────────────────────────────────────▼──────────┐          │
│              │  🗄️  CENTRAL LOG STORE                              │          │
│              │                                                     │          │
│              │  Elasticsearch / Loki / CloudWatch / Splunk        │          │
│              │         │                                          │          │
│              │         ▼                                          │          │
│              │  📊 Kibana / Grafana   (visualization & alerts)   │          │
│              └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
│                                                                              │
│  THREE LOGGING PATTERNS:                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────────┐             │
│  │ Node-level Agent │ Sidecar Streaming│ Sidecar with Agent   │             │
│  │ (DaemonSet)      │ (sidecar → stdout│ (sidecar ships logs) │             │
│  │ ✅ Recommended   │  → node agent)   │ ⚠️ Resource heavy   │             │
│  │ 1 agent per node │ Multi-format logs│ Direct to backend    │             │
│  └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────────┘             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 CKA Scope: Logging

The CKA exam tests kubectl logs commands, not deploying full logging stacks. Know the architecture concepts (DaemonSet agent, node-level logs, sidecar patterns) but focus your practice on the kubectl logs flags in section 33.1.

Sidecar Logging Pattern — When Apps Don't Log to stdout

📖 Why Sidecar Logging?

Some applications write logs to files instead of stdout. Since kubectl logs only captures stdout/stderr, you need a sidecar container that reads the log file and streams it to its own stdout — making it visible via kubectl logs.

sidecar-logging.yaml 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  containers:
  # Main application — writes logs to a file
  - name: django
    image: easypj:v1
    volumeMounts:
    - name: log-volume
      mountPath: /var/log/django

  # Sidecar — streams the log file to stdout
  - name: log-streamer
    image: busybox:1.36
    args: ['sh', '-c', 'tail -F /var/log/django/app.log']
    volumeMounts:
    - name: log-volume
      mountPath: /var/log/django

  volumes:
  - name: log-volume
    emptyDir: {}

# Now you can read the app logs via:
# kubectl logs easypj-web -c log-streamer

Container Log Rotation

Setting Default Purpose
containerLogMaxSize 10Mi Max size of a single log file before rotation
containerLogMaxFiles 5 Max number of rotated log files kept per container
💡 Log Rotation Config

These are set in the kubelet configuration (/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml). Default: each container can use up to 50Mi of disk for logs (10Mi × 5 files). If a node has disk pressure, check if log rotation is properly configured.

33.3 Monitoring with Metrics Server

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

Metrics Server is a lightweight, in-cluster component that collects CPU and memory usage from kubelet on each node. It powers kubectl top and is required for HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler).

Metrics Server — How It Works

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     METRICS SERVER ARCHITECTURE                          │
│                                                                          │
│  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐                            │
│  │ kubelet  │   │ kubelet  │   │ kubelet  │                            │
│  │ (node 1) │   │ (node 2) │   │ (node 3) │                            │
│  │          │   │          │   │          │                            │
│  │ cAdvisor │   │ cAdvisor │   │ cAdvisor │   ← built into kubelet     │
│  │ collects │   │ collects │   │ collects │     collects container      │
│  │ metrics  │   │ metrics  │   │ metrics  │     CPU/memory metrics     │
│  └────┬─────┘   └────┬─────┘   └────┬─────┘                            │
│       │              │              │                                    │
│       └──────────────┼──────────────┘                                    │
│                      ▼                                                   │
│            ┌──────────────────┐                                         │
│            │  Metrics Server  │   ← Deployment in kube-system           │
│            │  (kube-system)   │     Scrapes /metrics/resource from      │
│            │                  │     each kubelet every 15 seconds       │
│            └────────┬─────────┘                                         │
│                     │ exposes                                            │
│                     ▼                                                    │
│            ┌──────────────────┐                                         │
│            │ metrics.k8s.io   │   ← Kubernetes API extension            │
│            │  API endpoint    │                                         │
│            └────────┬─────────┘                                         │
│                     │                                                    │
│           ┌─────────┼──────────────┐                                    │
│           ▼                        ▼                                    │
│  ┌──────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐                           │
│  │ kubectl top  │       │ HPA Controller   │                           │
│  │ pods / nodes │       │ (auto-scaling)   │                           │
│  └──────────────┘       └──────────────────┘                           │
│                                                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Metrics Server Installation & Usage 
# ═══ INSTALL METRICS SERVER ═══
# Download and apply the official manifest
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml

# For local clusters (kubeadm, kind, minikube) — add insecure TLS flag:
# Edit the Deployment and add to args:
# --kubelet-insecure-tls
kubectl edit deployment metrics-server -n kube-system

# Verify metrics server is running
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep metrics-server
kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics     # Should show v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io

# ═══ KUBECTL TOP — RESOURCE USAGE ═══
# Node-level metrics
kubectl top nodes                          # CPU and memory per node
kubectl top nodes --sort-by=cpu            # Sort by CPU usage

# Pod-level metrics
kubectl top pods                           # CPU and memory per pod
kubectl top pods -A                        # All namespaces
kubectl top pods --sort-by=memory          # Sort by memory usage
kubectl top pods --sort-by=cpu             # Sort by CPU usage
kubectl top pods -n kube-system            # Specific namespace

# Pod with containers breakdown
kubectl top pods --containers              # Per-container metrics

Interpreting Resource Metrics

Metric Unit Example What It Means
CPU millicores (m) 250m 25% of one CPU core
CPU cores 1 100% of one CPU core
Memory Mi (mebibytes) 128Mi ~134 MB of RAM
Memory Gi (gibibytes) 2Gi ~2.1 GB of RAM

33.4 Monitoring easypj Resource Usage

Let's apply monitoring to our easypj project — find resource-hungry pods, identify OOM risks, and set appropriate limits.

Monitoring easypj — Finding Resource Issues 
# Which pods are using the most CPU?
kubectl top pods -n easypj --sort-by=cpu
# NAME                          CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
# easypj-web-7d4f8c5-abc12      250m         128Mi
# easypj-db-0                   100m         512Mi     ← DB uses most memory
# easypj-worker-xxxx            50m          64Mi

# Which pods are using the most memory?
kubectl top pods -n easypj --sort-by=memory

# Per-container breakdown (useful for sidecar pods)
kubectl top pods -n easypj --containers
# NAME                  CONTAINER   CPU    MEMORY
# easypj-web-xxx        django      200m   100Mi
# easypj-web-xxx        nginx       50m    28Mi

# Node-level — is any node under pressure?
kubectl top nodes
# NAME           CPU(cores)  CPU%   MEMORY(bytes)  MEMORY%
# controlplane   350m        17%    1200Mi         62%
# worker01       800m        40%    3200Mi         80%     ← ⚠️ High memory!

# Compare against resource requests/limits
kubectl describe pod easypj-web-xxxx -n easypj | grep -A8 "Requests\|Limits"

Resource Monitoring — Requests vs Limits vs Actual Usage

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  easypj-web pod: CPU usage over time                                     │
│                                                                          │
│  CPU (millicores)                                                        │
│  500m ┤                                                                  │
│       │                                                                  │
│  400m ┤                              ╔═══════════════╗ ← LIMIT (400m)   │
│       │                        ┌─────╨───┐           ║                   │
│  300m ┤                   ┌────┘         └───┐       ║                   │
│       │              ┌────┘                  │       ║                   │
│  250m ┤─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─│─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─│─ ─ ─ ─║─ ← REQUEST (250m)│
│       │         ┌────┘                       └───┐   ║                   │
│  200m ┤    ┌────┘                                └───║──┐                │
│       │────┘                                         ║  └───             │
│  100m ┤                                              ║                   │
│       │                                              ║                   │
│    0m ┤──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ Time  │
│       │                                                                  │
│  REQUEST = guaranteed minimum (scheduler uses this for placement)        │
│  LIMIT   = maximum allowed (container is throttled/killed above this)    │
│  ACTUAL  = the wavy line (what kubectl top shows)                        │
│                                                                          │
│  ⚠️ If ACTUAL exceeds MEMORY LIMIT → OOMKilled (exit 137)              │
│  ⚠️ If ACTUAL exceeds CPU LIMIT → Throttled (not killed)               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🏋️ Practice Drill: Monitoring Commands

1
Install Metrics Server and verify: kubectl top nodes returns data
2
Find the pod using the most CPU: kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu | head -5
3
Find the node with highest memory usage: kubectl top nodes --sort-by=memory
Under the Hood — How Logging and Monitoring Architectures Work: kubelet Log Management, Container Runtime Logs, and the Metrics Pipeline
🗺️ Kubernetes Logging Architecture — Where Logs Live

kubectl logs doesn't connect to a central log server. It reads directly from the node's filesystem where the container runtime writes stdout/stderr.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  KUBERNETES LOGGING — Data Flow                                              │
│                                                                              │
│  Container stdout/stderr                                                      │
│       │                                                                       │
│       ▼                                                                       │
│  containerd captures output → writes to JSON file:                           │
│  /var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod-name>_<pod-uid>/<container>/0.log          │
│                                                                              │
│  kubectl logs → kubelet reads from this file via CRI                        │
│                                                                              │
│  NODE-LEVEL LOG LOCATIONS:                                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Application logs: /var/log/pods/                                       │   │
│  │ Container logs:   /var/log/containers/ (symlinks to pod logs)         │   │
│  │ kubelet logs:     journalctl -u kubelet                               │   │
│  │ containerd logs:  journalctl -u containerd                             │   │
│  │ API Server logs:  /var/log/kube-apiserver.log OR crictl logs <id>    │   │
│  │ etcd logs:        crictl logs <id>                                     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  LOG ROTATION (kubelet-managed):                                             │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ kubelet rotates logs when:                                            │   │
│  │   containerLogMaxSize: "10Mi"  ← Max size per log file               │   │
│  │   containerLogMaxFiles: 5      ← Max rotated files to keep           │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ After rotation: 0.log → 0.log.1 → 0.log.2 → ... → deleted            │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ ⚠️  kubectl logs --previous reads from the PREVIOUS (rotated) file    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  METRICS PIPELINE — How kubectl top Works:                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ cAdvisor (in kubelet) → collects CPU/memory per container            │   │
│  │       │                                                                │   │
│  │       ▼                                                                │   │
│  │ metrics-server → aggregates cAdvisor data from all nodes              │   │
│  │       │  (Deployment in kube-system, needs metrics-server installed)  │   │
│  │       ▼                                                                │   │
│  │ kubectl top pod/node → queries metrics-server API                     │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ WITHOUT metrics-server: kubectl top returns "error: Metrics API not    │   │
│  │   available". Install: kubectl apply -f metrics-server components.yaml │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  EVENTS — The Cluster's Timeline:                                            │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -A | tail -30            │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Events are kept for 1 hour by default. They tell you:                 │   │
│  │ • Why a pod was killed (OOMKilling)                                   │   │
│  │ • Why a pod can't start (FailedMount, FailedScheduling)               │   │
│  │ • Why a probe failed (Unhealthy)                                      │   │
│  │ • When nodes changed state (NodeReady→NodeNotReady)                   │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Events are your FIRST stop for any cluster issue.                     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CKA Insight: On the CKA, kubectl logs is your primary diagnostic tool. Remember: --previous for crashed container logs, --tail=50 for last N lines, --since=5m for time-windowed logs, --all-containers for multi-container pods, -l app=web for aggregate logs across pods. For control plane component logs, use crictl logs on the node since they run as static pods (not accessible via kubectl logs in kube-system).

🔑 Key Takeaways

Bulleted key takeaways go here.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • ✗ Wrong Expecting kubectl top to work without Metrics Server installed
  • ✓ Right Install Metrics Server first — it's not included by default in kubeadm clusters
  • ✗ Wrong Thinking Metrics Server stores historical data
  • ✓ Right Metrics Server provides current snapshot only — for history use Prometheus
  • ✗ Wrong Forgetting --kubelet-insecure-tls in lab environments
  • ✓ Right Add this flag in kubeadm/kind/minikube — otherwise Metrics Server can't scrape kubelet
  • Metrics Server must be installed — kubectl top nodes and kubectl top pods fail without it. The exam cluster usually has it pre-installed, but verify first: kubectl get deployment metrics-server -n kube-system
  • kubectl top shows CURRENT usage, not limits — A pod using 450Mi doesn't mean its limit is 450Mi. Compare with kubectl describe pod to see limits vs actual usage. Exam may ask "which pod is closest to its memory limit"
  • Log rotation — Node-level logs at /var/log/containers/ are rotated by the container runtime. If a pod restarted 5 times, only the current + previous logs are available via kubectl logs
  • Sidecar logging pattern — App writes to a file on a shared emptyDir volume. A sidecar container tails that file to stdout. This makes logs accessible via kubectl logs <pod> -c sidecar
  • --sort-by flag — kubectl top pods --sort-by=memory or --sort-by=cpu. The exam may ask to find the pod consuming the most resources. Know these flags
⚡ Speed Tips

CKA Speed Tip — Resource usage commands:
kubectl top nodes — CPU/memory per node
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu — highest CPU across all namespaces
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory | head -5 — top 5 memory consumers
kubectl logs <pod> -f --tail=50 — follow last 50 lines (live tail)

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 33)

ActionCommand
Current container stdout/stderr — First check for running podskubectl logs <pod>
Previous crashed container output — CrashLoopBackOff debuggingkubectl logs <pod> --previous
Follow / stream live — Watch realtime during testingkubectl logs <pod> -f
Last N lines only — Quick check without scrollingkubectl logs <pod> --tail=100
Logs from last hour — Recent errors onlykubectl logs <pod> --since=1h
Specific container — Multi-container pods (sidecars)kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>
All containers in a pod — Sidecar/init container logskubectl logs <pod> --all-containers
All pods matching label — Deployments with multiple replicaskubectl logs -l app=name
all containers, last 10 minkubectl logs <pod> --all-containers --since=10m
logs from multiple pods by labelkubectl logs -l app=web --max-log-requests=10
per-container resource usagekubectl top pods -n <ns> --containers
recent cluster eventskubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
previous crashed container's logskubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous
