⚙️ Chapter 33 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Quick recall of logging & metrics tooling — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
How do you get the last 100 lines of logs from a pod and stream new logs in real time?
Show Answer
Answer
last 100 lines
# Last 100 lines:
kubectl logs web-pod --tail=100

# Stream (follow) logs in real time:
kubectl logs web-pod -f

# Combine: last 100 lines THEN stream:
kubectl logs web-pod --tail=100 -f

# Logs since a specific time:
kubectl logs web-pod --since=1h     # Last 1 hour
kubectl logs web-pod --since=30m    # Last 30 minutes
kubectl logs web-pod --since=5s     # Last 5 seconds

# Logs since a timestamp:
kubectl logs web-pod --since-time="2024-01-15T10:00:00Z"

# Add timestamps to log lines:
kubectl logs web-pod --timestamps=true
# 2024-01-15T10:30:00Z  [INFO] Server started on port 8080

# Previous container logs (after crash/restart):
kubectl logs web-pod --previous

# Combine for exam speed:
kubectl logs web-pod --tail=50 --timestamps -f
Explanation

--tail=N shows the last N lines (avoids flooding). -f follows/streams new logs. --since accepts durations (1h, 30m) or timestamps. --timestamps prepends timestamps to each line. On the CKA, use --tail=50 -f to quickly see recent logs and watch for new errors. --previous gets logs from the previous container instance (crucial after crashes).

Q2
Create a sidecar container that reads the main application's log file and streams it to stdout.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: app-with-sidecar
spec:
containers:
- name: app
image: busybox
command: ['sh', '-c',
  'while true; do echo "$(date) - Processing request" >> /var/log/app.log; sleep 5; done']
volumeMounts:
- name: log-volume
  mountPath: /var/log

- name: log-sidecar
image: busybox
command: ['sh', '-c', 'tail -f /var/log/app.log']
volumeMounts:
- name: log-volume
  mountPath: /var/log

volumes:
- name: log-volume
emptyDir: {}

# Now you can view app logs via kubectl:
# kubectl logs app-with-sidecar -c log-sidecar
# 2024-01-15 10:30:00 - Processing request
# 2024-01-15 10:30:05 - Processing request
Explanation

Sidecar logging pattern: the main app writes logs to a file, the sidecar reads that file with tail -f and outputs to stdout. Both containers share a volume (emptyDir). This makes file-based logs accessible via kubectl logs. On the CKA, you may need to add a sidecar container to stream logs from a file. Key: shared volume, tail -f in the sidecar, and matching mountPath.

Q3
How do you install Metrics Server and get resource usage with kubectl top?
Show Answer
Answer
check if metrics-server is installed
# Check if metrics-server is installed:
kubectl top nodes
# Error: Metrics API not available
# ← Metrics Server is NOT installed

# Install Metrics Server:
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml

# For lab environments (self-signed certs), add --kubelet-insecure-tls:
kubectl patch deployment metrics-server -n kube-system \
--type='json' -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'

# Wait for it to be ready (~60 seconds):
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep metrics-server

# Node resource usage:
kubectl top nodes
# NAME       CPU(cores)  CPU%  MEMORY(bytes)  MEMORY%
# master     250m        12%   1500Mi         75%
# worker-1   150m        7%    800Mi          40%

# Pod resource usage:
kubectl top pods -A
kubectl top pods -n default

# Sort by CPU or memory:
kubectl top pods --sort-by=cpu
kubectl top pods --sort-by=memory

# Per-container metrics:
kubectl top pods --containers

# Specific namespace, sorted:
kubectl top pods -n production --sort-by=memory
Explanation

Metrics Server collects CPU/memory metrics from kubelets. kubectl top requires Metrics Server to be installed. On the CKA, Metrics Server is usually pre-installed, but you should know how to verify. --sort-by=cpu or --sort-by=memory sorts the output — useful for finding resource-hungry pods. --containers shows per-container breakdown. In lab environments, --kubelet-insecure-tls is often needed.

Q4
How do you find the pod consuming the most CPU in a specific namespace?
Show Answer
Answer
sort by cpu usage (highest first)
# Sort by CPU usage (highest first):
kubectl top pods -n production --sort-by=cpu
# NAME          CPU(cores)  MEMORY(bytes)
# data-proc     950m        2Gi          ← Highest CPU!
# web-server    200m        512Mi
# api-gateway   150m        256Mi
# cache         50m         128Mi

# Sort by memory:
kubectl top pods -n production --sort-by=memory
# NAME          CPU(cores)  MEMORY(bytes)
# data-proc     950m        2Gi          ← Also highest memory!
# web-server    200m        512Mi

# All namespaces, top CPU consumers:
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu | head -10

# Per-container breakdown:
kubectl top pods -n production --containers --sort-by=cpu
# POD          CONTAINER    CPU(cores)  MEMORY(bytes)
# data-proc    worker       800m        1.5Gi
# data-proc    sidecar      150m        512Mi

# Node-level: which node is busiest?
kubectl top nodes --sort-by=cpu

# CKA tip: Redirect output to a file
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu > /opt/heavy-cpu.txt
# Or extract just the pod name:
kubectl top pods -n production --sort-by=cpu \
--no-headers | head -1 | awk '{print $1}' > /opt/answer.txt
# data-proc
Explanation

On the CKA, you'll be asked to find the highest resource consumer and write the answer to a file. kubectl top pods --sort-by=cpu sorts by CPU. Use --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{print $1}' to extract just the pod name. Common exam question: "find the pod using the most CPU in namespace X and write its name to /opt/answer.txt".

Q5
How do you view and filter Kubernetes events?
Show Answer
Answer
all events in current namespace
# All events in current namespace:
kubectl get events

# All events, sorted by time (most recent first):
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

# All events across all namespaces:
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

# Only Warning events (errors):
kubectl get events --field-selector type=Warning

# Events for a specific object:
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=web-pod
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=my-deploy

# Events by reason:
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=FailedScheduling
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=BackOff
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Killing

# Watch events in real time:
kubectl get events -w

# Custom output:
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp \
-o custom-columns=\
'TIME:.lastTimestamp,TYPE:.type,REASON:.reason,OBJECT:.involvedObject.name,MESSAGE:.message'

# Events in describe (per-object):
kubectl describe pod web-pod | tail -20
# Events section shows events specific to this pod

# Note: Events expire after ~1 hour by default
# (controlled by --event-ttl flag on kube-apiserver)
Explanation

Events record what's happening in the cluster. On the CKA: --sort-by=.lastTimestamp shows newest first, --field-selector type=Warning filters to only errors. Events expire after ~1 hour, so check them early during troubleshooting. kubectl describe also shows events for a specific resource. Use -w to watch events in real time while reproducing an issue.

Q6
How do you check resource requests and limits for all pods and compare with node capacity?
Show Answer
Answer
pod resource requests/limits
# Pod resource requests/limits:
kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=\
'NAME:.metadata.name,CPU_REQ:.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu,CPU_LIM:.spec.containers[0].resources.limits.cpu,MEM_REQ:.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.memory,MEM_LIM:.spec.containers[0].resources.limits.memory'
# NAME       CPU_REQ  CPU_LIM  MEM_REQ  MEM_LIM
# web-pod    100m     500m     128Mi    512Mi
# api-pod    250m     1        256Mi    1Gi

# Node capacity:
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A5 "Capacity"
# Capacity:
#   cpu:     4
#   memory:  8Gi

# Node allocatable (after system reservations):
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A5 "Allocatable"
# Allocatable:
#   cpu:     3800m
#   memory:  7500Mi

# What's allocated on the node:
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A10 "Allocated"
# Allocated resources:
#   CPU Requests  (Limits)    Memory Requests  (Limits)
#   1500m (39%)   3000m (78%) 2Gi (26%)        4Gi (53%)

# Available = Allocatable - Allocated
# CPU: 3800m - 1500m = 2300m free for scheduling
# Memory: 7500Mi - 2048Mi = 5452Mi free

# Actual usage vs requests (are pods using what they asked for?):
kubectl top pods
# Compare kubectl top (actual) vs requests (reserved)
Explanation

Three levels: Capacity (total), Allocatable (after reservations), Allocated (sum of requests). On the CKA: scheduling uses requests (not limits or actual usage). If a pod requests 500m CPU and the node only has 300m allocatable, it won't schedule. kubectl describe node shows all three levels. kubectl top shows actual real-time usage. Common pitfall: pods requesting more than they use wastes resources.

Q7
How do you redirect pod logs to a file for a CKA exam question?
Show Answer
Answer
basic: all logs to a file
# Basic: All logs to a file
kubectl logs web-pod > /opt/web-pod-logs.txt

# Specific container in multi-container pod:
kubectl logs web-pod -c nginx > /opt/nginx-logs.txt

# Only error lines:
kubectl logs web-pod | grep -i error > /opt/errors.txt
kubectl logs web-pod | grep -i "ERROR\|WARN" > /opt/issues.txt

# Last 100 lines to file:
kubectl logs web-pod --tail=100 > /opt/recent-logs.txt

# With timestamps:
kubectl logs web-pod --timestamps > /opt/timestamped.txt

# Previous crashed container:
kubectl logs web-pod --previous > /opt/crash-logs.txt

# Multiple pods by label:
kubectl logs -l app=web > /opt/all-web-logs.txt

# CKA common question patterns:
# "Write the logs of pod X to /opt/logs.txt"
kubectl logs web-pod > /opt/logs.txt

# "Write only error logs of pod X to /opt/errors.txt"
kubectl logs web-pod | grep -i error > /opt/errors.txt

# "Write the name of the pod with most restarts to /opt/answer.txt"
kubectl get pods --sort-by='.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount' \
--no-headers | tail -1 | awk '{print $1}' > /opt/answer.txt
Explanation

CKA exam frequently asks you to write output to specific files. Use > to redirect. Key patterns: kubectl logs pod > file, kubectl logs pod | grep error > file, kubectl top pods --sort-by=cpu --no-headers | head -1 | awk '{print $1}' > file. Always verify: cat /opt/answer.txt to confirm the content is correct. Use pipe + grep + awk for extracting specific values.

Q8
A cluster has multiple pods with high restart counts. How do you investigate?
Show Answer
Answer
find pods with high restart counts
# Step 1: Find pods with high restart counts
kubectl get pods -A --sort-by='.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount'
# Shows ascending — look at the bottom for highest

# Reverse sort trick (show highest first):
kubectl get pods -A --sort-by='.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount' \
-o custom-columns=\
'NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount,STATUS:.status.phase'
# NS        NAME         RESTARTS  STATUS
# default   crash-app    45        Running  ← Lots of restarts!
# prod      buggy-api    23        Running
# default   web-app      0         Running

# Step 2: Check WHY it's restarting
kubectl describe pod crash-app | grep -A5 "Last State"
# Last State:  Terminated
#   Reason:    OOMKilled    ← Memory issue
#   Exit Code: 137

# Step 3: Check recent restarts with events
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=crash-app \
--sort-by=.lastTimestamp

# Step 4: Check liveness probe
kubectl describe pod crash-app | grep -A5 Liveness
# If liveness probe fails → pod gets killed and restarted

# Common restart causes:
# OOMKilled (137) → Increase memory limit
# Exit Code 1     → App error, check logs --previous
# Liveness failed → Fix probe path/port/threshold
# Readiness fail  → Doesn't cause restart, but indicates issues
Explanation

Sort by restart count to find the most unstable pods. --sort-by='.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount' sorts ascending (highest at bottom). Check describe pod for "Last State: Terminated" with the reason. Top causes of restarts: OOMKilled (exit 137), liveness probe failures, and app errors (exit 1). Note: high restart count + Running status = the pod keeps crashing and recovering.

Q9
How do you monitor cluster-wide resource usage and identify capacity issues?
Show Answer
Answer
node-level overview
# Node-level overview:
kubectl top nodes
# NAME       CPU(cores)  CPU%  MEMORY(bytes)  MEMORY%
# master     250m        12%   1500Mi         75%
# worker-1   1800m       90%   6000Mi         80%  ← High!
# worker-2   100m        5%    400Mi          20%

# Identify overloaded node:
# worker-1 at 90% CPU and 80% memory → capacity issue!

# Check what's on the overloaded node:
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName=worker-1 \
-o custom-columns='NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,CPU:.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu'

# Check if pods are unevenly distributed:
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | awk '{print $8}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
#  15 worker-1    ← Too many pods!
#   3 worker-2
#   2 master

# Check node allocations:
for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o name); do
echo "=== $node ==="
kubectl describe $node | grep -A8 "Allocated resources"
done

# Check for resource quotas:
kubectl get resourcequotas -A

# Check for limit ranges:
kubectl get limitranges -A

# Quick cluster health:
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running | grep -v Completed
kubectl top nodes
kubectl get events -A --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | head -10
Explanation

kubectl top nodes gives CPU% and Memory% per node — look for nodes above 80%. Check pod distribution with -o wide and count per node. If pods are unevenly distributed, it might indicate affinity rules or the scheduler choosing based on available resources. describe node shows allocated vs allocatable, which tells you what the scheduler sees. ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges control resource usage at the namespace level.

Q10
How do you get logs from all pods matching a label selector?
Show Answer
Answer
logs from all pods with label app=web
# Logs from all pods with label app=web:
kubectl logs -l app=web
# (shows logs from up to 5 pods by default)

# Increase the limit:
kubectl logs -l app=web --max-log-requests=20

# All containers in matching pods:
kubectl logs -l app=web --all-containers=true

# Stream logs from all matching pods:
kubectl logs -l app=web -f --max-log-requests=10

# With prefix (shows pod name before each line):
kubectl logs -l app=web --prefix=true
# [pod/web-abc12/nginx] 10.0.0.1 - GET /api/health 200
# [pod/web-def34/nginx] 10.0.0.2 - GET /api/users 500 ← Error!

# Only last 10 lines from each:
kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=10

# Filter specific namespace:
kubectl logs -l app=web -n production

# Combine with grep:
kubectl logs -l app=web --all-containers | grep -i error

# Labels with multiple selectors:
kubectl logs -l app=web,tier=frontend

# CKA tip: When you need to check multiple replicas
# Use -l with --prefix to identify which pod has the error
Explanation

-l (label selector) with kubectl logs fetches logs from all matching pods at once. Default limit is 5 concurrent pods — increase with --max-log-requests. --prefix=true prepends the pod/container name to each line, making it easy to identify which pod generated each log entry. On the CKA, this is faster than checking pods one by one when a Deployment has multiple replicas.

34.1 Scenario Collection — 10 Must-Practice Scenarios

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

Each scenario presents a broken cluster state and walks you through the exact commands and thinking process to diagnose and fix it. These mirror real CKA exam tasks.

The 5-Step Troubleshooting Method

1
IDENTIFY

What's broken? kubectl get pods/nodes/svc — find the failing resource and its status.

2
GATHER

kubectl describe + kubectl logs — collect Events, conditions, and error messages.

3
ANALYZE

Read the error messages. Match symptoms to known causes. Narrow down root cause.

4
FIX

Apply the fix — edit YAML, restart service, add missing resource. Make ONE change at a time.

5
VERIFY

Confirm the fix worked. kubectl get + kubectl describe — status should be healthy.

Troubleshooting Priority Layers

🏗️
Infrastructure Layer

Nodes NotReady, kubelet down, etcd unhealthy, certificates expired, kubeconfig issues. Fix infrastructure first — nothing else works if the cluster is broken.

📦
Workload Layer

Pod Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, PVC not binding, resource limits. Most common exam tasks — fix pod/deployment configs.

🌐
Networking Layer

Service not accessible, DNS failing, NetworkPolicy blocking. Hardest to debug — check selectors, endpoints, kube-proxy, CoreDNS.

⏱️
CKA Time Strategy

Easy tasks first (2-3 min each), hard tasks last. Skip if stuck >8 minutes. Return to skipped tasks at the end. Never zero a question.

│  ├── Scenario 4:  CrashLoopBackOff            ███████░░░  Difficulty: 7/10  │
│  └── Scenario 9:  PVC Not Binding             ██████░░░░  Difficulty: 6/10  │
│                                                                              │
│  NETWORKING LAYER                                                            │
│  ├── Scenario 3:  Service Not Accessible      ███████░░░  Difficulty: 7/10  │
│  ├── Scenario 5:  DNS Resolution Failing      ████████░░  Difficulty: 8/10  │
│  └── Scenario 8:  Network Policy Blocking     ███████░░░  Difficulty: 7/10  │
│                                                                              │
│  💡 Practice order: 2 → 4 → 3 → 10 → 9 → 1 → 8 → 5 → 7 → 6              │
│     (easiest first, build confidence before the hard ones)                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Scenario 1: Worker Node NotReady

⚠️ Problem

kubectl get nodes shows worker01 NotReady. Pods on this node are being evicted.

🔴 Worker Node NotReady — Step-by-Step Walkthrough

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. IDENTIFY:                                                           │
│     $ kubectl get nodes                                                 │
│     NAME       STATUS     ROLES    AGE   VERSION                        │
│     master     Ready      master   30d   v1.31.0                        │
│     worker01   NotReady   <none>   30d   v1.31.0    ◄── PROBLEM        │
│     worker02   Ready      <none>   30d   v1.31.0                        │
│                                                                         │
│  2. GATHER — Describe the node:                                         │
│     $ kubectl describe node worker01                                    │
│     Conditions:                                                         │
│       Ready   False   KubeletNotReady   container runtime not running   │
│                                                                         │
│  3. ANALYZE — SSH to the node:                                          │
│     $ ssh worker01                                                      │
│     $ systemctl status kubelet                                          │
│     → Active: inactive (dead)    ◄── kubelet is not running!            │
│                                                                         │
│     $ systemctl status containerd                                       │
│     → Active: inactive (dead)    ◄── container runtime also down!       │
│                                                                         │
│  4. FIX — Restart services:                                             │
│     $ systemctl restart containerd                                      │
│     $ systemctl restart kubelet                                         │
│     $ systemctl enable kubelet    (ensure it starts on boot)            │
│                                                                         │
│  5. VERIFY — Back on the master:                                        │
│     $ kubectl get nodes                                                 │
│     worker01   Ready   <none>   30d   v1.31.0   ← ✅ Fixed!            │
│                                                                         │
│  ⚠️  OTHER COMMON CAUSES:                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐            │
│  │ • kubelet config wrong → /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   │            │
│  │ • swap enabled → swapoff -a                             │            │
│  │ • disk pressure → df -h (clear space)                   │            │
│  │ • CNI plugin missing → ls /etc/cni/net.d/               │            │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Scenario 2: Pod Stuck in Pending

⚠️ Problem

easypj-web pod in the easypj namespace is stuck in Pending state and won't schedule.

🟡 Pod Pending — Scheduling Failure Walkthrough

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. IDENTIFY:                                                           │
│     $ kubectl get pods -n easypj                                        │
│     NAME                 READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE               │
│     easypj-web-xxxx      0/1     Pending   0          5m                │
│                                                                         │
│  2. GATHER — Describe the pod (Events are KEY):                         │
│     $ kubectl describe pod easypj-web-xxxx -n easypj                    │
│     Events:                                                             │
│       Warning  FailedScheduling  0/3 nodes are available:               │
│         1 node(s) had taint {node-role.kubernetes.io/master: },    ◄──  │
│         that the pod didn't tolerate,                                   │
│         2 Insufficient cpu.                                        ◄──  │
│                                                                         │
│  3. ANALYZE — Two issues revealed:                                      │
│     a) Master node has taint → pod can't schedule there                 │
│     b) Worker nodes don't have enough CPU for the request               │
│                                                                         │
│  4. FIX — Reduce resource requests:                                     │
│     $ kubectl edit deployment easypj-web -n easypj                      │
│     resources:                                                          │
│       requests:                                                         │
│         cpu: "100m"       ← was "2000m", reduced to fit                 │
│         memory: "256Mi"                                                 │
│                                                                         │
│  5. VERIFY:                                                             │
│     $ kubectl get pods -n easypj -w                                     │
│     easypj-web-xxxx   1/1   Running   0   15s   ← ✅ Scheduled!        │
│                                                                         │
│  📋 COMMON PENDING CAUSES:                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┐           │
│  │ Event Message            │ Fix                           │           │
│  ├──────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤           │
│  │ Insufficient cpu/memory  │ Reduce requests or add nodes  │           │
│  │ pod didn't tolerate      │ Add toleration or remove taint│           │
│  │ no nodes match selector  │ Fix nodeSelector or label node│           │
│  │ PVC not found            │ Create the missing PVC        │           │
│  └──────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Scenario 3: Service Not Accessible

⚠️ Problem

Can't reach easypj via the NodePort service. Requests to http://<node-ip>:<nodeport> time out.

🔵 Service Not Accessible — Label Mismatch Walkthrough

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. IDENTIFY — Check the service:                                       │
│     $ kubectl get svc easypj-svc -n easypj                              │
│     NAME         TYPE       CLUSTER-IP    PORT(S)        AGE            │
│     easypj-svc   NodePort   10.96.45.12   80:30080/TCP   2h             │
│                                                                         │
│  2. GATHER — Check if endpoints exist:                                  │
│     $ kubectl get endpoints easypj-svc -n easypj                        │
│     NAME         ENDPOINTS   AGE                                        │
│     easypj-svc   <none>      2h   ◄── NO ENDPOINTS! Service has        │
│                                         no matching pods!               │
│                                                                         │
│  3. ANALYZE — Compare selector vs pod labels:                           │
│     $ kubectl get svc easypj-svc -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A3 selector │
│       selector:                                                         │
│         app: easypj-web       ◄── Service looks for this label          │
│                                                                         │
│     $ kubectl get pods -n easypj --show-labels                          │
│       easypj-web-xxxx   Running   app=easypj   ◄── Pod has THIS label  │
│                                                                         │
│     → MISMATCH! Service: "easypj-web" vs Pod: "easypj"                 │
│                                                                         │
│  4. FIX — Correct the service selector:                                 │
│     $ kubectl edit svc easypj-svc -n easypj                             │
│     selector:                                                           │
│       app: easypj         ← changed from "easypj-web" to "easypj"      │
│                                                                         │
│  5. VERIFY:                                                             │
│     $ kubectl get endpoints easypj-svc -n easypj                        │
│     ENDPOINTS: 10.244.1.5:8000   ← ✅ Pod is now connected!            │
│                                                                         │
│     $ curl http://<node-ip>:30080                                       │
│     → ✅ easypj responds!                                               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Scenario 4: CrashLoopBackOff

⚠️ Problem

easypj-db pod keeps crashing — restart count is climbing and backoff interval increasing.

🔴 CrashLoopBackOff — Missing Environment Variable

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. IDENTIFY:                                                           │
│     $ kubectl get pods -n easypj                                        │
│     NAME         READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE           │
│     easypj-db-0  0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   7 (3m ago)    15m           │
│                                                                         │
│  2. GATHER — Logs from the PREVIOUS crash:                              │
│     $ kubectl logs easypj-db-0 -n easypj --previous                     │
│                                                                         │
│     Error: Database is uninitialized and superuser password              │
│     is not specified. You must specify POSTGRES_PASSWORD to a    ◄──    │
│     non-empty value for the superuser.                                  │
│                                                                         │
│  3. ANALYZE — Check pod spec:                                           │
│     $ kubectl describe pod easypj-db-0 -n easypj                        │
│     Containers:                                                         │
│       postgres:                                                         │
│         Image: postgres:15                                              │
│         Environment: <none>    ◄── No env vars set! Missing            │
│                                    POSTGRES_PASSWORD                     │
│     Last State: Terminated (Exit Code 1)  ← App error                   │
│                                                                         │
│  4. FIX — Add the required env var via Secret:                          │
│     $ kubectl create secret generic db-creds \                          │
│         --from-literal=POSTGRES_PASSWORD=securepass123 -n easypj        │
│                                                                         │
│     Then patch the StatefulSet:                                          │
│     $ kubectl edit statefulset easypj-db -n easypj                       │
│     env:                                                                │
│     - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD                                           │
│       valueFrom:                                                        │
│         secretKeyRef:                                                   │
│           name: db-creds                                                │
│           key: POSTGRES_PASSWORD                                        │
│                                                                         │
│  5. VERIFY:                                                             │
│     $ kubectl get pods -n easypj -w                                     │
│     easypj-db-0   1/1   Running   0   20s   ← ✅ No more crashes!      │
│     $ kubectl logs easypj-db-0 -n easypj                                │
│     → "database system is ready to accept connections"                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Scenario 5: DNS Resolution Failing

⚠️ Problem

Pods can't resolve service names. easypj-web can't reach easypj-db by hostname.

🔴 DNS Failure — CoreDNS Troubleshooting

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. IDENTIFY — Test DNS from inside a pod:                              │
│     $ kubectl run dns-test --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=    │
│       Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default                              │
│     → ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached     ◄──     │
│                                                                         │
│  2. GATHER — Check CoreDNS pods:                                       │
│     $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns              │
│     NAME                       READY   STATUS             RESTARTS     │
│     coredns-5644d7b6d9-abc12   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   4            │
│     coredns-5644d7b6d9-def34   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   4            │
│                                                                         │
│  3. ANALYZE — Check CoreDNS logs:                                      │
│     $ kubectl logs -n kube-system coredns-5644d7b6d9-abc12              │
│     → plugin/forward: no nameservers found                              │
│                                                                         │
│     $ kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml                     │
│     → Corefile has forward . /etc/resolv.conf                           │
│     → But /etc/resolv.conf in the pod is empty or wrong                 │
│                                                                         │
│  4. FIX — Correct the CoreDNS ConfigMap:                               │
│     $ kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system                            │
│     forward . 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4    ← use specific DNS servers            │
│                                                                         │
│     $ kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system         │
│                                                                         │
│  5. VERIFY:                                                             │
│     $ kubectl run dns-test --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=    │
│       Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default                              │
│     Name:    kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local                       │
│     Address: 10.96.0.1   ← ✅ DNS is working!                          │
│                                                                         │
│  🔍 ALSO CHECK:                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐            │
│  │ • CoreDNS service IP:  kubectl get svc kube-dns         │            │
│  │   -n kube-system (must match pod's /etc/resolv.conf)    │            │
│  │ • Network plugin: is the CNI functional?                │            │
│  │ • Firewall rules blocking UDP port 53?                  │            │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Scenario 6: etcd Cluster Unhealthy

⚠️ Problem

API server is intermittently unavailable. kubectl commands sometimes time out. Suspected etcd issue.

🔴 etcd Unhealthy — Diagnosis and Recovery

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. IDENTIFY — Check etcd health:                                       │
│     $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health \                           │
│       --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \                              │
│       --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \                        │
│       --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \                      │
│       --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key                         │
│                                                                         │
│     https://127.0.0.1:2379 is unhealthy: failed to commit    ◄──       │
│                                                                         │
│  2. GATHER — Check etcd member list and logs:                           │
│     $ etcdctl member list (with same cert flags above)                  │
│     $ kubectl logs etcd-master -n kube-system                           │
│     OR if API is down:                                                  │
│     $ crictl logs $(crictl ps -a | grep etcd | awk '{print $1}')       │
│                                                                         │
│  3. ANALYZE — Common causes:                                           │
│     → Disk too slow (WAL write latency)                                 │
│     → Member removed/added incorrectly                                  │
│     → Data corruption                                                   │
│                                                                         │
│  4. FIX — If data corruption, restore from backup:                     │
│     a) Move API server manifest out to stop it:                         │
│        $ mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/         │
│                                                                         │
│     b) Restore etcd from snapshot:                                      │
│        $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/snapshot.db \   │
│          --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored                              │
│                                                                         │
│     c) Update etcd manifest with new data-dir:                          │
│        $ vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml                         │
│        → Change --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored                       │
│        → Update hostPath volume to /var/lib/etcd-restored               │
│                                                                         │
│     d) Move API server manifest back:                                   │
│        $ mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/         │
│                                                                         │
│  5. VERIFY:                                                             │
│     $ kubectl get nodes        ← API responds                          │
│     $ etcdctl endpoint health  ← etcd is healthy                       │
│     ✅ Cluster recovered!                                               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ CKA Gotcha: etcd Restore Flags

When restoring etcd, you must use a new data-dir path (--data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored). Don't restore in-place to /var/lib/etcd — it will fail if the existing data conflicts. Also update both the --data-dir flag AND the hostPath volume in the etcd static pod manifest.

Scenario 7: Certificates Expired

⚠️ Problem

kubectl commands fail with "Unable to connect to the server: x509: certificate has expired".

🔴 Certificates Expired — Renewal Walkthrough

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. IDENTIFY — Check certificate expiry:                                │
│     $ kubeadm certs check-expiration                                    │
│                                                                         │
│     CERTIFICATE                EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME   │
│     admin.conf                 Jan 15, 2024 09:30 UTC   expired    ◄── │
│     apiserver                  Jan 15, 2024 09:30 UTC   expired    ◄── │
│     apiserver-kubelet-client   Jan 15, 2024 09:30 UTC   expired        │
│     controller-manager.conf    Jan 15, 2024 09:30 UTC   expired        │
│     front-proxy-client         Jan 15, 2024 09:30 UTC   expired        │
│     scheduler.conf             Jan 15, 2024 09:30 UTC   expired        │
│                                                                         │
│  2. FIX — Renew all certificates:                                      │
│     $ kubeadm certs renew all                                           │
│                                                                         │
│     certificate embedded in admin.conf renewed                          │
│     certificate for serving the Kubernetes API renewed                  │
│     certificate for the API server to connect to kubelet renewed        │
│     ... (all renewed)                                                   │
│                                                                         │
│  3. RESTART — Control plane components:                                │
│     $ systemctl restart kubelet                                         │
│     (Static pods will automatically restart and pick up new certs)      │
│                                                                         │
│  4. UPDATE — kubeconfig with new certs:                                │
│     $ cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config                      │
│     $ chown $(id -u):$(id -g) ~/.kube/config                           │
│                                                                         │
│  5. VERIFY:                                                             │
│     $ kubectl get nodes                                                 │
│     → Should work without cert errors   ← ✅ Fixed!                    │
│                                                                         │
│     $ kubeadm certs check-expiration                                    │
│     → All certs show ~1 year residual time                              │
│                                                                         │
│  💡 PREVENTION: kubeadm auto-renews on control plane upgrade.          │
│     Set a calendar reminder before cert expiry!                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Scenario 8: Network Policy Blocking Traffic

⚠️ Problem

Frontend pods can't reach backend pods after a NetworkPolicy was applied. curl backend:80 from frontend times out.

🟠 Network Policy Blocking — Label Selector Fix

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. IDENTIFY — Confirm the connectivity issue:                          │
│     $ kubectl exec -n easypj frontend-pod -- curl -s --max-time 3      │
│       http://backend-svc:80                                             │
│     → curl: (28) Connection timed out   ◄── blocked!                   │
│                                                                         │
│  2. GATHER — List and inspect NetworkPolicies:                          │
│     $ kubectl get networkpolicy -n easypj                               │
│     NAME             POD-SELECTOR    AGE                                │
│     backend-policy   app=backend     10m                                │
│                                                                         │
│     $ kubectl describe netpol backend-policy -n easypj                  │
│     Spec:                                                               │
│       PodSelector:   app=backend                                        │
│       Allowing ingress traffic:                                         │
│         From:                                                           │
│           PodSelector: role=api       ◄── Only allows "role=api" pods  │
│       Policy Types: Ingress                                             │
│                                                                         │
│  3. ANALYZE — Check frontend pod labels:                               │
│     $ kubectl get pods -n easypj --show-labels                          │
│     frontend-pod   Running   app=frontend,tier=web   ◄── No "role=api" │
│                                                                         │
│     → The policy allows ingress from pods with "role=api"               │
│     → Frontend has "app=frontend,tier=web" — NO MATCH!                 │
│                                                                         │
│  4. FIX — Either add the label or update the policy:                   │
│     Option A: Add label to frontend pod                                 │
│     $ kubectl label pod frontend-pod -n easypj role=api                 │
│                                                                         │
│     Option B: Fix the NetworkPolicy selector                           │
│     $ kubectl edit netpol backend-policy -n easypj                      │
│     ingress:                                                            │
│     - from:                                                             │
│       - podSelector:                                                    │
│           matchLabels:                                                  │
│             app: frontend      ← match actual frontend labels          │
│                                                                         │
│  5. VERIFY:                                                             │
│     $ kubectl exec -n easypj frontend-pod -- curl -s --max-time 3      │
│       http://backend-svc:80                                             │
│     → ✅ Response received! Traffic is flowing.                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Scenario 9: PVC Not Binding

⚠️ Problem

easypj-db PVC is stuck in Pending state. The database pod can't start without its volume.

🟡 PVC Not Binding — StorageClass Mismatch

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. IDENTIFY:                                                           │
│     $ kubectl get pvc -n easypj                                         │
│     NAME          STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   STORAGECLASS   AGE      │
│     easypj-data   Pending                       fast-ssd       10m ◄── │
│                                                                         │
│  2. GATHER — Describe PVC for events:                                  │
│     $ kubectl describe pvc easypj-data -n easypj                        │
│     Events:                                                             │
│       Warning  ProvisioningFailed  no persistent volumes available      │
│       for this claim and no storage class "fast-ssd" found     ◄──     │
│                                                                         │
│  3. ANALYZE — Check available storage classes and PVs:                 │
│     $ kubectl get storageclass                                          │
│     NAME              PROVISIONER          RECLAIMPOLICY               │
│     standard (def.)   rancher.io/local     Delete                      │
│     → "fast-ssd" doesn't exist! PVC asks for a non-existent class     │
│                                                                         │
│     $ kubectl get pv                                                    │
│     NAME     CAPACITY   ACCESS   RECLAIM   STATUS      STORAGECLASS    │
│     pv-01    10Gi       RWO      Retain    Available   standard        │
│     → PV exists but with "standard" class, not "fast-ssd"             │
│                                                                         │
│  4. FIX — Option A: Change PVC to use "standard":                      │
│     (PVC storageClassName is immutable — recreate it)                   │
│     $ kubectl delete pvc easypj-data -n easypj                          │
│     $ cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -                                    │
│     apiVersion: v1                                                      │
│     kind: PersistentVolumeClaim                                         │
│     metadata:                                                           │
│       name: easypj-data                                                 │
│       namespace: easypj                                                 │
│     spec:                                                               │
│       accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]                                    │
│       storageClassName: standard                                        │
│       resources:                                                        │
│         requests:                                                       │
│           storage: 5Gi                                                  │
│     EOF                                                                 │
│                                                                         │
│  5. VERIFY:                                                             │
│     $ kubectl get pvc -n easypj                                         │
│     easypj-data   Bound   pv-01   10Gi   RWO   standard   ← ✅ Bound! │
│                                                                         │
│  💡 "WaitForFirstConsumer" is NOT an error — PV binds only when        │
│     a pod actually mounts the PVC. This is normal behavior.            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Scenario 10: kubeconfig Issues

⚠️ Problem

kubectl can't connect to the cluster: "The connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused".

🟠 kubeconfig Issues — Connection Diagnosis

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. IDENTIFY — Check current config:                                    │
│     $ kubectl config current-context                                    │
│     error: current-context is not set   ◄── no context configured!     │
│                                                                         │
│     $ kubectl config view                                               │
│     apiVersion: v1                                                      │
│     clusters: null                                                      │
│     contexts: null       ◄── kubeconfig is empty/wrong                 │
│                                                                         │
│  2. GATHER — Check where kubectl looks for config:                     │
│     $ echo $KUBECONFIG                                                  │
│     → empty (uses default ~/.kube/config)                               │
│                                                                         │
│     $ ls -la ~/.kube/config                                             │
│     → No such file or directory   ◄── config file is missing!          │
│                                                                         │
│  3. ANALYZE — The kubeconfig wasn't copied after cluster setup.        │
│     On a kubeadm cluster, the admin config is on the master node.       │
│                                                                         │
│  4. FIX — Copy the kubeconfig from the master:                         │
│     $ mkdir -p ~/.kube                                                  │
│     $ cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config                      │
│     $ chown $(id -u):$(id -g) ~/.kube/config                           │
│                                                                         │
│     If on a different machine, SCP from master:                         │
│     $ scp master:/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config              │
│                                                                         │
│  5. VERIFY:                                                             │
│     $ kubectl cluster-info                                              │
│     Kubernetes control plane is running at https://10.0.0.10:6443       │
│     CoreDNS is running at https://10.0.0.10:6443/api/v1/...            │
│                                                                         │
│     $ kubectl get nodes                                                 │
│     → All nodes listed   ← ✅ Connected!                               │
│                                                                         │
│  📋 OTHER KUBECONFIG ISSUES:                                            │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐         │
│  │ Symptom                      │ Fix                         │         │
│  ├──────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤         │
│  │ Wrong context active         │ kubectl config use-context  │         │
│  │ Wrong server URL             │ Edit server: in config      │         │
│  │ KUBECONFIG env overriding    │ unset KUBECONFIG            │         │
│  │ Permission denied            │ chown the config file       │         │
│  └──────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🏋️ Practice Drill: Time Yourself on All 10 Scenarios

Set up a practice cluster (kubeadm or kind). Intentionally break it in each of these 10 ways, then fix it. Target: solve each scenario in under 5 minutes. On the CKA exam, speed matters.

  1. Stop kubelet on a worker node → diagnose and fix NotReady
  2. Set impossible resource requests → fix Pending pod
  3. Mismatch service selector → fix endpoints
  4. Remove required env var → fix CrashLoopBackOff
  5. Break CoreDNS config → fix DNS resolution
  6. Corrupt etcd data → restore from snapshot
  7. Let certs expire (kubeadm certs) → renew and recover
  8. Apply overly restrictive NetworkPolicy → fix traffic flow
  9. Create PVC with wrong StorageClass → fix binding
  10. Delete kubeconfig → recreate from admin.conf

Symptom → First Response Quick-Reference

Symptom You See Most Likely Cause First Command to Run Scenario #
Node NotReady kubelet stopped / misconfigured ssh <node>; systemctl status kubelet #1
Pod Pending Insufficient resources / node affinity kubectl describe pod <name> → Events #2
Service returns no response Selector mismatch / wrong port kubectl get endpoints <svc> #3
CrashLoopBackOff Missing config / bad entrypoint kubectl logs <pod> --previous #4
DNS not resolving CoreDNS crash / bad ConfigMap kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns #5
API server errors / cluster unstable etcd unhealthy or data loss etcdctl endpoint health (with certs) #6
x509: certificate has expired Cluster certificates expired kubeadm certs check-expiration #7
Pod-to-pod traffic blocked NetworkPolicy too restrictive kubectl get netpol -A #8
PVC Pending StorageClass mismatch / no provisioner kubectl get sc + kubectl describe pvc #9
connection refused from kubectl kubeconfig missing or corrupted ls -la ~/.kube/config #10
⚠️ Common Gotcha: Multiple Symptoms, One Root Cause

On the CKA exam, a single failure (e.g., kubelet down) can produce many symptoms at once — Pods in Terminating state, Services returning errors, DNS failing. Always start at the infrastructure layer (nodes → control plane → workloads) and work upward. Fixing the root cause often resolves several visible symptoms simultaneously.

Essential Troubleshooting Commands — Quick Reference

💡 Part 9 Key Takeaways
  • Troubleshooting flow: kubectl get → describe → logs → exec → events. ALWAYS follow this order.
  • Pod statuses: CrashLoopBackOff (app crashes), ImagePullBackOff (wrong image/tag), Pending (no node/resources), Error (exit non-zero)
  • Node troubleshooting: Check kubelet (systemctl status), certificates (kubeadm certs), connectivity
  • Control plane down? Check static pod manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and kubelet logs
  • 5-step method: IDENTIFY → GATHER → ANALYZE → FIX → VERIFY — never skip VERIFY!
  • Use --previous to see logs from crashed containers. Use -f to follow logs in real-time.
  • CKA weight: 30% — the heaviest domain! Practice every scenario until you can solve it in under 5 minutes.
✅ Part 9 Competency Checklist
  • Can you debug a CrashLoopBackOff pod in under 3 minutes?
  • Can you diagnose a NotReady node and bring it back?
  • Can you restore etcd from a snapshot backup?
  • Can you fix a broken service with no endpoints?
  • Can you troubleshoot DNS failure by inspecting CoreDNS?
  • Can you renew expired certificates and restore API access?
  • Can you identify and fix NetworkPolicy blocking traffic?
  • Do you follow IDENTIFY → GATHER → ANALYZE → FIX → VERIFY every time?

🔥

Multi-Issue Scenario: "Application Not Reachable"

ADVANCED

Situation: A 3-tier app (frontend → backend → database) reports "Connection refused" from outside the cluster. Multiple things are broken.

Layer 1 — Infrastructure

Run kubectl get nodes. Worker node is NotReady. SSH in, find kubelet stopped → systemctl start kubelet. Node recovers. Pods reschedule.

Layer 2 — Workload

Backend pod is CrashLoopBackOff. kubectl logs backend --previous shows missing DB_HOST env var. Fix: add envFrom referencing the ConfigMap. Pod starts.

Layer 3 — Networking

Frontend Service has no Endpoints. kubectl get endpoints frontend-svc → empty. Selector says app: front but pod label is app: frontend. Fix selector → endpoints populate → app reachable.

Lesson: On the CKA, one question can have 2-3 issues across different layers. Always re-verify the whole stack after each fix. Don't stop at the first symptom.
Under the Hood — How Multi-Layer Troubleshooting Scenarios Work: The Systematic Debugging Methodology, Dependency Chain Analysis, and the CKA Troubleshooting Mindset
🗺️ The CKA Troubleshooting Methodology — Systematic Root Cause Analysis

Complex CKA scenarios involve multiple failing components. The key is a systematic top-down approach that isolates the root cause layer by layer.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SYSTEMATIC TROUBLESHOOTING METHODOLOGY                                       │
│                                                                              │
│  LAYER MODEL (debug from top down):                                           │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ LAYER 1: APPLICATION (logs, exit codes, probes)                       │   │
│  │   └── LAYER 2: POD (status, events, describe, resource usage)         │   │
│  │       └── LAYER 3: CONTROLLER (Deployment/RS/DaemonSet status)        │   │
│  │           └── LAYER 4: SERVICE/NETWORK (endpoints, DNS, NetworkPolicy)│   │
│  │               └── LAYER 5: NODE (kubelet, containerd, disk, memory)   │   │
│  │                   └── LAYER 6: CONTROL PLANE (API, etcd, scheduler)   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  SCENARIO: "Deployment is running but unreachable"                           │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. APP: kubectl logs → app listening on correct port? ✅              │   │
│  │ 2. POD: kubectl describe → probes passing? ready? ✅                  │   │
│  │ 3. CONTROLLER: kubectl get deploy,rs → desired=ready? ✅              │   │
│  │ 4. SERVICE: kubectl get svc → selector matches pod labels?           │   │
│  │    kubectl get endpoints → ENDPOINTS is <none>? ❌                   │   │
│  │    → Service selector doesn't match pod labels!                      │   │
│  │    → Fix: update Service selector or pod labels                      │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ 5. VERIFY: curl <svc-ip>:<port> → works now ✅                       │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  DEPENDENCY CHAIN ANALYSIS — Finding the Root Cause:                         │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ When multiple things are broken, find the DEPENDENCY that broke first│   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  Chain: DNS down → Services unreachable → Pods can't talk → app dead  │   │
│  │  ROOT CAUSE: CoreDNS pods crashed (check kube-system)                 │   │
│  │  FIX: Restart CoreDNS → everything recovers                            │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  Chain: Node disk full → kubelet can't write → node NotReady           │   │
│  │  → pods evicted → Deployment shows fewer replicas                      │   │
│  │  ROOT CAUSE: DiskPressure on node (check df -h)                       │   │
│  │  FIX: Clean disk → node recovers                                       │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  CKA TROUBLESHOOTING MINDSET — Rules for the Exam:                           │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. ALWAYS check namespace first: -n <ns> (most common mistake)       │   │
│  │ 2. ALWAYS check context: kubectl config current-context               │   │
│  │ 3. DESCRIBE before LOGS: describe gives events + state; logs gives    │   │
│  │    application-level details                                          │   │
│  │ 4. CHECK EVENTS: kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp          │   │
│  │ 5. WHEN STUCK: Move up one layer. Pod broken? Check node. Node        │   │
│  │    broken? Check kubelet. Kubelet broken? Check disk/containerd.      │   │
│  │ 6. VERIFY AFTER FIXING: Don't assume. Run a test command.             │   │
│  │ 7. ONE FIX AT A TIME: Fix one thing, verify, then fix the next.       │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CKA Insight: Troubleshooting is 30% of the CKA — the largest single domain. Exam questions often have 2-3 cascading failures. Fix the ROOT CAUSE first (not the symptoms). Common root causes: wrong namespace, wrong context, label mismatch, missing ConfigMap/Secret, insufficient resources, expired certs. After every fix, verify with a test command before moving on. Don't fix-and-forget.

🔑 Key Takeaways

Bulleted key takeaways go here.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions

When restoring etcd, you must use a new data-dir path (--data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored). Don't restore in-place to /var/lib/etcd — it will fail if the existing data conflicts. Also update both the --data-dir flag AND the hostPath volume in the etcd static pod manifest.

  • Always VERIFY after fixing — The exam checks the end state. If you fix a broken service but don't verify with curl or kubectl get endpoints, you might have missed something. Follow the 5-step method: IDENTIFY → GATHER → ANALYZE → FIX → VERIFY
  • Multiple issues per question — A single scenario may have 2-3 things broken (wrong label + wrong port + missing service). Fix one, test, then check for more. Don't assume one fix solves everything
  • Read the question TWICE — "Ensure the pod runs on node01" could mean nodeSelector, nodeName, or taint toleration. "Fix the deployment" could mean image, resources, selectors, or mount issues. Misreading costs 5-10 minutes
  • Use kubectl explain as your API reference — kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources --recursive. Faster than searching docs. Works offline (exam environment)
  • Time management — 17 questions in 2 hours = ~7 min per question. If stuck for 10 minutes, flag it and move on. Come back with fresh eyes. Easy questions first
⚡ Speed Tips

CKA Speed Tip — Troubleshooting decision tree:
Pod not running? → kubectl describe pod → check Events
Service not reachable? → kubectl get endpoints → if empty, fix selector
Node NotReady? → SSH + systemctl status kubelet + journalctl -u kubelet
API server down? → Check /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
DNS broken? → kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns

⚙️ Chapter 34 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Multi-layer troubleshooting recall — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
A Deployment's pods are running but the Service returns no response. Walk through the troubleshooting methodology.
Show Answer
Answer
systematic 5-step approach
# Systematic 5-step approach:

# Step 1: Check pods are running and ready
kubectl get pods -l app=web
# NAME        READY  STATUS   RESTARTS
# web-abc12   1/1    Running  0        ← Looks good

# Step 2: Check Service exists and has correct selector
kubectl get svc web-svc
kubectl describe svc web-svc
# Selector: app=web
# Port:     80/TCP
# TargetPort: 8080

# Step 3: Check Endpoints (MOST CRITICAL STEP)
kubectl get endpoints web-svc
# NAME      ENDPOINTS
# web-svc   <none>     ← NO ENDPOINTS! Selector mismatch!

# Step 4: Compare selector with pod labels
kubectl get pods --show-labels
# NAME        LABELS
# web-abc12   app=webapp    ← "webapp" not "web"!

# Step 5: Fix the selector
kubectl edit svc web-svc
# Change selector from app: web → app: webapp

# OR fix the pod labels:
kubectl label pod web-abc12 app=web --overwrite

# Verify:
kubectl get endpoints web-svc
# web-svc   10.244.1.5:8080   ← Endpoints populated!

# Test:
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- web-svc
# <html>...</html> ✓
Explanation

The #1 CKA troubleshooting pattern: Service → Endpoints → Pods. If Endpoints shows <none>, the Service selector doesn't match any pod labels. Always: (1) check pods are Running+Ready, (2) check Service selector, (3) check Endpoints, (4) compare labels, (5) fix. This scenario appears in almost every CKA exam. The targetPort (container port) must match what the app listens on.

Q2
A Deployment isn't rolling out new pods after an image update. What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer
check rollout status
# Check rollout status:
kubectl rollout status deployment web
# Waiting for deployment "web" rollout to finish:
# 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
# ← Stuck! New pods aren't becoming ready

# Check the new ReplicaSet:
kubectl get rs
# NAME          DESIRED  CURRENT  READY
# web-abc123    3        3        3     ← OLD (still running)
# web-def456    1        1        0     ← NEW (0 ready!)

# Check the new pod:
kubectl get pods | grep web-def456
# web-def456-xyz   0/1   ImagePullBackOff   0   2m

# Root cause: Wrong image name
kubectl describe pod web-def456-xyz | grep Image
# Image: nginxx:latest  ← Typo! "nginxx"

# Fix:
kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:latest
# OR
kubectl rollout undo deployment web

# If rollout was paused:
kubectl rollout status deployment web
# "deployment is paused" ← Someone paused it!
kubectl rollout resume deployment web

# If maxUnavailable=0 and cluster is at capacity:
# New pod can't schedule → old pod can't terminate → deadlock
# Fix: Increase maxSurge or reduce replicas temporarily

# Verify:
kubectl rollout status deployment web
# deployment "web" successfully rolled out ✓
Explanation

Stuck rollouts happen when new pods can't become Ready. Common causes: (1) wrong image name/tag (ImagePullBackOff), (2) readiness probe fails, (3) resource constraints, (4) rollout paused. On the CKA: check `kubectl rollout status`, then check the new ReplicaSet's pods. kubectl rollout undo is the fastest way to revert. Deadlock scenario: maxUnavailable=0 + maxSurge=0 = can't add new or remove old pods.

Q3
DNS resolution isn't working inside pods. How do you debug?
Show Answer
Answer
test dns from inside a pod
# Step 1: Test DNS from inside a pod
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup kubernetes
# Server:    10.96.0.10
# nslookup: can't resolve 'kubernetes'  ← DNS broken!

# Step 2: Check CoreDNS pods
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
# NAME                      READY  STATUS
# coredns-5d78c9869d-abc12  0/1    CrashLoopBackOff  ← Problem!

# Step 3: Check CoreDNS logs
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns

# Step 4: Check CoreDNS ConfigMap
kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml
# Look for syntax errors in Corefile

# Step 5: Check kube-dns Service
kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system
# Should be ClusterIP 10.96.0.10

# Step 6: Check pod DNS config
kubectl exec dns-test -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# nameserver 10.96.0.10     ← Should point to kube-dns
# search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local

# Common fixes:
# CoreDNS crash → Check ConfigMap for syntax errors
# Wrong nameserver → Check kubelet --cluster-dns flag
# Loop detected → Remove "loop" plugin from Corefile
# Upstream DNS → Check forward . directive in Corefile

# Fix CoreDNS ConfigMap:
kubectl edit configmap coredns -n kube-system
# Then restart:
kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system
Explanation

DNS is CoreDNS running in kube-system. Pods get the DNS IP (10.96.0.10) from kubelet config. On the CKA: test with nslookup kubernetes, check CoreDNS pods, check the Corefile ConfigMap. Common issue: loop detection plugin causes crashes on some setups — fix by editing the ConfigMap. The kube-dns Service name is kept for backward compatibility, but it routes to CoreDNS pods.

Q4
A user reports they can't create pods in a namespace. How do you check RBAC permissions?
Show Answer
Answer
check what the user can do
# Step 1: Check what the user CAN do
kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev --as=user1
# no  ← User can't create pods!

# Step 2: Check all permissions for the user
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=user1 -n dev
# Resources  Verbs
# (nothing relevant)  ← No roles bound!

# Step 3: Check existing RoleBindings
kubectl get rolebindings -n dev
# NAME       ROLE              SUBJECTS
# (empty)    ← No bindings!

# Step 4: Check ClusterRoleBindings
kubectl get clusterrolebindings | grep user1
# (nothing)

# Step 5: Create the necessary RBAC
# Option A: Create Role + RoleBinding
kubectl create role pod-manager -n dev \
--verb=create,get,list,delete \
--resource=pods

kubectl create rolebinding user1-pods -n dev \
--role=pod-manager \
--user=user1

# Option B: Use existing ClusterRole
kubectl create rolebinding user1-edit -n dev \
--clusterrole=edit \
--user=user1

# Step 6: Verify
kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev --as=user1
# yes ✓

# Debug: Check which role is blocking
kubectl auth can-i create pods -n dev --as=user1 -v=5
# Shows API calls and authorization decisions
Explanation

kubectl auth can-i tests permissions. --as=user1 impersonates the user. --list shows all allowed actions. On the CKA: if a user can't do something, check RoleBindings in the namespace and ClusterRoleBindings. The fix is creating a Role + RoleBinding. Built-in ClusterRoles (view, edit, admin, cluster-admin) save time. -v=5 shows verbose authorization debugging.

Q5
A NetworkPolicy is blocking expected traffic. How do you debug it?
Show Answer
Answer
symptom: pod a can't reach pod b
# Symptom: Pod A can't reach Pod B, but it worked before

# Step 1: Check NetworkPolicies in the namespace
kubectl get networkpolicies -n prod
# NAME           POD-SELECTOR  AGE
# deny-all       app=api       5m   ← Recently created!
# allow-web      app=web       30d

# Step 2: Examine the blocking policy
kubectl describe networkpolicy deny-all -n prod
# PodSelector: app=api
# Allowing ingress traffic: <none>   ← Blocks ALL ingress!
# Allowing egress traffic:  <none>   ← Blocks ALL egress!

# Step 3: Verify traffic is actually blocked
kubectl exec -n prod web-pod -- curl -s --max-time 3 api-svc:8080
# curl: (28) Connection timed out  ← Blocked!

# Step 4: Fix — Add allow rule for needed traffic
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
name: allow-web-to-api
namespace: prod
spec:
podSelector:
matchLabels:
  app: api
policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
ingress:
- from:
- podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
ports:
- port: 8080

# Step 5: Verify
kubectl exec -n prod web-pod -- curl -s api-svc:8080
# {"status": "ok"} ✓

# Key rules:
# - If ANY NetworkPolicy selects a pod, only allowed traffic works
# - No NetworkPolicy = all traffic allowed
# - Multiple policies are ADDITIVE (union of all allow rules)
Explanation

NetworkPolicies are default-deny once applied. If a pod has ANY NetworkPolicy selecting it, only explicitly allowed traffic passes. On the CKA: check which policies select the target pod (via podSelector), verify with curl/wget from source pod, then add an allow rule if needed. Multiple NetworkPolicies are additive — the union of all rules determines what's allowed. Common trap: creating a deny-all without corresponding allow rules.

Q6
You have 5 minutes left on the CKA exam and 3 questions remaining. What's your strategy?
Show Answer
Answer
Strategy Action
Triage Check weights — do highest % question first
Imperative First Use kubectl run/create/expose not YAML
Skip Stuck If stuck >60s, flag and move on
Partial Credit Create the resource even if incomplete — partial credit exists
Context! Always check kubectl config use-context — wrong context = 0 points
speed aliases (should already be set)
# Speed aliases (should already be set):
export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"
export now="--force --grace-period 0"

# Fast pod creation:
k run web --image=nginx --port=80 $do > pod.yaml
vi pod.yaml  # Quick edit
k apply -f pod.yaml

# Fast service:
k expose pod web --port=80 --target-port=80

# Fast delete and recreate:
k delete pod broken $now
k run broken --image=nginx
Explanation

Time management is critical on the CKA. With 5 minutes left: (1) do the highest-weight question, (2) use imperative commands exclusively, (3) don't debug — create from scratch if faster, (4) always verify the context with kubectl config use-context. Partial credit exists, so creating an incomplete resource is better than skipping entirely. The $do and $now variables save significant time.

Q7
A pod can't resolve an external domain (e.g., google.com) but can resolve cluster services. What's the issue?
Show Answer
Answer
verify internal dns works
# Step 1: Verify internal DNS works
kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup kubernetes.default
# Name:   kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
# Address: 10.96.0.1  ← Internal DNS works!

# Step 2: Test external DNS
kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup google.com
# ** server can't find google.com: SERVFAIL ← External fails!

# Step 3: Check CoreDNS forward config
kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml
# Corefile:
#   .:53 {
#     forward . /etc/resolv.conf    ← Should forward to upstream DNS
#   }

# Step 4: Check the node's /etc/resolv.conf
# CoreDNS forwards external queries to the node's DNS
ssh worker-1
cat /etc/resolv.conf
# nameserver 127.0.0.53  ← systemd-resolved (might cause loops!)

# Step 5: Fix — Point CoreDNS to a real DNS server
kubectl edit configmap coredns -n kube-system
# Change: forward . /etc/resolv.conf
# To:     forward . 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4

# Step 6: Restart CoreDNS
kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system

# Step 7: Verify
kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup google.com
# Name:   google.com
# Address: 142.250.80.46 ✓

# Alternative: Check NetworkPolicy blocking DNS egress
kubectl get networkpolicies -n <namespace>
# If egress restricted, must allow UDP port 53 to kube-dns
Explanation

Internal DNS works (CoreDNS resolves .cluster.local) but external fails = upstream DNS forwarding issue. CoreDNS forwards external queries using the forward directive. If the node uses systemd-resolved (127.0.0.53), CoreDNS may loop. Fix by pointing to real upstream DNS (8.8.8.8). Also check NetworkPolicies — if egress is restricted, UDP port 53 to kube-dns must be explicitly allowed.

Q8
You need to fix a broken cluster where kubectl commands timeout. Where do you start?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl timeout = api server unreachable
# kubectl timeout = API server unreachable

# Step 1: SSH to the master node
ssh master

# Step 2: Check kubelet (manages static pods)
systemctl status kubelet
# If stopped → systemctl start kubelet

# Step 3: Check API server container
crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver
# If not listed → Check static pod manifest

# Step 4: Check API server manifest
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Look for:
# - Wrong image
# - Wrong port
# - Missing/wrong cert paths
# - Syntax errors

# Step 5: Check API server logs
crictl logs $(crictl ps -a | grep apiserver | awk '{print $1}')
# OR
journalctl -u kubelet | grep apiserver

# Step 6: Check etcd (API server depends on it)
crictl ps | grep etcd
# If etcd is down → API server can't work
# Check: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml

# Step 7: Check certificates
openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -dates
# notAfter=... ← Expired?

# Fix sequence:
# 1. Fix manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# 2. kubelet auto-restarts static pods
# 3. Wait 30-60 seconds
# 4. Test: kubectl get nodes

# Common CKA causes:
# - Wrong port in kube-apiserver.yaml
# - Cert file path typo
# - etcd endpoint wrong
# - Image tag wrong
Explanation

kubectl timeout = API server down. On the CKA: SSH to master, use crictl (not kubectl!), check kubelet, check static pod manifests. API server is a static pod managed by kubelet. Common exam scenario: a deliberate error is placed in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Fix the manifest → kubelet detects the change → API server restarts. Check etcd too — if etcd is down, API server won't work even if its config is correct.

Q9
How do you use kubectl explain to quickly find the correct YAML field paths during the exam?
Show Answer
Answer
basic: what fields does a pod spec have?
# Basic: What fields does a Pod spec have?
kubectl explain pod.spec
# Lists all fields with descriptions

# Recursive: ALL nested fields
kubectl explain pod.spec --recursive
# Shows the full tree without descriptions
# Perfect for finding the exact path

# Specific field:
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources
# Shows: limits, requests sub-fields

# Common exam lookups:
kubectl explain pod.spec.volumes --recursive
# Shows all volume types and their fields

kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.volumeMounts
# mountPath, name, subPath, readOnly

kubectl explain pod.spec.tolerations
# effect, key, operator, tolerationSeconds, value

kubectl explain pod.spec.affinity --recursive
# nodeAffinity, podAffinity, podAntiAffinity

kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy
# type, rollingUpdate (maxSurge, maxUnavailable)

kubectl explain pv.spec --recursive
# All PV fields: capacity, accessModes, hostPath, nfs...

# CKA shortcut: Use with aliases
alias kx="kubectl explain"
kx pod.spec.securityContext --recursive
kx pod.spec.initContainers

# Can't remember the field name? Use recursive + grep:
kubectl explain pod.spec --recursive | grep -i "toleration"
#   tolerations  <[]Toleration>
Explanation

kubectl explain is your built-in documentation during the CKA — it's faster than searching docs. --recursive shows the full field tree. Use it when you can't remember the exact YAML path (e.g., "is it spec.containers.resources.limits or spec.resources.limits?"). grep with recursive output helps find field names. On the CKA, alias it as kx for speed.

Q10
A multi-issue scenario: pods are Pending, a Service has no endpoints, and a node is NotReady. Solve it systematically.
Show Answer
Answer
multi-issue diagnosis order
# Multi-issue diagnosis order: Infrastructure → Workloads → Networking

# PHASE 1: FIX INFRASTRUCTURE (Node)
kubectl get nodes
# NAME       STATUS     ROLES          AGE
# master     Ready      control-plane  30d
# worker-1   NotReady   <none>         30d  ← Fix this first!

ssh worker-1
systemctl status kubelet
# Active: inactive (dead)
systemctl start kubelet
systemctl enable kubelet
exit
# Wait: kubectl get nodes → worker-1 Ready ✓

# PHASE 2: FIX WORKLOADS (Pending Pods)
kubectl get pods
# NAME       READY  STATUS   RESTARTS
# web-abc    0/1    Pending  0
kubectl describe pod web-abc | tail -10
# "0/1 nodes available: 1 node had taint {NoSchedule}"
# (Before we fixed the node, no node was available)
# After node fix → pod auto-schedules!
kubectl get pods  # web-abc → Running ✓

# PHASE 3: FIX NETWORKING (Service)
kubectl get endpoints web-svc
# web-svc   <none>  ← Still no endpoints!

kubectl get svc web-svc -o yaml | grep -A2 selector
# selector:
#   app: website      ← Wrong label!

kubectl get pods --show-labels
# web-abc   app=web   ← Label is "web" not "website"

kubectl patch svc web-svc -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"web"}}}'
kubectl get endpoints web-svc
# web-svc   10.244.1.5:80 ✓

# VERIFY ALL:
kubectl get nodes        # All Ready ✓
kubectl get pods         # All Running ✓
kubectl get endpoints    # All populated ✓
Explanation

Multi-issue scenarios test your ability to prioritize. Fix order: Infrastructure (nodes) → Workloads (pods) → Networking (services). Fixing the node first often auto-resolves the Pending pods (they were waiting for a schedulable node). Then fix the Service selector to populate endpoints. On the CKA, issues are often cascading — one root cause creates multiple symptoms. Fix the root cause first and check if downstream issues self-resolve before spending time on them.
