🔴 Part 9 · Recap · Complete

Troubleshooting — What You Now Know

You can now run a disciplined fault-finding loop across the whole stack: pods (status → events → logs), nodes and the control plane (NotReady, crictl/journalctl, static-pod manifests), logs and metrics, and the Service/DNS/NetworkPolicy playbook. This is the CKA’s single biggest domain — 30%.

🔑 🔴 Part 9 — Key Takeaways

  • Pods (Ch 31): read STATUS (Pending/ImagePullBackOff/CrashLoopBackOff/OOMKilled) → describe Events → logs (+--previous) → exec/debug. Status names the cause.
  • Nodes & control plane (Ch 32): NotReady → check kubelet (journalctl -u kubelet) and the CNI; when kubectl is down, use crictl ps/logs and inspect /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.
  • Logs & metrics (Ch 33): kubectl logs, node/pod kubectl top (needs metrics-server), and Events are your evidence; there’s no built-in log aggregation.
  • Scenario playbook (Ch 34): Service has no endpoints (selector mismatch), DNS fails (CoreDNS), traffic blocked (NetworkPolicy/kube-proxy) — a fixed symptom → command → cause → fix routine.
  • 🎯 Exam: 30% lives here — it’s the largest domain; speed and a methodical loop win the most marks.
📌 Part 9 Visual Summary — the symptom → command → cause → fix loop
   🔎 SYMPTOM ──▶ 🧪 COMMAND ──▶ 🧠 CAUSE ──▶ 🔧 FIX ──▶ ✅ VERIFY
   pod:  get → describe(Events) → logs --previous → exec/debug
   node: get nodes → journalctl -u kubelet → crictl ps/logs → manifests
   net:  endpoints? → CoreDNS? → NetworkPolicy/kube-proxy?
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   a repeatable loop turns "broken easypj" into a fixed, verified task.

In words: Part 9 gave you a method. Every failure follows symptom → command → cause → fix → verify: a pod’s status and events name the problem, a node’s kubelet/crictl/journalctl reveal a NotReady cause, and the networking playbook (endpoints → DNS → policy) finds why traffic doesn’t flow.

The takeaway: practise the loop until it’s automatic and you own the 30% Troubleshooting domain — the difference between passing and failing the CKA. easypj can now be broken and fixed at every layer. Next: Parts 10+ take it to production HA, packaging, hardening, and observability.

🔴 Part 10 · Production and Beyond

Run It in Production

Chapters 35–37 · Advanced · "No single point of failure, anywhere"

A single-control-plane cluster is a demo, not production. Part 10 takes easypj to a real operating posture: highly-available control planes with etcd quorum, the managed cloud Kubernetes services (EKS/GKE/AKS) and how your kubeadm skills map onto them, and the CI/CD + GitOps pipelines that ship changes automatically and safely.

🎯 What you’ll be able to do by the end: design an HA control plane (stacked vs external etcd, quorum math, leader election); map self-managed concepts onto EKS/GKE/AKS; and build a CI/CD + GitOps flow that deploys easypj from a git commit with rollback.

35.1 HA Architecture

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

A single control plane node is a single point of failure. If it goes down, the API server becomes unreachable, no new pods can be scheduled, and the cluster is essentially frozen. High Availability (HA) eliminates this by running multiple control plane nodes.

Single vs HA Control Plane — Why HA Matters

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                              │
│  ❌ SINGLE CONTROL PLANE                ✅ HIGH AVAILABILITY (HA)            │
│  ════════════════════════               ═══════════════════════════           │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────┐                       ┌────────────────────┐              │
│  │ Control Plane│ ← Single point        │   LOAD BALANCER    │              │
│  │              │    of failure!         │  (HAProxy/nginx)   │              │
│  │ API Server   │                       └───────┬────────────┘              │
│  │ etcd         │                      ┌────────┼────────┐                  │
│  │ Scheduler    │                      ▼        ▼        ▼                  │
│  │ Ctrl-Manager │               ┌──────────┐┌──────────┐┌──────────┐       │
│  └──────┬───────┘               │  CP-1    ││  CP-2    ││  CP-3    │       │
│         │                       │ API ✅    ││ API ✅    ││ API ✅    │       │
│    ┌────┼────┐                  │ etcd ✅   ││ etcd ✅   ││ etcd ✅   │       │
│    ▼    ▼    ▼                  │ sched ✅  ││ sched ⏸  ││ sched ⏸  │       │
│  W-1  W-2  W-3                  │ c-mgr ✅  ││ c-mgr ⏸  ││ c-mgr ⏸  │       │
│                                 └──────────┘└──────────┘└──────────┘       │
│  If CP goes down:                     (leader)   (standby)   (standby)      │
│  ❌ No new scheduling                                                        │
│  ❌ No API access                ┌────┼────┐                                │
│  ❌ No self-healing              ▼    ▼    ▼                                │
│  ❌ Cluster is FROZEN           W-1  W-2  W-3                               │
│                                                                              │
│  Existing pods keep running     If CP-1 goes down:                          │
│  but nothing new can happen     ✅ LB routes to CP-2/CP-3                   │
│                                 ✅ New leader elected in seconds             │
│                                 ✅ Full cluster operations continue          │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 Key HA Principle

Only ONE scheduler and controller-manager are active at any time (the "leader"). The others are on hot standby — they watch and are ready to take over in seconds. All API servers, however, handle requests simultaneously (active-active behind the load balancer).

HA Cluster Architecture — Complete View

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                       HA CLUSTER ARCHITECTURE                                │
│                                                                              │
│                    ┌──────────────────────────┐                              │
│                    │     LOAD BALANCER         │                              │
│                    │   (HAProxy / nginx)       │                              │
│                    │   VIP: 10.0.0.100:6443    │                              │
│                    └────────────┬─────────────┘                              │
│                     ┌──────────┼──────────┐                                  │
│                     │          │          │                                   │
│                     ▼          ▼          ▼                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │                  CONTROL PLANE TIER                                  │     │
│  │                                                                     │     │
│  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐             │     │
│  │  │ cp-1 (10.0.1)│  │ cp-2 (10.0.2)│  │ cp-3 (10.0.3)│             │     │
│  │  ├──────────────┤  ├──────────────┤  ├──────────────┤             │     │
│  │  │ kube-apiserver│  │ kube-apiserver│  │ kube-apiserver│             │     │
│  │  │ (active)     │  │ (active)     │  │ (active)     │             │     │
│  │  ├──────────────┤  ├──────────────┤  ├──────────────┤             │     │
│  │  │ kube-scheduler│  │ kube-scheduler│  │ kube-scheduler│             │     │
│  │  │ ★ LEADER     │  │ ⏸ standby    │  │ ⏸ standby    │             │     │
│  │  ├──────────────┤  ├──────────────┤  ├──────────────┤             │     │
│  │  │ ctrl-manager │  │ ctrl-manager │  │ ctrl-manager │             │     │
│  │  │ ★ LEADER     │  │ ⏸ standby    │  │ ⏸ standby    │             │     │
│  │  ├──────────────┤  ├──────────────┤  ├──────────────┤             │     │
│  │  │ etcd         │  │ etcd         │  │ etcd         │             │     │
│  │  │ (peer)       │  │ (peer)       │  │ (peer)       │             │     │
│  │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘             │     │
│  │                                                                     │     │
│  │  etcd replication: cp-1 ◀──▶ cp-2 ◀──▶ cp-3 (Raft consensus)      │     │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │                   WORKER NODE TIER                                   │     │
│  │                                                                     │     │
│  │  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐       │     │
│  │  │ worker-1  │  │ worker-2  │  │ worker-3  │  │ worker-N  │       │     │
│  │  │┌─────────┐│  │┌─────────┐│  │┌─────────┐│  │┌─────────┐│       │     │
│  │  ││ easypj  ││  ││ easypj  ││  ││ easypj  ││  ││ jobpost ││       │     │
│  │  ││ web-1   ││  ││ web-2   ││  ││ db-0    ││  ││ worker  ││       │     │
│  │  │└─────────┘│  │└─────────┘│  │└─────────┘│  │└─────────┘│       │     │
│  │  │ kubelet   │  │ kubelet   │  │ kubelet   │  │ kubelet   │       │     │
│  │  │ kube-proxy│  │ kube-proxy│  │ kube-proxy│  │ kube-proxy│       │     │
│  │  └───────────┘  └───────────┘  └───────────┘  └───────────┘       │     │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🎯 CKA Exam: Know the Components

You must know what runs on control plane nodes vs worker nodes. API server is active-active (all serve requests). Scheduler and controller-manager are active-passive (only the leader acts). etcd uses Raft consensus (all peers participate but one is the Raft leader).

35.2 Stacked vs External etcd

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

There are two ways to deploy etcd in an HA cluster. The choice affects fault tolerance, complexity, and cost. You must understand both for the CKA exam.

Stacked etcd Topology — etcd on Control Plane Nodes

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STACKED etcd TOPOLOGY (Default with kubeadm)                                │
│                                                                              │
│  Each control plane node runs BOTH Kubernetes components AND etcd            │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌───────────────┐    ┌───────────────┐    ┌───────────────┐                │
│  │  CP Node 1    │    │  CP Node 2    │    │  CP Node 3    │                │
│  │ ┌───────────┐ │    │ ┌───────────┐ │    │ ┌───────────┐ │                │
│  │ │API Server │ │    │ │API Server │ │    │ │API Server │ │                │
│  │ │Scheduler  │ │    │ │Scheduler  │ │    │ │Scheduler  │ │                │
│  │ │Ctrl-Mgr   │ │    │ │Ctrl-Mgr   │ │    │ │Ctrl-Mgr   │ │                │
│  │ ├───────────┤ │    │ ├───────────┤ │    │ ├───────────┤ │                │
│  │ │  etcd  📀 │ │    │ │  etcd  📀 │ │    │ │  etcd  📀 │ │                │
│  │ └───────────┘ │    │ └───────────┘ │    │ └───────────┘ │                │
│  └───────┬───────┘    └───────┬───────┘    └───────┬───────┘                │
│          │                    │                    │                          │
│          └─────── Raft Replication ───────────────┘                          │
│                                                                              │
│  ✅ Simpler setup — fewer nodes to manage                                   │
│  ✅ Default kubeadm topology                                                │
│  ⚠️ Risk: If a node dies, you lose both CP and an etcd member              │
│  📊 Minimum: 3 nodes (for etcd quorum)                                     │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

External etcd Topology — etcd on Dedicated Servers

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  EXTERNAL etcd TOPOLOGY                                                      │
│                                                                              │
│  etcd runs on SEPARATE dedicated nodes — decoupled from control plane        │
│                                                                              │
│  Control Plane Tier:                                                         │
│  ┌───────────────┐    ┌───────────────┐    ┌───────────────┐                │
│  │  CP Node 1    │    │  CP Node 2    │    │  CP Node 3    │                │
│  │ ┌───────────┐ │    │ ┌───────────┐ │    │ ┌───────────┐ │                │
│  │ │API Server │ │    │ │API Server │ │    │ │API Server │ │                │
│  │ │Scheduler  │ │    │ │Scheduler  │ │    │ │Scheduler  │ │                │
│  │ │Ctrl-Mgr   │ │    │ │Ctrl-Mgr   │ │    │ │Ctrl-Mgr   │ │                │
│  │ └───────────┘ │    │ └───────────┘ │    │ └───────────┘ │                │
│  └───────┬───────┘    └───────┬───────┘    └───────┬───────┘                │
│          └────────────┬───────┘                    │                          │
│                       │  Connect via TLS            │                          │
│          ┌────────────┼────────────────────────────┘                          │
│          ▼            ▼            ▼                                          │
│  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐                                │
│  │ etcd-1 📀 │  │ etcd-2 📀 │  │ etcd-3 📀 │  ← Dedicated etcd cluster    │
│  └─────┬─────┘  └─────┬─────┘  └─────┬─────┘                                │
│        └───── Raft Replication ───────┘                                      │
│                                                                              │
│  ✅ etcd survives control plane failures                                    │
│  ✅ Can scale etcd independently                                            │
│  ⚠️ More complex — requires 6+ nodes minimum (3 CP + 3 etcd)               │
│  ⚠️ More certs to manage (API→etcd TLS)                                    │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Topology Comparison

Aspect Stacked (default) External etcd
etcd location On control plane node Separate dedicated servers
Setup complexity Easier — kubeadm init handles it Harder — manual etcd cluster setup
Fault isolation ⚠️ CP failure = etcd member lost too ✅ etcd survives CP node failure
Minimum nodes 3 (combined CP + etcd) 6 (3 CP + 3 etcd)
Cost Lower — fewer servers Higher — 2× the infrastructure
CKA Exam Most tested topology ✅ Conceptual understanding needed
Best for Most production clusters Critical workloads with strict SLAs

⚠️ CKA Gotcha: Which Topology Is on the Exam?

The CKA exam uses stacked etcd topology (kubeadm default). When asked to backup/restore etcd, the etcd data dir is on the control plane node at /var/lib/etcd. The API server connects to etcd on localhost:2379. Know both topologies conceptually, but practice stacked for the exam.

35.3 Setting Up HA with kubeadm

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

Setting up an HA cluster with kubeadm follows a specific sequence: configure the load balancer first, initialize the first control plane, then join additional control planes and workers.

HA Setup Sequence — Step by Step

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    HA CLUSTER SETUP SEQUENCE                                  │
│                                                                              │
│  Step 1          Step 2           Step 3           Step 4                    │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐              │
│  │ Setup    │    │ Init 1st │    │ Join     │    │ Join     │              │
│  │ Load     │───▶│ Control  │───▶│ More CP  │───▶│ Worker   │              │
│  │ Balancer │    │ Plane    │    │ Nodes    │    │ Nodes    │              │
│  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘              │
│  HAProxy/nginx    kubeadm init    kubeadm join    kubeadm join              │
│  on :6443         --control-      --control-      (no flag)                 │
│                   plane-endpoint  plane                                      │
│                   =LB_IP:6443                                                │
│                                                                              │
│  Step 5          Step 6           Step 7                                     │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐                               │
│  │ Install  │    │ Verify   │    │ Test     │                               │
│  │ CNI      │───▶│ etcd     │───▶│ Failover │                               │
│  │ Plugin   │    │ Health   │    │          │                               │
│  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘                               │
│  Calico/Cilium    etcdctl         Kill a CP node                             │
│                   endpoint        → verify LB                                │
│                   health          reroutes                                    │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Step 1: HAProxy Configuration

/etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg 
# HAProxy configuration for Kubernetes API Server HA
frontend kubernetes-api
    bind *:6443
    mode tcp
    option tcplog
    default_backend kubernetes-api-backend

backend kubernetes-api-backend
    mode tcp
    option tcp-check
    balance roundrobin
    # Health check: API server /healthz endpoint
    server cp-1 10.0.0.1:6443 check fall 3 rise 2
    server cp-2 10.0.0.2:6443 check fall 3 rise 2
    server cp-3 10.0.0.3:6443 check fall 3 rise 2

Step 2: Initialize First Control Plane

Terminal — cp-1 (first control plane) 
# Initialize first control plane — point to the load balancer!
$ sudo kubeadm init \
    --control-plane-endpoint "10.0.0.100:6443" \
    --upload-certs \
    --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16

# Output includes TWO join commands:
# 1. For additional control plane nodes (has --control-plane flag)
# 2. For worker nodes (no --control-plane flag)

# Copy kubeconfig
$ mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
$ sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
$ sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config

Steps 3 & 4: Join Additional Nodes

Terminal — cp-2 and cp-3 
# Join as additional control plane (note --control-plane flag!)
$ sudo kubeadm join 10.0.0.100:6443 \
    --token <token> \
    --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash> \
    --control-plane \
    --certificate-key <cert-key>
Terminal — worker nodes 
# Join as worker node (NO --control-plane flag)
$ sudo kubeadm join 10.0.0.100:6443 \
    --token <token> \
    --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>

Step 6: Verify Cluster Health

Terminal — verify HA cluster 
# Verify all nodes are Ready
$ kubectl get nodes
NAME   STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
cp-1   Ready    control-plane   10m   v1.31.0
cp-2   Ready    control-plane   8m    v1.31.0
cp-3   Ready    control-plane   6m    v1.31.0
w-1    Ready    <none>          4m    v1.31.0
w-2    Ready    <none>          3m    v1.31.0
w-3    Ready    <none>          2m    v1.31.0

# Verify etcd cluster health
$ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list \
    --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
    --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
    --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
# Should show 3 members: cp-1, cp-2, cp-3

✅ Verify: HA Setup Checklist

  • kubectl get nodes — all control plane nodes show Ready
  • etcdctl member list — shows 3 etcd members
  • etcdctl endpoint health — all endpoints healthy
  • Load balancer health check — all backends UP
  • Kill one CP node → API still responds via LB

35.4 etcd Quorum and Leader Election

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm. A majority of etcd members must agree before any write is committed. This majority is called the quorum. Understanding quorum math is essential for CKA.

etcd Quorum Formula: (N/2) + 1

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ETCD QUORUM — THE MATH                                    │
│                                                                              │
│  Formula: Quorum = floor(N/2) + 1                                            │
│  Tolerated Failures = N - Quorum                                             │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌─────────┬────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Members │ Quorum │ Tolerated Failures  │ Recommendation               │  │
│  ├─────────┼────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │    1    │   1    │         0           │ ❌ Dev/test only              │  │
│  │    2    │   2    │         0           │ ❌ NEVER — worse than 1!     │  │
│  │    3    │   2    │         1           │ ✅ Standard production       │  │
│  │    4    │   3    │         1           │ ❌ Same tolerance as 3!      │  │
│  │    5    │   3    │         2           │ ✅ Large-scale production    │  │
│  │    6    │   4    │         2           │ ❌ Same tolerance as 5!      │  │
│  │    7    │   4    │         3           │ ⚠️ Rare — more latency       │  │
│  └─────────┴────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                              │
│  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Even numbers are WASTEFUL!                                 │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────                                   │
│  3 members → tolerate 1 failure                                              │
│  4 members → STILL only tolerate 1 failure (need 3 for quorum)              │
│  → You added a node but got ZERO extra fault tolerance!                      │
│                                                                              │
│  ALWAYS USE ODD NUMBERS: 1, 3, 5, 7                                        │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Quorum in Action — What Happens During Failures

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  3-MEMBER CLUSTER FAILURE SCENARIOS                                          │
│                                                                              │
│  Normal (3/3 alive):         1 Node Down (2/3 alive):                        │
│  ┌────┐  ┌────┐  ┌────┐     ┌────┐  ┌────┐  ┌────┐                        │
│  │ E1 │  │ E2 │  │ E3 │     │ E1 │  │ E2 │  │ ╳╳ │  ← Node 3 down       │
│  │ ✅ │  │ ✅ │  │ ✅ │     │ ✅ │  │ ✅ │  │ ❌ │                        │
│  └────┘  └────┘  └────┘     └────┘  └────┘  └────┘                        │
│  Quorum: 2 of 3 = ✅         Quorum: 2 of 3 = ✅ (still works!)            │
│  Writes: ✅                  Writes: ✅                                      │
│  Reads:  ✅                  Reads:  ✅                                      │
│                                                                              │
│  2 Nodes Down (1/3 alive):   Split Brain (network partition):                │
│  ┌────┐  ┌────┐  ┌────┐     ┌────┐  │  ┌────┐  ┌────┐                     │
│  │ E1 │  │ ╳╳ │  │ ╳╳ │     │ E1 │  │  │ E2 │  │ E3 │                     │
│  │ ✅ │  │ ❌ │  │ ❌ │     │ ✅ │  │  │ ✅ │  │ ✅ │                     │
│  └────┘  └────┘  └────┘     └────┘  │  └────┘  └────┘                     │
│  Quorum: 1 of 3 = ❌         Side A: 1 (no quorum ❌)                       │
│  Writes: ❌ CLUSTER DOWN!    Side B: 2 (has quorum ✅)                       │
│  Reads:  ❌ (stale reads     → Side B continues serving                      │
│             may be possible)  → Side A becomes read-only                     │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🎯 CKA Exam Quick Recall

If asked "how many etcd node failures can a 5-member cluster tolerate?" — the answer is 2. Formula: floor(5/2) + 1 = 3 needed for quorum, so 5 - 3 = 2 failures tolerated. Always use odd numbers for etcd cluster size.

💡 Why Even Numbers Are Dangerous

A 4-member etcd cluster tolerates only 1 failure — the same as a 3-member cluster — but uses more resources. Worse, with 4 members a network partition can create two equal groups (2 vs 2), and neither has quorum, causing a total outage. Odd numbers eliminate this symmetric split risk.

etcd Backup & Restore in HA — Critical CKA Skill

Backing up and restoring etcd is a guaranteed CKA exam topic. In an HA cluster, you must back up from one member and restore to all members.

Terminal — etcd backup & restore (CKA exam critical) 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 1: BACKUP — Take snapshot from any healthy member
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
$ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/etcd-backup.db \
    --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
    --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
    --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# Verify the backup
$ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/etcd-backup.db --write-table
+----------+----------+------------+------------+
|   HASH   | REVISION | TOTAL KEYS | TOTAL SIZE |
+----------+----------+------------+------------+
| abc12def |   150234 |       1847 |     4.2 MB |
+----------+----------+------------+------------+

# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 2: RESTORE — Stop API server, restore, restart
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# On EACH control plane node:
$ mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/

# Restore with a NEW data directory (don't overwrite!)
$ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /tmp/etcd-backup.db \
    --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored \
    --name=cp-1 \
    --initial-cluster="cp-1=https://10.0.0.1:2380,cp-2=https://10.0.0.2:2380,cp-3=https://10.0.0.3:2380" \
    --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://10.0.0.1:2380

# Update etcd manifest to point to new data dir
$ sed -i 's|/var/lib/etcd|/var/lib/etcd-restored|g' \
    /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml

# Restart API server
$ mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/

etcd Backup Strategy — When & Where

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  etcd BACKUP BEST PRACTICES                                                  │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐               │
│  │  BACKUP SCHEDULE:                                         │               │
│  │                                                           │               │
│  │  CronJob every 30 min ──▶ /backups/etcd-{timestamp}.db   │               │
│  │  Keep last 48 backups (24 hours of 30-min snapshots)      │               │
│  │  Store offsite: S3 / Azure Blob / GCS bucket ✅           │               │
│  │  NEVER store backups only on the etcd nodes! ❌            │               │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘               │
│                                                                              │
│  RESTORE SCENARIOS:                                                          │
│  ┌───────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐               │
│  │ Scenario          │ Action                               │               │
│  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤               │
│  │ 1 etcd member     │ Remove & re-add member (simpler)   │               │
│  │ lost              │ etcdctl member add                   │               │
│  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤               │
│  │ Quorum lost       │ Full restore from snapshot on ALL    │               │
│  │ (majority down)   │ remaining members                    │               │
│  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤               │
│  │ Data corruption   │ Full restore from known-good         │               │
│  │                   │ snapshot + verify cluster health      │               │
│  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤               │
│  │ Disaster recovery │ Restore snapshot to new cluster +    │               │
│  │                   │ update certificates if needed         │               │
│  └───────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘               │
│                                                                              │
│  ⚠️  REMEMBER: etcd restore creates a NEW cluster ID — all members          │
│     must restore from the SAME snapshot to form a consistent cluster!        │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Common Mistake: Forgetting TLS Flags

The #1 reason etcdctl commands fail on the CKA exam: missing the --cacert, --cert, and --key flags. These certs are always at /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/. Also remember to set ETCDCTL_API=3 — version 2 has different commands!

35.5 Leader Election Deep Dive

🎯 CKA EXAM TOPIC

In an HA cluster, only one instance of the kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager is actively making decisions at any time. This is managed through leader election using the Kubernetes Lease API.

Leader Election — How It Works

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LEADER ELECTION MECHANISM                                                   │
│                                                                              │
│  Component        │ Active Instances │ Election Method                       │
│  ─────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────               │
│  kube-apiserver   │ ALL (active-     │ No election needed —                  │
│                   │ active)          │ stateless, LB distributes             │
│  ─────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────               │
│  kube-scheduler   │ ONE (leader)     │ Lease object in kube-system          │
│                   │                  │ --leader-elect=true                   │
│  ─────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────               │
│  kube-controller  │ ONE (leader)     │ Lease object in kube-system          │
│  -manager         │                  │ --leader-elect=true                   │
│  ─────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────               │
│  etcd             │ ALL (Raft        │ Raft protocol — internal             │
│                   │ consensus)       │ leader for write ordering            │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐            │
│  │  LEASE-BASED LEADER ELECTION FLOW:                          │            │
│  │                                                              │            │
│  │  1. All instances try to acquire a Lease object              │            │
│  │  2. Winner writes its identity + timestamp to Lease          │            │
│  │  3. Leader renews Lease every ~2 seconds (leaseDuration)     │            │
│  │  4. Other instances watch — if Lease expires, they compete   │            │
│  │  5. Fastest to write wins → new leader in ~15 seconds        │            │
│  │                                                              │            │
│  │  Timeline:                                                   │            │
│  │  ─────────── Leader CP-1 ──────────── ╳ (dies)              │            │
│  │  ───── standby CP-2 ────────────────── ★ new leader ──────  │            │
│  │  ───── standby CP-3 ────────────────── standby ───────────  │            │
│  │                               ~15s gap                       │            │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘            │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Inspecting Leader Election

Terminal — check current leaders 
# List all leases in kube-system
$ kubectl get lease -n kube-system
NAME                      HOLDER       AGE
kube-scheduler            cp-1_xxx     3d
kube-controller-manager   cp-1_xxx     3d

# Describe scheduler lease — see who holds it
$ kubectl describe lease kube-scheduler -n kube-system
Name:         kube-scheduler
Namespace:    kube-system
Spec:
  Holder Identity:    cp-1_xxxxxxxx-xxxx  ← THIS is the active leader
  Lease Duration:     15s
  Renew Time:         2024-03-15T10:45:32Z

# Check leader-elect flags in scheduler manifest
$ cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml | grep leader
    - --leader-elect=true    ← Enables leader election (default)
💡 What Happens During Leader Failover

When the leader dies, there's a brief gap (~15 seconds) before a new leader is elected. During this time, no new pods are scheduled and no controller actions happen (like scaling Deployments). Existing pods continue running — they don't depend on the scheduler or controller-manager once scheduled.

🏋️ Practice Drill — Leader Election Investigation

Scenario: Your team reports that new pods aren't being scheduled. You suspect the scheduler leader may have failed over. Investigate and verify.

  1. Check which node currently holds the scheduler lease:
    kubectl get lease kube-scheduler -n kube-system -o yaml
  2. Check the controller-manager lease as well:
    kubectl get lease kube-controller-manager -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.holderIdentity}'
  3. Verify the lease renewTime is recent (within last ~15 seconds). If stale → the leader may have crashed
  4. Check scheduler pod logs for election events:
    kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-scheduler-cp-1 | grep -i "leader\|elected\|lost"
  5. Verify all control plane nodes are healthy:
    kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane

Expected outcome: You can identify which control plane node is the active leader and confirm the lease is being renewed.

35.6 Load Balancer Configuration for HA

The load balancer is the front door to your HA cluster. All kubectl commands, worker node registrations, and internal API calls go through it. If the LB fails, the entire cluster is unreachable — making the LB itself another critical HA component.

Load Balancer Health Check Flow

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LOAD BALANCER HEALTH CHECK & ROUTING                                       │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                        │
│  │        kubectl / kubelet        │                                        │
│  │        All API requests         │                                        │
│  └───────────────┬─────────────────┘                                        │
│                  │                                                            │
│                  ▼ :6443                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                        │
│  │        LOAD BALANCER            │      Health Check:                      │
│  │      (HAProxy / nginx)          │      GET /healthz on :6443              │
│  │                                 │      Every 5 seconds                    │
│  │   Rules:                        │                                        │
│  │   - TCP mode (Layer 4)          │      Response 200 → Backend UP ✅      │
│  │   - Round-robin distribution    │      No response  → Remove from pool ❌│
│  │   - 3 failed checks → remove   │                                        │
│  │   - 2 passed checks → re-add   │                                        │
│  └──┬──────────┬──────────┬───────┘                                        │
│     │          │          │                                                  │
│     ▼          ▼          ▼                                                  │
│  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                                              │
│  │CP-1  │  │CP-2  │  │CP-3  │                                              │
│  │:6443 │  │:6443 │  │:6443 │                                              │
│  │ ✅   │  │ ✅   │  │ ❌   │  ← CP-3 failed health check                 │
│  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘    → removed from pool                       │
│  ▲ 50%     ▲ 50%     (0%)       → traffic split between CP-1 & CP-2       │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

nginx Stream Proxy Configuration (Alternative to HAProxy)

/etc/nginx/nginx.conf — stream proxy for K8s API 
stream {
    upstream kubernetes_api {
        # Round-robin between control plane nodes
        server 10.0.0.1:6443 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
        server 10.0.0.2:6443 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
        server 10.0.0.3:6443 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
    }

    server {
        listen 6443;
        proxy_pass kubernetes_api;
        proxy_timeout 10m;
        proxy_connect_timeout 1s;
    }
}
⚠️ LB Single Point of Failure?

Yes — a single load balancer is itself a SPOF. In production, use keepalived + VRRP for LB failover (two LB hosts sharing a virtual IP), or use a cloud-managed load balancer (AWS NLB, Azure LB, GCP TCP LB) which is inherently HA.

keepalived + VRRP — Making the Load Balancer HA

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LOAD BALANCER HIGH AVAILABILITY WITH keepalived                             │
│                                                                              │
│  Problem: Single LB = Single Point of Failure                                │
│  Solution: Two LBs sharing a Virtual IP (VIP) via VRRP protocol             │
│                                                                              │
│                     ┌──────────────┐                                        │
│   kubectl ────▶     │  VIP:        │     ← Clients connect to VIP           │
│   kubelet           │  10.0.0.100  │        NOT individual LB IPs            │
│                     └──────┬───────┘                                        │
│                            │                                                 │
│              ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐                                  │
│              │                           │                                   │
│     ┌────────▼────────┐        ┌────────▼────────┐                          │
│     │  LB-1 (MASTER)  │  VRRP  │  LB-2 (BACKUP)  │                          │
│     │  10.0.0.10      │◄──────▶│  10.0.0.11       │                          │
│     │  Owns VIP ✅    │ health  │  Standby ⏳      │                          │
│     │  Priority: 101  │ checks  │  Priority: 100   │                          │
│     └────────┬────────┘        └────────┬─────────┘                          │
│              │                           │                                   │
│              └─────────┬─┬───────────────┘                                  │
│                        │ │ │                                                 │
│                   CP-1 CP-2 CP-3                                             │
│                                                                              │
│  Failover Flow:                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐            │
│  │  1. LB-1 sends VRRP advertisements every 1 second          │            │
│  │  2. LB-2 monitors — if no VRRP from LB-1 for 3 seconds    │            │
│  │  3. LB-2 claims the VIP → sends gratuitous ARP             │            │
│  │  4. Traffic redirects to LB-2 in <5 seconds ✅            │            │
│  │  5. When LB-1 recovers → reclaims VIP (preempt mode)       │            │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘            │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Production Readiness Checklist

Category Requirement Status
Control Plane 3+ CP nodes across availability zones ✅ Required
etcd backup CronJob every 6 hours ✅ Required
Load balancer with health checks on /healthz ✅ Required
Workloads PodDisruptionBudget on easypj (minAvailable: 2) ✅ Required
Anti-affinity: spread easypj pods across nodes ✅ Required
Resource requests/limits on all containers ✅ Required
Liveness and readiness probes configured ✅ Required
Monitoring Alerts for node NotReady and pod crash loops ✅ Required
Central logging (Fluentd/Fluent Bit → ELK/Loki) ✅ Required
Security RBAC: least-privilege ServiceAccounts ✅ Required
NetworkPolicies: restrict inter-namespace traffic ✅ Required
Secrets encrypted at rest in etcd ✅ Required
Anti-Patterns ❌ Never run single-replica Deployments in prod ⚠️ Avoid
❌ Never run without resource limits ⚠️ Avoid
❌ Never skip PodDisruptionBudgets ⚠️ Avoid
easypj-pdb.yaml — PodDisruptionBudget 
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-pdb
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  minAvailable: 2          # At least 2 pods must always be running
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
---
# Anti-affinity in Deployment to spread pods across nodes
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - weight: 100
            podAffinityTerm:
              labelSelector:
                matchExpressions:
                - key: app
                  operator: In
                  values:
                  - easypj-web
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      containers:
      - name: easypj
        image: easypj/web:v2.0
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 15
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10

Under the Hood — How High Availability Clusters Actually Work: Stacked vs External etcd, Quorum Math, and Leader Election Across Components
🗺️ HA Topologies — Stacked vs External etcd

Kubernetes HA comes in two architectures. Understanding the trade-offs helps you choose the right topology and debug HA failures on the CKA.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HA TOPOLOGIES — Stacked vs External etcd                                     │
│                                                                              │
│  STACKED ETCD (default, simpler):                                            │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  CP Node 1          CP Node 2          CP Node 3                     │   │
│  │  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐              │   │
│  │  │ API Server  │    │ API Server  │    │ API Server  │              │   │
│  │  │ etcd        │◀──▶│ etcd        │◀──▶│ etcd        │              │   │
│  │  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘              │   │
│  │                                                                       │   │
│  │  ✅ Simpler to set up (1 command: kubeadm join --control-plane)      │   │
│  │  ✅ Fewer nodes needed (3 CP nodes = 3 etcd nodes)                   │   │
│  │  ⚠️  etcd competes for resources with API Server                    │   │
│  │  ⚠️  If CP node fails, lose BOTH API Server AND etcd member         │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  EXTERNAL ETCD (separate etcd cluster):                                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  CP Node 1          CP Node 2          CP Node 3                     │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐            │   │
│  │  │  API Server  │   │  API Server  │   │  API Server  │            │   │
│  │  └──────┬───────┘   └──────┬───────┘   └──────┬───────┘            │   │
│  │         │                 │                 │                        │   │
│  │         └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘                        │   │
│  │                           ▼                                           │   │
│  │  etcd Node 1        etcd Node 2        etcd Node 3                   │   │
│  │  ┌────────────┐     ┌────────────┐     ┌────────────┐               │   │
│  │  │   etcd     │◀───▶│   etcd     │◀───▶│   etcd     │               │   │
│  │  └────────────┘     └────────────┘     └────────────┘               │   │
│  │                                                                       │   │
│  │  ✅ API Server and etcd failures are independent                      │   │
│  │  ✅ etcd on dedicated nodes → better performance                     │   │
│  │  ⚠️  More nodes (3 CP + 3 etcd = 6 minimum)                         │   │
│  │  ⚠️  More complex setup                                               │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  QUORUM MATH — How Many Failures Can Your Cluster Survive:                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  etcd uses RAFT — needs MAJORITY (N/2 + 1) to commit writes          │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  ┌───────┬──────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐   │   │
│  │  │ Nodes │ Majority │ Max Failures │ Notes                        │   │   │
│  │  ├───────┼──────────┼──────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤   │   │
│  │  │   1   │    1     │      0       │ No HA — single point of      │   │   │
│  │  │       │          │              │ failure                       │   │   │
│  │  │   2   │    2     │      0       │ Worse than 1 — needs both!    │   │   │
│  │  │   3   │    2     │      1       │ Minimum for production HA     │   │   │
│  │  │   4   │    3     │      1       │ Still only 1 failure allowed  │   │   │
│  │  │   5   │    3     │      2       │ Production recommendation     │   │   │
│  │  │   7   │    4     │      3       │ Maximum recommended            │   │   │
│  │  └───────┴──────────┴──────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘   │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  RULE: ALWAYS use ODD number of etcd nodes (3, 5, 7).                 │   │
│  │  Even numbers waste resources with NO reliability gain.               │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│  API SERVER LOAD BALANCING:                                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  ┌──────────┐                                                         │   │
│  │  │  kubectl │────▶ haproxy/nginx LB (10.0.1.200:6443)                │   │
│  │  └──────────┘        │                                                 │   │
│  │              ┌───────┼───────┐                                         │   │
│  │              ▼       ▼       ▼                                         │   │
│  │         CP-Node1  CP-Node2  CP-Node3                                  │   │
│  │         :6443     :6443     :6443                                      │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  All API Servers are ACTIVE (no leader election for API Server).      │   │
│  │  Any API Server can serve read requests.                              │   │
│  │  Writes go through ANY API Server → etcd (Raft leader handles).      │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CKA Insight: On the CKA, you may be asked about etcd quorum. Formula: quorum = floor(N/2) + 1, max failures = floor((N-1)/2). Always use odd numbers (3, 5, 7). 3 etcd nodes tolerate 1 failure. API Servers have NO leader election — ALL are active. Controller manager and scheduler DO have leader election (only one active at a time). Check with: kubectl get leases -n kube-system.

🔑 Key Takeaways

Bulleted key takeaways go here.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions

The CKA exam uses stacked etcd topology (kubeadm default). When asked to backup/restore etcd, the etcd data dir is on the control plane node at /var/lib/etcd. The API server connects to etcd on localhost:2379. Know both topologies conceptually, but practice stacked for the exam.

  • Stacked vs External etcd — Stacked: etcd runs on control plane nodes (simpler, fewer machines). External: etcd on dedicated nodes (better isolation, harder to set up). The CKA uses stacked topology. Know both for conceptual questions
  • etcd quorum formula — (N/2) + 1 members must be alive. 3 nodes = tolerate 1 failure. 5 nodes = tolerate 2. Always use ODD numbers. Even numbers waste a node without improving fault tolerance
  • Leader election — Only ONE controller-manager and ONE scheduler are active at a time (the leader). Others are standby. Check leader: kubectl get lease -n kube-system. If the leader dies, a new one is elected in ~15s
  • --control-plane-endpoint is critical — Must point to a load balancer, not a single node IP. Without this, adding control plane nodes later fails. Set during kubeadm init and it CANNOT be changed after
  • Pod anti-affinity for HA workloads — Without podAntiAffinity, all replicas could land on the same node. If that node dies, 100% downtime. Always spread critical workloads across nodes
⚡ Speed Tips

CKA Speed Tip — HA concepts to know:
kubectl get lease -n kube-system — see leader election leases
kubectl get endpoints -n kube-system kube-scheduler -o yaml — current leader annotation
Quorum table: 1 node=no HA, 3=tolerate 1, 5=tolerate 2, 7=tolerate 3
Rule: Never run production with fewer than 3 control plane nodes

⚙️ Chapter 35 — Scenario & Command Drills (12)

Quick recall of HA control-plane architecture — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
How many etcd nodes are needed to tolerate 2 node failures? Explain the quorum formula.
Show Answer
Answer
Total Nodes Quorum Needed Failures Tolerated Useful?
1 1 0 ❌ No HA
2 2 0 ❌ Worse than 1
3 2 1 ✅ Minimum HA
4 3 1 ⚠️ Wastes a node
5 3 2 ✅ Answer!
7 4 3 ✅ Large clusters
formula: quorum = (n / 2) + 1 (integer division)
# Formula: Quorum = (N / 2) + 1 (integer division)
# Failures tolerated = N - Quorum

# 5 nodes: Quorum = (5/2) + 1 = 3
# Failures = 5 - 3 = 2 ← Answer!

# Check etcd members:
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list \
--endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
--cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
--cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
--key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
Explanation

etcd uses Raft consensus: a majority (quorum) must agree on every write. Formula: quorum = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1. To tolerate 2 failures, you need 5 nodes (quorum of 3, so 2 can fail). Always use odd numbers — 4 nodes tolerates the same failures as 3 but costs more. On the CKA, know this table cold. Two nodes is WORSE than one because you need both alive for quorum.

Q2
What's the difference between stacked etcd and external etcd topologies?
Show Answer
Answer
Aspect Stacked etcd External etcd
Where etcd runs On control plane nodes On dedicated separate nodes
Min machines (HA) 3 (total) 6 (3 CP + 3 etcd)
Failure coupling Coupled: node failure loses both CP + etcd Decoupled: CP failure ≠ etcd failure
Complexity Simpler setup More complex
CKA exam ✅ Default (kubeadm) Know conceptually
kubeadm init flag (default) --external-etcd-endpoints
stacked: etcd is a local static pod
# Stacked: etcd is a local static pod
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml  # Exists on CP nodes

# External: API server points to remote etcd
grep etcd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# --etcd-servers=https://etcd1:2379,https://etcd2:2379,https://etcd3:2379
Explanation

Stacked = etcd runs on the same nodes as the control plane (simpler, fewer machines). External = etcd on dedicated nodes (better isolation, requires more machines). The CKA uses stacked topology (kubeadm default). In stacked, losing a control plane node also loses an etcd member. In external, control plane and etcd fail independently, providing better resilience at the cost of complexity.

Q3
How do you check which node is the current leader for kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler?
Show Answer
Answer
check lease objects (modern way)
# Method 1: Check Lease objects (modern way)
kubectl get lease -n kube-system
# NAME                          HOLDER            AGE
# kube-controller-manager       master-1_abc123   30d
# kube-scheduler                master-2_def456   30d
# ← HOLDER shows which node is the current leader

# Method 2: Detailed lease info
kubectl describe lease kube-controller-manager -n kube-system
# Spec:
#   Holder Identity:   master-1_abc123
#   Lease Duration:    15s
#   Renew Time:        2024-01-15 10:30:00

# Method 3: Check endpoint annotations (legacy)
kubectl get endpoints kube-controller-manager -n kube-system -o yaml
# metadata:
#   annotations:
#     control-plane.alpha.kubernetes.io/leader:
#       holderIdentity: master-1_abc123

# How leader election works:
# 1. Multiple instances compete for a Lease object
# 2. Winner writes its identity + holds the lease
# 3. Winner renews every ~10s (leaseDuration: 15s)
# 4. If leader stops renewing, another takes over (~15s)
# 5. Only the leader actively processes work

# On each control plane node, check:
kubectl logs kube-scheduler-master-2 -n kube-system | head -5
# "successfully acquired lease kube-system/kube-scheduler"
# ← This node is the scheduler leader
Explanation

In HA clusters, only ONE controller-manager and ONE scheduler are active (the leader). Others are standby. Leaders use Lease objects (in kube-system) for election. The HOLDER field shows which node is leading. If the leader dies, a new one is elected within the lease duration (~15s). On the CKA, kubectl get lease -n kube-system is the fastest way to check.

Q4
What is the --control-plane-endpoint flag and why is it critical for HA?
Show Answer
Answer
kubeadm init with ha setup
# kubeadm init with HA setup:
kubeadm init \
--control-plane-endpoint="lb.example.com:6443" \
--upload-certs \
--pod-network-cidr=192.168.0.0/16

# --control-plane-endpoint sets the API server address for ALL nodes
# Must be a load balancer or DNS name that fronts all CP nodes

# What it configures:
# 1. All kubeconfigs point to lb.example.com:6443
# 2. All kubelet configs use this address
# 3. Workers join via this address (not a single master IP)

# WITHOUT --control-plane-endpoint:
# kubeadm uses the first master's IP (e.g., 10.0.0.1:6443)
# If that master dies → ALL kubeconfigs point to dead IP
# Workers can't reach API server → cluster is down
# CANNOT be changed after kubeadm init!

# Load balancer options:
# - HAProxy (common for bare-metal)
# - nginx (also common)
# - Cloud LB (ELB, ALB, Azure LB)
# - keepalived + virtual IP

# Verify current endpoint:
kubectl cluster-info
# Kubernetes control plane is running at https://lb.example.com:6443

# Check kubeconfig:
cat ~/.kube/config | grep server
# server: https://lb.example.com:6443
Explanation

--control-plane-endpoint must be a load balancer address that distributes traffic across all control plane nodes. It's set during kubeadm init and is IMMUTABLE — changing it later requires rebuilding the cluster. Without it, all configs point to a single master IP, making HA impossible. On the CKA, know this conceptually: it ensures API access survives individual master node failures.

Q5
How do you ensure critical workloads are spread across nodes for high availability?
Show Answer
Answer
problem: all 3 replicas land on the same node
# Problem: All 3 replicas land on the same node
kubectl get pods -l app=web -o wide
# NAME       NODE
# web-abc    worker-1
# web-def    worker-1
# web-ghi    worker-1  ← All on one node! Not HA!

# Solution: Pod Anti-Affinity
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
name: web
spec:
replicas: 3
selector:
matchLabels:
  app: web
template:
metadata:
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  affinity:
    podAntiAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - labelSelector:
          matchExpressions:
          - key: app
            operator: In
            values:
            - web
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx

# Result: 1 pod per node
# web-abc  worker-1
# web-def  worker-2
# web-ghi  worker-3  ← Spread across nodes!

# Softer version (preferred, not required):
# preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution
# → Best effort spread, won't block scheduling

# Topology Spread Constraints (newer API):
spec:
topologySpreadConstraints:
- maxSkew: 1
topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
labelSelector:
  matchLabels:
    app: web
Explanation

Pod anti-affinity prevents pods with the same label from running on the same node. requiredDuringScheduling = hard rule (pod stays Pending if no unique node). preferredDuringScheduling = soft rule (best effort). topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname means one pod per node. On the CKA, you might need to add anti-affinity to ensure HA. topologySpreadConstraints is the newer, more flexible alternative.

Q6
How do you add a new control plane node to an existing HA cluster?
Show Answer
Answer
prerequisites
# Prerequisites:
# - Initial cluster created with --control-plane-endpoint
# - Load balancer configured for existing + new CP node
# - New node meets prerequisites (OS, container runtime, kubeadm)

# Step 1: On existing control plane, generate join command
kubeadm token create --print-join-command
# kubeadm join lb.example.com:6443 --token abc123 \
#   --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:xyz789

# Step 2: Upload certificates (need key for new CP node)
kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs
# [upload-certs] Using certificate key: abc123def456...

# Step 3: On new node, join as control plane
kubeadm join lb.example.com:6443 \
--token abc123 \
--discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:xyz789 \
--control-plane \
--certificate-key abc123def456

# Step 4: Update load balancer
# Add new node's IP to the LB backend pool

# Step 5: Verify
kubectl get nodes
# NAME       STATUS  ROLES          VERSION
# master-1   Ready   control-plane  v1.31.0
# master-2   Ready   control-plane  v1.31.0
# master-3   Ready   control-plane  v1.31.0  ← New!

# Check etcd is healthy:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep etcd
# etcd-master-1  1/1  Running
# etcd-master-2  1/1  Running
# etcd-master-3  1/1  Running  ← New etcd member!
Explanation

Adding a control plane node uses kubeadm join with the --control-plane flag and --certificate-key to download shared certificates. The cluster must have been initialized with --control-plane-endpoint. On the CKA, know this workflow conceptually. The key steps: generate token, upload certs, join with control-plane flag, update load balancer. Stacked etcd automatically adds a new member when a control plane node joins.

Q7
What is a PodDisruptionBudget and how does it protect HA during maintenance?
Show Answer
Answer
create pdb imperatively
# Create PDB imperatively:
kubectl create pdb web-pdb --selector=app=web --min-available=2

# OR declaratively:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
name: web-pdb
spec:
minAvailable: 2          # At least 2 pods must be running
# OR: maxUnavailable: 1  # At most 1 pod can be down
selector:
matchLabels:
  app: web

# What PDB protects against:
# ✅ kubectl drain (node maintenance)
# ✅ Cluster autoscaler removing nodes
# ✅ kubeadm upgrade
# ❌ Does NOT protect against: node crash, OOMKill, pod deletion

# Without PDB (3 replicas, draining 2 nodes):
kubectl drain worker-1 --delete-emptydir-data --ignore-daemonsets
kubectl drain worker-2 --delete-emptydir-data --ignore-daemonsets
# Both succeed → 0 pods running → DOWNTIME!

# With PDB (minAvailable: 2):
kubectl drain worker-1  # Succeeds (2 pods remain on worker-2,3)
kubectl drain worker-2  # BLOCKS! "Cannot evict pod: would violate PDB"
# Service stays up with 2 pods ✓

# Check PDB status:
kubectl get pdb
# NAME     MIN-AVAILABLE  MAX-UNAVAILABLE  ALLOWED-DISRUPTIONS  AGE
# web-pdb  2              N/A              1                    5m
# ALLOWED-DISRUPTIONS: 1 = can safely evict 1 more pod
Explanation

PDB sets limits on voluntary disruptions (drain, upgrades, autoscaler). minAvailable = minimum pods that must stay running. maxUnavailable = maximum pods that can be down. PDB blocks drain commands that would violate the budget. On the CKA, create PDBs to protect critical workloads during node maintenance. kubectl create pdb is the fastest imperative method. PDB does NOT prevent involuntary disruptions (node crashes, OOMKill).

Q8
An HA cluster has 3 control plane nodes and one goes down. What happens?
Show Answer
Answer
3 cp nodes → quorum = 2 → can tolerate 1 failure ✓
# 3 CP nodes → Quorum = 2 → Can tolerate 1 failure ✓

# What happens when master-2 goes down:

# API Server:
# master-1 API server: ✅ Still serving requests
# master-3 API server: ✅ Still serving requests
# Load balancer routes to remaining 2 nodes
# kubectl commands still work (via LB)

# etcd:
# 3 members, 1 down → 2 alive → Quorum (2) met ✅
# Reads work, writes work
# "etcdctl member list" shows member as unreachable

# Controller Manager:
# If master-2 was the leader → new leader elected (~15s)
# If master-2 was standby → no impact
kubectl get lease kube-controller-manager -n kube-system
# HOLDER changes to master-1 or master-3

# Scheduler:
# Same as controller manager — leader election kicks in
kubectl get lease kube-scheduler -n kube-system

# Impact on workloads:
# ✅ Existing pods keep running (kubelet is independent)
# ✅ New pods can be created (scheduler on remaining CP)
# ✅ Self-healing works (controller-manager re-elected)
# ⚠️ But now: ONE MORE failure = total cluster loss!

# Action: Fix/replace master-2 ASAP
# 1. Fix the node if recoverable
# 2. OR remove and re-add: kubeadm reset + re-join
Explanation

With 3 CP nodes and 1 down: quorum is still met (2/3 alive), so the cluster functions normally. API server (via LB), etcd, controller-manager, and scheduler all continue. Leader election replaces the lost leader in ~15 seconds. Critical: you now have ZERO fault tolerance. If another node fails, you lose quorum and the cluster becomes read-only (no writes to etcd). Fix the failed node immediately.

Q9
How do you verify an HA cluster is properly configured?
Show Answer
Answer
check all control plane nodes
# 1. Check all control plane nodes:
kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
# NAME       STATUS  ROLES          VERSION
# master-1   Ready   control-plane  v1.31.0
# master-2   Ready   control-plane  v1.31.0
# master-3   Ready   control-plane  v1.31.0  ✓ 3 nodes

# 2. Check all control plane pods running:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "apiserver|etcd|scheduler|controller"
# All should show 1/1 Running for each master node

# 3. Check etcd cluster health:
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health \
--endpoints=https://master-1:2379,https://master-2:2379,https://master-3:2379 \
--cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
--cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
--key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key
# master-1:2379 is healthy
# master-2:2379 is healthy
# master-3:2379 is healthy  ✓

# 4. Check leader election:
kubectl get lease -n kube-system
# Controller-manager and scheduler should have HOLDERs ✓

# 5. Check API server endpoint:
kubectl cluster-info
# Should show LB address, not single node IP

# 6. Check PDBs for critical workloads:
kubectl get pdb -A
# Critical apps should have PDBs ✓

# 7. Test failover (carefully!):
# Simulate by stopping kubelet on one master
# Verify cluster still works after ~30s
Explanation

HA verification checklist: (1) 3+ control plane nodes all Ready, (2) all CP pods running (3 of each), (3) etcd cluster healthy, (4) leader election active, (5) API endpoint is a load balancer, (6) PDBs protect workloads. On the CKA, these verification steps help you understand what a working HA cluster looks like, which helps you diagnose when something is broken.

Q10
What is the role of the load balancer in an HA Kubernetes cluster?
Show Answer
Answer
load balancer sits in front of all api servers
# Load Balancer sits in front of ALL API servers:
#
#   kubectl → Load Balancer → API Server 1 (master-1)
#                           → API Server 2 (master-2)
#                           → API Server 3 (master-3)
#
# Workers also connect through the LB:
#   kubelet → Load Balancer → API Server (any)

# Configuration (HAProxy example):
# /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg
# frontend k8s-api
#   bind *:6443
#   default_backend k8s-api-backend
#
# backend k8s-api-backend
#   balance roundrobin
#   option httpchk GET /healthz
#   server master-1 10.0.0.1:6443 check
#   server master-2 10.0.0.2:6443 check
#   server master-3 10.0.0.3:6443 check

# What the LB does:
# ✅ Distributes API requests across CP nodes
# ✅ Health checks — removes dead nodes from rotation
# ✅ Single endpoint for all clients (kubectl, kubelet, etc.)
# ✅ Survives individual CP node failures

# What the LB does NOT do:
# ❌ Doesn't handle etcd traffic (etcd peers talk directly)
# ❌ Doesn't load balance pod-to-pod traffic (that's kube-proxy)
# ❌ Doesn't replace Ingress controllers

# LB is a SPOF — must also be HA in production:
# keepalived + virtual IP (active/passive)
# Cloud LB (inherently HA)
Explanation

The load balancer provides a single stable endpoint for the Kubernetes API, distributing requests across all control plane nodes. It's what --control-plane-endpoint points to. Health checks automatically remove unresponsive masters from the pool. On the CKA, understand that the LB only handles API server traffic (port 6443). etcd uses separate peer-to-peer communication. The LB itself must be HA in production (keepalived, cloud LB).

Q11
Write an HAProxy configuration for load balancing across 3 API servers. What health checks ensure traffic only goes to healthy masters?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
# /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg

frontend kubernetes-api
bind *:6443
mode tcp
option tcplog
default_backend api-servers

backend api-servers
mode tcp
option tcp-check
balance roundrobin
# Health check: TCP connect to port 6443
server master1 192.168.1.10:6443 check fall 3 rise 2 inter 5s
server master2 192.168.1.11:6443 check fall 3 rise 2 inter 5s
server master3 192.168.1.12:6443 check fall 3 rise 2 inter 5s

# Alternative: HTTP health check against /healthz
backend api-servers-http-check
mode tcp
option httpchk GET /healthz
http-check expect status 200
server master1 192.168.1.10:6443 check check-ssl verify none
server master2 192.168.1.11:6443 check check-ssl verify none
server master3 192.168.1.12:6443 check check-ssl verify none

# Health check explanation:
# check        → enable health checking
# fall 3       → mark down after 3 consecutive failures
# rise 2       → mark up after 2 consecutive successes
# inter 5s     → check every 5 seconds

# Start HAProxy:
sudo systemctl enable --now haproxy

# Verify:
curl -k https://<haproxy-ip>:6443/healthz
# ok

# kubeadm init with LB:
kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint="<haproxy-ip>:6443" \
--upload-certs
Explanation

The load balancer sits in front of all API servers and is the address all clients (kubectl, kubelet, kube-proxy) connect to. HAProxy in TCP mode passes through TLS without terminating it mode tcp. Health checks (fall 3 rise 2) automatically remove a crashed master from the rotation and re-add it when it recovers. This is what --control-plane-endpoint points to during kubeadm init. On the CKA, you won't configure HAProxy, but understanding that the LB is needed for HA and what port it forwards (6443 only) is essential for HA cluster questions.

Q12
What is the production readiness checklist for an HA Kubernetes cluster? List the key items you should verify before considering a cluster production-ready.
Show Answer
Answer
production ha readiness checklist
# Production HA Readiness Checklist:

# 1. Control Plane HA
kubectl get nodes | grep control-plane
# At least 3 control plane nodes (odd number for quorum)

# 2. etcd Cluster Health
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health --cluster \
--cacert=... --cert=... --key=...
# All members healthy, leader elected

# 3. Load Balancer
curl -k https://<lb-endpoint>:6443/healthz
# ok — LB routing to healthy API servers

# 4. Automated etcd Backups
kubectl get cronjob -n kube-system | grep etcd-backup
# Backup CronJob running on schedule

# 5. Pod Disruption Budgets
kubectl get pdb -A
# Critical workloads have PDBs preventing total downtime

# 6. Resource Requests & Limits
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] |
select(.spec.containers[].resources.requests == null) |
.metadata.name'
# No pods without resource requests (prevents scheduling chaos)

# 7. Node Redundancy
kubectl get nodes
# Multiple worker nodes across failure domains

# 8. Monitoring & Alerting
kubectl get pods -n monitoring
# Prometheus/Grafana or equivalent running

# 9. RBAC Configured
kubectl get clusterrolebindings | grep -v system
# Custom roles set up, no default service account abuse

# 10. Certificate Expiration
kubeadm certs check-expiration
# All certs valid, auto-renewal configured

# 11. Network Policies
kubectl get networkpolicies -A
# Default deny + explicit allow rules

# 12. Storage
kubectl get sc
# StorageClass with appropriate reclaim policy (Retain for prod)
Explanation

A production HA cluster needs more than just multiple masters. The key areas: (1) etcd quorum — odd number of members (3 or 5), (2) load balancer with health checks, (3) automated backups, (4) PDBs for critical workloads, (5) resource requests on all pods for proper scheduling, (6) certificate management, (7) RBAC and network policies. On the CKA, you're tested on individual pieces (etcd backup, PDBs, RBAC), but understanding how they fit together as a production readiness checklist shows mastery of the full stack.
