38.1 Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)

CONCEPT 📝 CKA EXAM

A Custom Resource Definition (CRD) lets you create entirely new resource types in Kubernetes. Once registered, your custom resources behave just like built-in ones — you can kubectl get, describe, delete, and apply them.

💡 Why CRDs Matter

Every popular Kubernetes tool uses CRDs: cert-manager creates Certificate resources, Prometheus Operator creates ServiceMonitor resources, ArgoCD creates Application resources. Understanding CRDs is understanding how the K8s ecosystem works.

CRD vs Built-in Resources

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                    Kubernetes API Server                  │
 ├──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┤
 │   BUILT-IN RESOURCES │       CUSTOM RESOURCES (CRDs)     │
 │   ─────────────────  │       ───────────────────────     │
 │   Pod          v1    │       Certificate   cert-manager  │
 │   Deployment   apps  │       ServiceMonitor prometheus   │
 │   Service      v1    │       Application   argocd        │
 │   ConfigMap    v1    │       DjangoApp     easypj (ours!)│
 │   Secret       v1    │       VirtualService istio        │
 │                      │                                   │
 │   API Group: core,   │       API Group: custom defined   │
 │   apps, networking   │       e.g. apps.easypj.io/v1     │
 └──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

Creating a CRD — easypj DjangoApp Example

Let's create a custom DjangoApp resource type that describes a Django application deployment:

djangoapp-crd.yaml — Custom Resource Definition 
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: djangoapps.apps.easypj.io    # Must match: plural.group
spec:
  group: apps.easypj.io              # API group for our custom resources
  versions:
    - name: v1                        # Version of our API
      served: true                    # Enable this version
      storage: true                   # Store objects in this version
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:              # Validation schema (required!)
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              required: ["image", "replicas"]
              properties:
                image:
                  type: string
                  description: "Container image for the Django app"
                replicas:
                  type: integer
                  minimum: 1
                  maximum: 20
                database:
                  type: object
                  properties:
                    engine:
                      type: string
                      enum: ["postgresql", "mysql", "sqlite3"]
                    host:
                      type: string
                port:
                  type: integer
                  default: 8000
            status:
              type: object
              properties:
                availableReplicas:
                  type: integer
                phase:
                  type: string
      subresources:
        status: {}                    # Enable /status subresource
      additionalPrinterColumns:       # Custom columns for kubectl get
        - name: Image
          type: string
          jsonPath: .spec.image
        - name: Replicas
          type: integer
          jsonPath: .spec.replicas
        - name: Phase
          type: string
          jsonPath: .status.phase
        - name: Age
          type: date
          jsonPath: .metadata.creationTimestamp
  scope: Namespaced                   # Namespaced (vs Cluster)
  names:
    plural: djangoapps                # kubectl get djangoapps
    singular: djangoapp               # kubectl get djangoapp
    kind: DjangoApp                   # kind: DjangoApp in YAML
    shortNames:
      - dja                           # kubectl get dja

Registering and Using the CRD

terminal — CRD lifecycle 
# Step 1: Register the CRD
kubectl apply -f djangoapp-crd.yaml
# customresourcedefinition.apiextensions.k8s.io/djangoapps.apps.easypj.io created

# Step 2: Verify CRD is registered
kubectl get crd djangoapps.apps.easypj.io
# NAME                          CREATED AT
# djangoapps.apps.easypj.io     2026-04-02T10:00:00Z

# Step 3: The new resource type is now available!
kubectl api-resources | grep djangoapp
# djangoapps   dja   apps.easypj.io/v1   true   DjangoApp

# Step 4: kubectl explain works on CRDs too!
kubectl explain djangoapp.spec
# KIND:     DjangoApp
# VERSION:  apps.easypj.io/v1
# FIELD:    spec
# FIELDS:
#   database     Object   ...
#   image        string   Container image for the Django app
#   replicas     integer  ...

Creating a Custom Resource Instance

easypj-djangoapp.yaml — Custom Resource instance 
apiVersion: apps.easypj.io/v1
kind: DjangoApp
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  image: easypj/jobpost:v2.1
  replicas: 3
  database:
    engine: postgresql
    host: postgres-svc.easypj.svc.cluster.local
  port: 8000
terminal — managing custom resources 
# Create the custom resource
kubectl apply -f easypj-djangoapp.yaml

# List custom resources (short name works!)
kubectl get dja -n easypj
# NAME         IMAGE                  REPLICAS   PHASE   AGE
# easypj-web   easypj/jobpost:v2.1    3                  5s

# Describe it — just like any built-in resource
kubectl describe djangoapp easypj-web -n easypj

# Edit it
kubectl edit djangoapp easypj-web -n easypj

# Delete it
kubectl delete djangoapp easypj-web -n easypj

# Delete the CRD (WARNING: deletes ALL custom resources of this type!)
kubectl delete crd djangoapps.apps.easypj.io
⚠️ CRD Deletion Warning

Deleting a CRD deletes ALL custom resources of that type across all namespaces. This is a cluster-wide destructive operation. Always back up custom resources before deleting a CRD: kubectl get djangoapps --all-namespaces -o yaml > backup.yaml

38.2 The Operator Pattern

CONCEPT

An Operator = CRD + Custom Controller. The CRD defines what your custom resource looks like, and the controller watches for those resources and takes action to make reality match the desired state.

Operator Pattern — How It Works

 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                     THE OPERATOR PATTERN                     │
 ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │                                                              │
 │  YOU create:        DjangoApp YAML                          │
 │       │              (desired state)                         │
 │       ▼                                                      │
 │  ┌──────────┐     ┌────────────────────┐                    │
 │  │ API      │────▶│ Controller (Watch)  │                    │
 │  │ Server   │     │                    │                    │
 │  │ (stores  │     │ "DjangoApp created" │                    │
 │  │  CRD)    │     │  → Create Deployment│                    │
 │  └──────────┘     │  → Create Service   │                    │
 │                   │  → Create ConfigMap  │                    │
 │                   │  → Create Ingress    │                    │
 │                   │  → Run migrations    │                    │
 │                   │  → Update status     │                    │
 │                   └────────────────────┘                    │
 │                           │                                  │
 │                           ▼                                  │
 │             ┌─────────────────────────┐                     │
 │             │    RECONCILIATION LOOP   │                     │
 │             │  Watch → Compare → Act   │                     │
 │             │  (desired vs actual)     │                     │
 │             └─────────────────────────┘                     │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Real-World Operators You Already Use

OperatorCRD It CreatesWhat It Automates
cert-managerCertificate, ClusterIssuerTLS certificate provisioning and renewal via Let's Encrypt
Prometheus OperatorServiceMonitor, PrometheusRuleMonitoring target discovery and alerting rules
PostgreSQL OperatorPostgresClusterDatabase provisioning, backups, failover, upgrades
ArgoCDApplication, AppProjectGitOps deployment sync and health monitoring
Ingress NGINXIngressClassHTTP routing based on Ingress resource specs
terminal — exploring Operators in your cluster 
# List ALL CRDs in the cluster — see what Operators installed
kubectl get crd
# NAME                                      CREATED AT
# certificates.cert-manager.io              2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
# clusterissuers.cert-manager.io            2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
# applications.argoproj.io                  2026-01-15T00:00:00Z
# servicemonitors.monitoring.coreos.com     2026-02-01T00:00:00Z

# List custom resources for a specific CRD
kubectl get certificates --all-namespaces
kubectl get servicemonitors --all-namespaces

# Check which controller manages a CRD
kubectl get deployment -n cert-manager
# NAME                      READY   AGE
# cert-manager              1/1     90d
# cert-manager-cainjector   1/1     90d
# cert-manager-webhook      1/1     90d
💡 Operator vs Controller

All Operators are controllers, but not all controllers are Operators. The built-in Deployment controller is a controller (it reconciles Deployments), but it's not called an "Operator" because it manages generic workloads. An Operator specifically manages a complex, stateful application with domain-specific knowledge (e.g., how to back up PostgreSQL, how to rotate TLS certificates).

🔄 Operator Reconciliation Loop

The controller continuously watches for changes and reconciles desired state with actual state — the same pattern Kubernetes uses internally for Deployments, Services, etc.

1
Watch

Controller subscribes to CRD events via the API server — create, update, delete notifications for DjangoApp resources

2
Compare

Read the DjangoApp spec (desired: 3 replicas, v2.1 image) and check current cluster state (actual: 2 replicas, v2.0)

3
Act

Create/update child resources — scale Deployment to 3, update image to v2.1, run database migrations

4
Update Status

Write back to DjangoApp .status — set phase to "Running", availableReplicas to 3

5
Repeat

Loop back to Watch — any drift (pod crash, manual change) triggers re-reconciliation automatically

38.3 API Aggregation Layer

CONCEPT

The API Aggregation Layer allows you to extend the Kubernetes API by registering additional API servers. Unlike CRDs (which store data in etcd via the main API server), aggregated APIs run their own backend — useful for resources that need custom storage or complex logic.

CRD vs API Aggregation — When to Use Each

 ┌──────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐
 │     CRD APPROACH          │    │   API AGGREGATION         │
 ├──────────────────────────┤    ├──────────────────────────┤
 │ ✅ Simple to create       │    │ ✅ Custom storage backend │
 │ ✅ No extra server needed │    │ ✅ Custom validation logic│
 │ ✅ Stored in etcd         │    │ ✅ Protocol translation   │
 │ ❌ Limited validation     │    │ ❌ Complex to build       │
 │ ❌ No custom storage      │    │ ❌ Requires running server│
 │                          │    │                          │
 │ USE FOR:                  │    │ USE FOR:                  │
 │ Most custom resources     │    │ metrics-server            │
 │ App configuration         │    │ Custom metrics API        │
 │ Operator CRDs             │    │ Complex sub-resources     │
 └──────────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────────┘

The most common example you interact with daily is metrics-server — it registers an aggregated API at /apis/metrics.k8s.io so that kubectl top pods and kubectl top nodes work. It doesn't store data in etcd; it collects real-time metrics from kubelets.

📋 Use CRDs When
  • You need simple CRUD operations on custom types
  • Data fits naturally in etcd (configs, specs, state)
  • You want easy setup with just a YAML file
  • Validation via OpenAPI schema is sufficient
  • Examples: cert-manager, ArgoCD, Prometheus Operator
🔌 Use API Aggregation When
  • You need a custom storage backend (not etcd)
  • Data is real-time/ephemeral (metrics, logs)
  • You need complex protocol translation
  • Sub-resources need custom behavior
  • Examples: metrics-server, custom metrics API
terminal — check registered API services 
# List all registered API services
kubectl get apiservice | head -20
# NAME                       SERVICE                      AVAILABLE
# v1.                        Local                        True
# v1.apps                    Local                        True
# v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io     kube-system/metrics-server   True  ← aggregated!

# "Local" = built-in API, handled by main API server
# A service reference = aggregated API, handled by separate server

# Check a specific aggregated API
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io -o yaml
# spec:
#   group: metrics.k8s.io
#   service:
#     name: metrics-server
#     namespace: kube-system

38.4 kubectl Plugins and krew

COMMANDS

kubectl supports a plugin mechanism — any executable named kubectl-PLUGINNAME in your PATH becomes a kubectl subcommand. krew is the plugin package manager (like apt/yum for kubectl).

terminal — kubectl plugins 
# List installed plugins
kubectl plugin list

# Install krew (the plugin manager)
# See: https://krew.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user-guide/setup/install/

# Install useful plugins via krew
kubectl krew install ctx       # Fast context switching
kubectl krew install ns        # Fast namespace switching
kubectl krew install neat      # Clean up kubectl output (remove managed fields)
kubectl krew install tree      # Show resource ownership hierarchy
kubectl krew install who-can   # RBAC analysis — who can do what?

# Usage examples
kubectl ctx production         # Switch to production context
kubectl ns easypj              # Switch to easypj namespace
kubectl neat get pod web-0 -o yaml   # Clean YAML output
kubectl tree deployment easypj-web   # Show: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods
kubectl who-can create pods -n easypj
📝 CKA Note

kubectl plugins (krew) are NOT available on the CKA exam. However, you should understand how the plugin mechanism works conceptually: any executable named kubectl-<name> in your PATH is automatically discovered as a plugin. This is relevant for understanding how organizations extend kubectl for their workflows.

38.5 Admission Webhooks

CONCEPT 📝 CKA EXAM

After a request passes authentication and authorization, it goes through admission control. Kubernetes has two types of dynamic admission webhooks:

API Request Flow — Where Webhooks Fit

 kubectl apply ──▶ API Server
                      │
            ┌─────────┼─────────┐
            ▼         ▼         ▼
       Authentication  Authorization  Admission Control
       (Who are you?)  (Can you do    ┌─────────────────┐
                        this?)        │ 1. Mutating      │
                                     │    Webhooks       │
                                     │    (modify req)   │
                                     │                   │
                                     │ 2. Schema         │
                                     │    Validation     │
                                     │                   │
                                     │ 3. Validating     │
                                     │    Webhooks       │
                                     │    (accept/reject)│
                                     └─────────────────┘
                                            │
                                            ▼
                                       etcd (persist)
FeatureMutatingWebhookConfigurationValidatingWebhookConfiguration
When it runsFirst — before validationAfter mutation + schema validation
Can modify request?✅ Yes — can add/change/remove fields❌ No — can only accept or reject
Use caseInject sidecars, add labels, set defaultsEnforce policies, block insecure configs
ExampleIstio sidecar injectionDeny pods without resource limits

Example: Validating Webhook — Require Labels on Pods

🎯 Admission Control — The API Server Gateway

Every resource mutation passes through admission control. Mutating webhooks run first (can change the request), then validating webhooks (can only accept/reject). This is your last chance to enforce policies before data hits etcd.

validating-webhook.yaml — require "team" label on all pods 
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
webhooks:
  - name: require-team-label.easypj.io
    admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
    sideEffects: None
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: webhook-server          # Your webhook service
        namespace: webhook-system
        path: /validate-pods
      caBundle: <base64-encoded-CA>   # CA cert for TLS
    rules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        resources: ["pods"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
    namespaceSelector:                # Only in labeled namespaces
      matchLabels:
        webhook-enabled: "true"
    failurePolicy: Fail               # Reject if webhook unreachable
    timeoutSeconds: 5
⚠️ failurePolicy: Fail vs Ignore

Fail (default) — if the webhook is down, ALL matching requests are rejected. Safe but can break your cluster if the webhook crashes. Ignore — if the webhook is down, requests pass through without validation. Less safe but prevents cluster lockout. For production, use Fail with high availability for the webhook server.

38.6 ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL-Based)

CONCEPT 📝 CKA EXAM

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (GA in Kubernetes v1.30) lets you write validation rules using Common Expression Language (CEL) — no external webhook server needed! This is the future of in-cluster policy enforcement.

require-replicas-policy.yaml — No single-replica deployments 
# Step 1: Define the policy
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-minimum-replicas
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: ["apps"]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["deployments"]
  validations:
    - expression: "object.spec.replicas >= 2"
      message: "Deployments must have at least 2 replicas for high availability"
    - expression: "has(object.spec.template.spec.containers) && object.spec.template.spec.containers.all(c, has(c.resources) && has(c.resources.limits))"
      message: "All containers must have resource limits defined"
---
# Step 2: Bind the policy to namespaces
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: require-minimum-replicas-binding
spec:
  policyName: require-minimum-replicas
  validationActions: [Deny]          # Deny, Warn, or Audit
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        environment: production       # Only enforce in production
terminal — testing the policy 
# Label namespace for policy enforcement
kubectl label namespace easypj environment=production

# Apply the policy
kubectl apply -f require-replicas-policy.yaml

# Test — this should be DENIED
kubectl create deployment test --image=nginx --replicas=1 -n easypj
# Error: Deployments must have at least 2 replicas for high availability

# This should SUCCEED
kubectl create deployment test --image=nginx --replicas=3 -n easypj
# deployment.apps/test created

# List policies
kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicies
kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicybindings
💡 CEL Expression Cheat Sheet

object = the resource being created/updated. oldObject = the previous version (for UPDATE). has(object.spec.field) = check if field exists. object.spec.containers.all(c, expr) = check all items. object.metadata.labels.exists(k, k == "team") = check labels.

38.7 RBAC for Custom Resources

COMMANDS 📝 CKA EXAM

Custom resources follow the same RBAC model as built-in resources. You need to grant access to the CRD's API group and resource name.

crd-rbac.yaml — RBAC for DjangoApp CRD 
# Role for managing DjangoApp custom resources
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: djangoapp-manager
  namespace: easypj
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps.easypj.io"]     # CRD API group
    resources: ["djangoapps"]          # CRD plural name
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
  - apiGroups: ["apps.easypj.io"]
    resources: ["djangoapps/status"]   # Status subresource
    verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: djangoapp-manager-binding
  namespace: easypj
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: easypj-operator
    namespace: easypj
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: djangoapp-manager
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

Verify RBAC for Custom Resources

# Check if a service account can access CRDs
kubectl auth can-i get djangoapps --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-operator -n easypj
# yes

kubectl auth can-i delete djangoapps --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-operator -n easypj
# yes

# Note: to CREATE CRDs themselves (not instances), you need cluster-level access:
kubectl auth can-i create customresourcedefinitions --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-operator
# no  ← only cluster admins should create/delete CRDs
Under the Hood — How Kubernetes API Extensions Actually Work: CRD Schema Validation, Operator Reconciliation Loop, Admission Webhook Flow, and API Aggregation Architecture
🗺️ CRD Internals — How Custom Resources Become Part of the API

A CRD is not just a YAML file — it registers a new resource type in the Kubernetes API, creates an etcd key prefix, and enables standard kubectl operations on custom objects.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CRD LIFECYCLE — Registration to Usable Resource                              │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 1: CREATE CRD                                                           │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ $ kubectl apply -f djangoapp-crd.yaml                                 │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1                                   │   │
│  │ kind: CustomResourceDefinition                                         │   │
│  │ metadata:                                                              │   │
│  │   name: djangoapps.easypj.io  ← Must be: <plural>.<group>             │   │
│  │ spec:                                                                  │   │
│  │   group: easypj.io                                                     │   │
│  │   versions:                                                            │   │
│  │   - name: v1                                                           │   │
│  │     served: true                                                       │   │
│  │     storage: true                                                      │   │
│  │     schema:                                                            │   │
│  │       openAPIV3Schema:  ← Defines structure + validation              │   │
│  │         type: object                                                   │   │
│  │         properties:                                                    │   │
│  │           spec:                                                        │   │
│  │             type: object                                               │   │
│  │             properties:                                                │   │
│  │               replicas: {type: integer, minimum: 1}                   │   │
│  │               image: {type: string}                                    │   │
│  │   scope: Namespaced  ← Namespaced or Cluster                           │   │
│  │   names:                                                               │   │
│  │     plural: djangoapps                                                 │   │
│  │     singular: djangoapp                                                │   │
│  │     kind: DjangoApp                                                    │   │
│  │     shortNames: [da]                                                   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 2: API SERVER REGISTERS THE CRD                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. API Server detects new CRD in etcd                                 │   │
│  │ 2. Registers new REST endpoint:                                       │   │
│  │    /apis/easypj.io/v1/namespaces/{ns}/djangoapps                      │   │
│  │ 3. Creates etcd key prefix:                                            │   │
│  │    /registry/easypj.io/djangoapps/                                     │   │
│  │ 4. OpenAPI schema updated → kubectl explain DjangoApp works!          │   │
│  │ 5. kubectl api-resources now shows: djangoapps da easypj.io/v1 true   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 3: CREATE CUSTOM RESOURCE INSTANCES                                    │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ $ kubectl apply -f my-djangoapp.yaml                                   │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ apiVersion: easypj.io/v1                                              │   │
│  │ kind: DjangoApp                                                        │   │
│  │ metadata:                                                              │   │
│  │   name: easypj-production                                              │   │
│  │ spec:                                                                  │   │
│  │   replicas: 3                                                          │   │
│  │   image: ghcr.io/user/easypj:v2.1                                     │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ CRD instances are just like any other K8s resource:                   │   │
│  │ $ kubectl get djangoapps                                               │   │
│  │ $ kubectl describe djangoapp easypj-production                         │   │
│  │ $ kubectl edit djangoapp easypj-production                             │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 Operator Pattern — Custom Controller Reconciliation

An Operator = CRD + Custom Controller. The controller watches CRD instances and reconciles actual state with desired state — the same pattern used by built-in controllers:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  OPERATOR RECONCILIATION LOOP                                                 │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  1. WATCH: DjangoApp CRD instances (via K8s API watch)                │   │
│  │     → djangoapp/easypj-production created                              │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  2. RECONCILE:                                                         │   │
│  │     Desired (CRD spec):        Actual (cluster):                       │   │
│  │     ┌──────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐                   │   │
│  │     │ replicas: 3       │       │ No Deployment yet │                   │   │
│  │     │ image: easypj:v2.1│  vs   │ No Service yet    │                   │   │
│  │     │ env: [DB_HOST,...] │       │ No ConfigMap yet  │                   │   │
│  │     └──────────────────┘       └──────────────────┘                   │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  3. ACT:                                                               │   │
│  │     → Create ConfigMap (from spec.env)                                 │   │
│  │     → Create Deployment (spec.replicas, spec.image)                    │   │
│  │     → Create Service (ClusterIP, port 8000)                            │   │
│  │     → Update CRD status: phase=Running, url=easypj-svc:8000           │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  4. LOOP: Watch for changes → reconcile again                          │   │
│  │     → User changes replicas: 3→5 → controller scales Deployment       │   │
│  │     → User updates image → controller updates Deployment → rollout    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  OPERATOR FRAMEWORKS (simplify controller development):                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ • Operator SDK (Go/Ansible/Helm) — Red Hat's framework                │   │
│  │ • Kubebuilder — Official k8s SIG project, Go-based                   │   │
│  │ • KUDO — Declarative operator building                                │   │
│  │ • Kopf — Python operator framework                                     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔧 Admission Webhooks — Mutating + Validating Request Interception

Webhooks let external services intercept and modify/validate API requests BEFORE they're persisted to etcd:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ADMISSION WEBHOOK FLOW                                                       │
│                                                                              │
│  kubectl create pod → API Server                                              │
│                               │                                               │
│                               ▼                                               │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  MUTATING WEBHOOKS (run FIRST, in order):                             │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │   │
│  │  │ 1. API Server sends AdmissionReview (JSON) to webhook URL     │    │   │
│  │  │ 2. Webhook modifies the object (e.g., inject sidecar,        │    │   │
│  │  │    add labels, set defaults)                                   │    │   │
│  │  │ 3. Webhook returns AdmissionResponse with JSON patch           │    │   │
│  │  │ 4. API Server applies the patch                                │    │   │
│  │  │                                                               │    │   │
│  │  │  Example: Istio injects sidecar container into every pod      │    │   │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                               │                                               │
│                               ▼                                               │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  VALIDATING WEBHOOKS (run AFTER mutating):                            │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │   │
│  │  │ 1. API Server sends AdmissionReview to webhook URL            │    │   │
│  │  │ 2. Webhook validates the object (policy checks)              │    │   │
│  │  │ 3. Returns: allowed: true OR allowed: false + message        │    │   │
│  │  │ 4. If false → API Server rejects the request (403 Forbidden) │    │   │
│  │  │                                                               │    │   │
│  │  │  Example: Require all pods to have resource limits           │    │   │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                               │                                               │
│                               ▼                                               │
│                          PERSIST TO etcd                                     │
│                                                                              │
│  WEBHOOK REQUIREMENTS:                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ • Must be accessible via HTTPS (TLS required)                         │   │
│  │ • Runs as a Service inside the cluster                                │   │
│  │ • Requires caBundle in webhook config (CA cert for TLS validation)    │   │
│  │ • Timeout: default 10s (webhook must respond in time)                 │   │
│  │ • Failure policy: Ignore (allow request) or Fail (reject request)     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CKA Insight: While CRDs and Operators are not heavily tested on the CKA, understanding the extension model helps with troubleshooting. Key points: (1) CRDs create new API endpoints — kubectl api-resources shows them, (2) CRD schema validation is OpenAPI v3 based, (3) Admission webhooks intercept ALL matching requests — a broken webhook with failurePolicy=Fail can BLOCK all pod creation, (4) Always check webhook configurations if pods suddenly can't be created: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations.

🔑 Key Takeaways

Bulleted key takeaways go here.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • ❌ Wrong metadata.name — must be plural.group (e.g., djangoapps.apps.easypj.io), not just the kind name
  • ❌ Missing openAPIV3Schema — required since K8s v1.16. Without it, the CRD won't be accepted
  • ❌ Forgetting served: true and storage: true — at least one version must have both set to true
  • ✅ Always verify — kubectl get crd | grep yourname after creating. If it's not listed, check kubectl describe crd for errors
⚡ Speed Tips

CKA Exam Context — You probably won't build a webhook server on the exam, but you need to understand the ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration resource structure. Know how to kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations and troubleshoot when a webhook blocks legitimate requests.

Q38.1
Create a CRD called backups.data.easypj.io with a Backup kind. It should be namespaced, have a v1 version, and require spec.source (string) and spec.schedule (string) fields. Then create a Backup resource in the easypj namespace.
Show Answer 
# CRD definition
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
name: backups.data.easypj.io
spec:
group: data.easypj.io
versions:
- name: v1
  served: true
  storage: true
  schema:
    openAPIV3Schema:
      type: object
      properties:
        spec:
          type: object
          required: ["source", "schedule"]
          properties:
            source:
              type: string
            schedule:
              type: string
scope: Namespaced
names:
plural: backups
singular: backup
kind: Backup
---
# Backup instance
apiVersion: data.easypj.io/v1
kind: Backup
metadata:
name: db-daily
namespace: easypj
spec:
source: postgresql
schedule: "0 2 * * *"
Explanation

CRD metadata.name MUST be plural.group — so backups.data.easypj.io. The schema is required and validates that source and schedule are strings. Once the CRD is registered, you create instances using the CRD's apiVersion (group/version) and kind. On the CKA, always apply the CRD first, verify with kubectl get crd, then create the custom resource.

Q38.2
List all CRDs in the cluster. Find which CRDs belong to cert-manager. Then check who can create certificates (cert-manager CRD) in the easypj namespace.
Show Answer 
# List all CRDs
kubectl get crd

# Filter for cert-manager CRDs
kubectl get crd | grep cert-manager
# certificates.cert-manager.io
# certificaterequests.cert-manager.io
# clusterissuers.cert-manager.io
# issuers.cert-manager.io
# orders.acme.cert-manager.io
# challenges.acme.cert-manager.io

# Check who can create certificates
kubectl auth can-i create certificates.cert-manager.io \
--as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:default -n easypj

# Use who-can (if available) for comprehensive RBAC analysis
kubectl who-can create certificates.cert-manager.io -n easypj
Explanation

CRDs are cluster-scoped resources — kubectl get crd lists all of them regardless of namespace. To filter by a specific operator, grep for the group name (e.g., cert-manager). When checking RBAC for custom resources, use the full resource name including the API group: certificates.cert-manager.io, not just certificates. The kubectl auth can-i command also works with --as= to test permissions for other users/service accounts.

Q38.3
Create a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy that prevents creating Pods with privileged: true security context. Bind it to the easypj namespace only.
Show Answer 
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
name: deny-privileged-pods
spec:
failurePolicy: Fail
matchConstraints:
resourceRules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    apiVersions: ["v1"]
    operations: ["CREATE"]
    resources: ["pods"]
validations:
- expression: >-
    object.spec.containers.all(c,
      !has(c.securityContext) ||
      !has(c.securityContext.privileged) ||
      c.securityContext.privileged == false)
  message: "Privileged containers are not allowed"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
name: deny-privileged-pods-binding
spec:
policyName: deny-privileged-pods
validationActions: [Deny]
matchResources:
namespaceSelector:
  matchLabels:
    kubernetes.io/metadata.name: easypj
Explanation

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy uses CEL expressions for in-cluster policy enforcement without external webhooks. The expression checks every container in the pod spec — if none has privileged: true, the pod is allowed. The binding uses namespaceSelector to limit enforcement to the easypj namespace (using the automatic label kubernetes.io/metadata.name). This replaces the need for OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno for simple policies. Available since K8s v1.30 GA.

Q38.4
Explain the difference between CRDs and API Aggregation. Give an example of when you'd use each approach. How does metrics-server use API aggregation?
Show Answer 
# Check if metrics-server uses API aggregation
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io -o yaml
# spec:
#   group: metrics.k8s.io
#   service:
#     name: metrics-server
#     namespace: kube-system

# Verify the aggregated API works
kubectl top pods -n easypj
kubectl top nodes
Explanation

CRDs: Store data in etcd, no custom server needed, simple to create. Use for: app configuration, operator-managed resources (Certificates, Applications). API Aggregation: Runs a separate API server, can have custom storage backend, complex to build. Use for: real-time data that shouldn't be in etcd (metrics), protocol translation. metrics-server uses API aggregation because it serves real-time CPU/memory metrics collected from kubelets — storing this in etcd would be wasteful and slow. It registers at metrics.k8s.io and proxies kubectl top requests to its own server.

Q38.5
A ValidatingWebhookConfiguration is blocking pod creation with the error "webhook denied the request". The webhook service is down. How do you temporarily fix this?
Show Answer 
# List validating webhooks
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations

# Check which webhook is failing
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration <name> -o yaml

# Option 1: Change failurePolicy to Ignore (temporary!)
kubectl patch validatingwebhookconfiguration <name> \
--type='json' -p='[{"op": "replace", "path": "/webhooks/0/failurePolicy", "value": "Ignore"}]'

# Option 2: Delete the webhook configuration entirely (if safe)
kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration <name>

# Option 3: Fix the webhook service (proper fix)
kubectl get svc -n webhook-system
kubectl get pods -n webhook-system
kubectl logs -n webhook-system <webhook-pod>
Explanation

When a webhook with failurePolicy: Fail is unreachable, ALL matching API requests are rejected — this can lock you out of creating/updating resources. Quick fix: patch the failurePolicy to Ignore so requests pass through while you fix the webhook server. The proper fix is to ensure the webhook service and pods are running. On the CKA, if you see "webhook denied the request" errors, check kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations and kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations.

39.1 The Kubernetes Security Hardening Checklist

CONCEPT 📝 CKA EXAM

Use this as a reference checklist when securing a cluster. Each item links to the detailed section below.

1
Infrastructure Layer

API server flags, etcd encryption at rest, audit logging, component TLS — secure the foundation

2
Auth & RBAC

Least-privilege roles, disable default SA token mounting, no wildcard permissions, audit bindings

3
Admission Control

Pod Security Standards (restricted), ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, image registry allowlisting

4
Workload Hardening

SecurityContext (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem), drop ALL capabilities, seccomp profiles

5
Network Isolation

Default-deny NetworkPolicy per namespace, egress filtering, DNS rules, mTLS with service mesh

6
Data Protection

Secrets encrypted at rest, mount as files (not env), external secret stores, credential rotation

Security Layers — Defense in Depth

 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                  DEFENSE IN DEPTH                            │
 ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │                                                              │
 │  Layer 1: CLUSTER INFRASTRUCTURE                            │
 │  ├── API server flags (--anonymous-auth=false)              │
 │  ├── etcd encryption at rest                                │
 │  ├── Audit logging enabled                                  │
 │  └── Component TLS (kubelet, etcd)                          │
 │                                                              │
 │  Layer 2: AUTHENTICATION & AUTHORIZATION                    │
 │  ├── RBAC with least privilege                              │
 │  ├── Disable default SA token auto-mount                    │
 │  ├── No cluster-admin for workloads                         │
 │  └── Audit who has wildcard permissions                     │
 │                                                              │
 │  Layer 3: ADMISSION CONTROL                                 │
 │  ├── Pod Security Admission (restricted)                    │
 │  ├── ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL)                        │
 │  ├── Image allowlisting                                     │
 │  └── Deny privileged containers                              │
 │                                                              │
 │  Layer 4: WORKLOAD SECURITY                                 │
 │  ├── SecurityContext (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem) │
 │  ├── Resource limits (CPU/memory)                           │
 │  ├── seccomp / AppArmor profiles                            │
 │  └── No hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC                       │
 │                                                              │
 │  Layer 5: NETWORK SECURITY                                  │
 │  ├── Default-deny NetworkPolicy                             │
 │  ├── Egress filtering                                       │
 │  ├── Namespace isolation                                    │
 │  └── mTLS (service mesh)                                    │
 │                                                              │
 │  Layer 6: DATA SECURITY                                     │
 │  ├── Secrets encrypted at rest                              │
 │  ├── External secret management (Vault, etc.)               │
 │  ├── No secrets in environment variables                    │
 │  └── Rotate credentials regularly                           │
 │                                                              │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

39.2 RBAC Hardening Deep Dive

CONCEPT 📝 CKA EXAM

Dangerous Permissions to Avoid

These RBAC rules grant far more access than they appear to. Treat them as red flags during security reviews.

Dangerous PermissionWhy It's DangerousWhat to Do Instead
verbs: ["*"] on any resourceGrants ALL operations including deleteList only the verbs you need: ["get", "list", "watch"]
resources: ["*"]Access to ALL resource types in the API groupList specific resources: ["pods", "services"]
apiGroups: ["*"]Access across ALL API groupsSpecify: ["", "apps", "networking.k8s.io"]
create on podsCan exec into nodes, mount secrets, escapeGrant create on deployments instead
escalate on rolesCan grant themselves cluster-adminNever grant to workload service accounts
bind on clusterrolesCan bind any role to any subjectLimit to specific roles with resourceNames
impersonate on users/groupsCan act as any user including cluster-adminNever grant unless absolutely required

RBAC Best Practices — easypj Example

rbac-hardened.yaml — least-privilege for easypj app 
# ❌ BAD — overly permissive
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: bad-example-do-not-use
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["*"]
    resources: ["*"]
    verbs: ["*"]           # This is basically cluster-admin!
---
# ✅ GOOD — least privilege for easypj web app
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-role
  namespace: easypj
rules:
  # Read-only access to ConfigMaps (for Django settings)
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    resourceNames: ["easypj-config"]  # Only THIS specific ConfigMap
    verbs: ["get", "watch"]
  
  # Read-only access to Secrets (for DB credentials)
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["secrets"]
    resourceNames: ["easypj-db-secret"]
    verbs: ["get"]
  
  # No access to pods, services, etc. — the app doesn't need it
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-binding
  namespace: easypj
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: easypj-web-sa
    namespace: easypj
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: easypj-web-role
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

Audit Existing RBAC Permissions

terminal — RBAC audit commands 
# Find all ClusterRoleBindings that reference cluster-admin
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") |
  .metadata.name + " → " + (.subjects[]? | .kind + "/" + .name)'

# Check what a specific ServiceAccount can do
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-web-sa -n easypj

# Find roles with wildcard permissions
kubectl get roles,clusterroles -A -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.rules[]? | .verbs[]? == "*") |
  .kind + "/" + .metadata.name'

# Verify no default SA has extra bindings
kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | .name == "default") |
  .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name'

RBAC Gotchas on the CKA

  • ❌ Role vs ClusterRole — Role is namespace-scoped, ClusterRole is cluster-wide. Use Role unless you need cross-namespace access
  • ❌ RoleBinding to ClusterRole — this is valid! It scopes the ClusterRole's permissions to a single namespace
  • ❌ Forgetting apiGroup — core resources (pods, services) use "", apps resources use "apps"
  • ✅ Use resourceNames — when possible, restrict access to specific named resources

39.3 Secrets Management Best Practices

CONCEPT 📝 CKA EXAM

Kubernetes Secrets are Base64-encoded, not encrypted by default. Anyone with RBAC access to Secrets or etcd can read them. Here's how to harden Secrets properly.

⚠️ Critical Security Truth

echo "cGFzc3dvcmQ=" | base64 -d → password. Base64 is encoding, NOT encryption. Without additional measures, Secrets in etcd are plaintext-equivalent. NEVER assume Secrets are safe by default.

Enable Encryption at Rest

encryption-config.yaml — encrypt secrets in etcd 
# /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
    providers:
      - aescbc:                      # AES-CBC encryption
          keys:
            - name: key1
              secret: <base64-encoded-32-byte-key>
      - identity: {}                 # Fallback: read unencrypted (for migration)
terminal — enable encryption at rest 
# 1. Generate a 32-byte encryption key
head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64

# 2. Add --encryption-provider-config flag to kube-apiserver
# Edit: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add to spec.containers[0].command:
#   --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml

# 3. Mount the encryption config into the API server pod
# Add volume and volumeMount to kube-apiserver.yaml

# 4. Re-encrypt existing Secrets (they're still unencrypted!)
kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -

# 5. Verify encryption is working
# Read a Secret directly from etcd — should be encrypted
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/easypj/easypj-db-secret \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt | hexdump -C | head

Secrets Anti-Patterns vs Best Practices

Anti-Pattern ❌Best Practice ✅Why
Secrets in env varsMount as files via volumeMountEnv vars appear in logs, process listings, and crash dumps
Secrets in Git reposUse SealedSecrets or external secret storesGit history is permanent — secrets can never be truly removed
Using the default SACreate dedicated ServiceAccountsDefault SA is shared by all pods in a namespace
Auto-mounting SA tokensSet automountServiceAccountToken: falseMost pods don't need API server access
Hardcoding secrets in YAMLUse kubectl create secret or external toolKeeps secret values out of manifest files
How should I provide secrets to my pod?
Need K8s-native?
✅ Use K8s Secret mounted as volume file
Production/enterprise?
✅ External secret store (Vault, AWS SM)
Never use these approaches:
❌ Environment variables — leak in logs/crashes
❌ Hardcoded in YAML — committed to Git history
easypj-secure-pod.yaml — proper secret handling 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  serviceAccountName: easypj-web-sa
  automountServiceAccountToken: false   # ✅ Don't mount SA token
  containers:
    - name: django
      image: easypj/jobpost:v2.1
      volumeMounts:
        - name: db-creds
          mountPath: /etc/secrets/db     # ✅ Mount as files
          readOnly: true                 # ✅ Read-only mount
  volumes:
    - name: db-creds
      secret:
        secretName: easypj-db-secret
        defaultMode: 0400                # ✅ Restrictive permissions

39.4 API Server & Control Plane Security

CONCEPT 📝 CKA EXAM

The API server is the front door to your cluster. Hardening it is your highest priority.

Critical API Server Flags

FlagRecommended ValuePurpose
--anonymous-authfalseDisable unauthenticated access to the API
--enable-admission-pluginsInclude NodeRestriction,PodSecurityRestrict node self-modification, enforce pod security
--audit-log-path/var/log/kubernetes/audit.logEnable audit logging for all API requests
--audit-policy-filePoint to policy YAMLDefine what events to record and at what level
--profilingfalseDisable profiling endpoints (information disclosure)
--insecure-port0 (disabled)No HTTP access — HTTPS only (deprecated, removed in 1.24)
--encryption-provider-configPoint to config fileEncrypt secrets at rest in etcd

Audit Logging — Tracking Who Did What

audit-policy.yaml — sample audit policy 
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
  # Log Secret access at Metadata level (don't log Secret content!)
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["secrets"]
  
  # Log all write operations at RequestResponse level
  - level: RequestResponse
    verbs: ["create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["pods", "services", "configmaps"]
      - group: "apps"
        resources: ["deployments", "statefulsets", "daemonsets"]
  
  # Log RBAC changes at RequestResponse level
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
      - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
        resources: ["roles", "rolebindings", "clusterroles", "clusterrolebindings"]
  
  # Don't log read-only requests to known non-sensitive endpoints
  - level: None
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["events"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  
  # Catch-all: log everything else at Metadata level
  - level: Metadata

CKA Exam — You may be asked to configure audit logging. Remember the four audit levels: None (no logging), Metadata (log request metadata only), Request (log request body), RequestResponse (log both request and response body). Never log Secret content — use Metadata level for Secrets.

39.5 Runtime Security — seccomp & AppArmor

CONCEPT

seccomp Profiles

seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) restricts which Linux system calls a container can make. By blocking dangerous syscalls, you reduce the attack surface if a container is compromised.

easypj-seccomp.yaml — seccomp profile for Django app 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-hardened
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault          # ✅ Use container runtime's default profile
  containers:
    - name: django
      image: easypj/jobpost:v2.1
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true           # ✅ Never run as root
        runAsUser: 1000
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true # ✅ Prevent filesystem writes
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # ✅ Block setuid/setgid
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]              # ✅ Drop ALL Linux capabilities
      volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp            # Django needs a writable temp dir
  volumes:
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir: {}                   # ✅ Provide writable tmp via emptyDir

AppArmor Profiles

AppArmor is a Linux Security Module that restricts a program's capabilities — file access, network access, and raw socket creation.

apparmor-pod.yaml — apply AppArmor profile 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-apparmor
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  containers:
    - name: django
      image: easypj/jobpost:v2.1
      securityContext:
        appArmorProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault       # Use runtime default AppArmor profile
          # type: Localhost           # Or use a custom profile:
          # localhostProfile: easypj-web-profile
📝 seccomp vs AppArmor

seccomp restricts system calls (kernel-level operations). AppArmor restricts file and network access (path-based). They are complementary — use both for defense in depth. The RuntimeDefault profile for both is a good starting point that blocks obviously dangerous operations without breaking most applications.

🔒 seccomp (System Call Filter)
  • Layer: Kernel syscalls
  • Blocks: mount, reboot, ptrace, raw sockets
  • Config: securityContext.seccompProfile
  • Types: RuntimeDefault, Localhost, Unconfined
  • Best for: Preventing kernel exploits
🛡️ AppArmor (Application Armor)
  • Layer: File/network access paths
  • Blocks: /etc/shadow reads, raw network, specific file writes
  • Config: securityContext.appArmorProfile
  • Types: RuntimeDefault, Localhost, Unconfined
  • Best for: Preventing file-based attacks

39.6 Supply Chain Security

CONCEPT

Securing the container image supply chain prevents compromised or vulnerable images from running in your cluster.

📌
Pin Image Versions

Use specific tags (v2.1) or SHA digests — never :latest

🔍
Scan Images

Run vulnerability scanners (Trivy, Grype) in CI/CD before deployment

✍️
Sign Images

Use cosign/Notation to verify image provenance and integrity

🏢
Allowlist Registries

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy to restrict image sources to trusted repos only

📦
Minimal Base Images

Use -slim or distroless images — fewer packages = fewer vulnerabilities

image-security-best-practices 
# ✅ Best Practice 1: Use specific image tags (NEVER use :latest)
containers:
  - name: django
    image: easypj/jobpost:v2.1        # ✅ Pinned version
    # image: easypj/jobpost:latest     # ❌ Mutable, unpredictable
    # image: easypj/jobpost             # ❌ Defaults to :latest

# ✅ Best Practice 2: Use image digests for maximum immutability
containers:
  - name: django
    image: easypj/jobpost@sha256:abc123...  # ✅ Content-addressable

# ✅ Best Practice 3: Set imagePullPolicy
containers:
  - name: django
    image: easypj/jobpost:v2.1
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent     # or Always for security-critical apps

# ✅ Best Practice 4: Use minimal base images
# Dockerfile:
# FROM python:3.12-slim              # ✅ Minimal — fewer vulnerabilities
# FROM python:3.12                    # ❌ Full — larger attack surface
# FROM ubuntu:24.04                   # ❌ General purpose — bloated

Restrict Image Sources with ValidatingAdmissionPolicy

restrict-registries.yaml — only allow trusted registries 
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-image-registries
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["pods"]
  validations:
    - expression: >-
        object.spec.containers.all(c,
          c.image.startsWith('easypj/') ||
          c.image.startsWith('registry.company.com/') ||
          c.image.startsWith('gcr.io/distroless/'))
      message: "Images must come from approved registries: easypj/, registry.company.com/, gcr.io/distroless/"

39.7 Multi-Tenancy & Namespace Isolation

CONCEPT 📝 CKA EXAM

In multi-tenant clusters, namespaces are the primary isolation boundary. But namespaces alone aren't enough — you need RBAC, NetworkPolicy, ResourceQuota, and Pod Security working together.

Multi-Tenancy Isolation Stack

 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │              MULTI-TENANCY ISOLATION STACK                 │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │                                                            │
 │  Namespace: team-a        │  Namespace: team-b             │
 │  ┌──────────────────┐    │  ┌──────────────────┐          │
 │  │ RBAC: team-a-role │    │  │ RBAC: team-b-role │          │
 │  │ (only team-a      │    │  │ (only team-b      │          │
 │  │  resources)       │    │  │  resources)       │          │
 │  ├──────────────────┤    │  ├──────────────────┤          │
 │  │ ResourceQuota:    │    │  │ ResourceQuota:    │          │
 │  │  CPU: 4 cores     │    │  │  CPU: 8 cores     │          │
 │  │  Memory: 8Gi      │    │  │  Memory: 16Gi     │          │
 │  ├──────────────────┤    │  ├──────────────────┤          │
 │  │ NetworkPolicy:    │    │  │ NetworkPolicy:    │          │
 │  │  deny-all +       │    │  │  deny-all +       │          │
 │  │  allow internal   │    │  │  allow internal   │          │
 │  ├──────────────────┤    │  ├──────────────────┤          │
 │  │ Pod Security:     │    │  │ Pod Security:     │          │
 │  │  restricted       │    │  │  restricted       │          │
 │  └──────────────────┘    │  └──────────────────┘          │
 │                           │                                │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
tenant-namespace.yaml — complete tenant isolation 
# 1. Namespace with Pod Security Standard
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: easypj
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
---
# 2. Default deny-all NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
---
# 3. Allow internal communication within namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-internal
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector: {}            # Allow from same namespace
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector: {}            # Allow to same namespace
    - to:                            # Allow DNS resolution
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
---
# 4. ResourceQuota to limit resource consumption
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: easypj-quota
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "20"
    services: "10"
    secrets: "20"
    configmaps: "20"

🔑 Key Takeaways

Bulleted key takeaways go here.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • ❌ Role vs ClusterRole — Role is namespace-scoped, ClusterRole is cluster-wide. Use Role unless you need cross-namespace access
  • ❌ RoleBinding to ClusterRole — this is valid! It scopes the ClusterRole's permissions to a single namespace
  • ❌ Forgetting apiGroup — core resources (pods, services) use "", apps resources use "apps"
  • ✅ Use resourceNames — when possible, restrict access to specific named resources
⚡ Speed Tips

CKA Exam — You may be asked to configure audit logging. Remember the four audit levels: None (no logging), Metadata (log request metadata only), Request (log request body), RequestResponse (log both request and response body). Never log Secret content — use Metadata level for Secrets.

⚙️ Chapter 39 — Scenario & Command Drills (5)

Quick recall of hardening checklist items — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q39.1
Create a Role in the easypj namespace called secret-reader that allows only get and list on Secrets. Bind it to a ServiceAccount called easypj-app. Then verify the binding works.
Show Answer 
# Create the SA
kubectl create serviceaccount easypj-app -n easypj

# Create the role
kubectl create role secret-reader -n easypj \
--verb=get,list \
--resource=secrets

# Create the binding
kubectl create rolebinding secret-reader-binding -n easypj \
--role=secret-reader \
--serviceaccount=easypj:easypj-app

# Verify
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n easypj \
--as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-app
# yes

kubectl auth can-i delete secrets -n easypj \
--as=system:serviceaccount:easypj:easypj-app
# no   ← correct! delete is not granted
Explanation

The imperative kubectl create role command is fastest for the CKA. The --verb=get,list flag sets allowed verbs, --resource=secrets sets the resource type. A RoleBinding connects the role to the service account. Verify with kubectl auth can-i using the --as flag to impersonate the service account. Note the ServiceAccount format: namespace:name.

Q39.2
Enable encryption at rest for Secrets. Create an EncryptionConfiguration using aescbc provider. Then update the API server to use it.
Show Answer 
# 1. Generate an encryption key
head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64
# Output: Bz4w1F...==

# 2. Create the encryption config
cat <<EOF > /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources:
  - secrets
providers:
  - aescbc:
      keys:
        - name: key1
          secret: Bz4w1F...==
  - identity: {}
EOF

# 3. Edit kube-apiserver manifest
vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add to command args:
#   --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
# Add volume:
#   - name: encryption-config
#     hostPath:
#       path: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#       type: File
# Add volumeMount:
#   - name: encryption-config
#     mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#     readOnly: true

# 4. API server restarts automatically (static pod)
# 5. Re-encrypt existing secrets
kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -
Explanation

The EncryptionConfiguration lists providers in order — the first provider is used for new writes, remaining providers are tried for reads (enabling migration). The identity: {} fallback allows reading pre-existing unencrypted Secrets. After enabling encryption, you must re-encrypt existing Secrets with kubectl get ... | kubectl replace. This is a common CKA task — remember to mount the config file into the API server pod.

Q39.3
Create a Pod in the easypj namespace that follows all security best practices: non-root user, read-only filesystem, drop all capabilities, seccomp profile, no SA token mounting.
Show Answer 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: easypj-hardened
namespace: easypj
spec:
automountServiceAccountToken: false
securityContext:
runAsNonRoot: true
runAsUser: 1000
runAsGroup: 3000
fsGroup: 2000
seccompProfile:
  type: RuntimeDefault
containers:
- name: django
  image: easypj/jobpost:v2.1
  ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
  securityContext:
    allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    capabilities:
      drop: ["ALL"]
  resources:
    limits:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 256Mi
    requests:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
  volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
volumes:
- name: tmp
  emptyDir:
    sizeLimit: 100Mi
Explanation

This pod follows all CKA security best practices: runAsNonRoot: true ensures no root processes, readOnlyRootFilesystem prevents filesystem writes (except mounted volumes), capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] removes all Linux capabilities, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault restricts syscalls, automountServiceAccountToken: false prevents API access, and resource limits prevent resource abuse. The emptyDir volume provides a writable /tmp directory since the root filesystem is read-only.

Q39.4
Configure audit logging for the API server. The policy should: log all Secret access at Metadata level, log RBAC changes at RequestResponse level, and skip logging events and health checks.
Show Answer 
# /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
# Skip health checks and events
- level: None
nonResourceURLs: ["/healthz*", "/readyz*", "/livez*"]
- level: None
resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["events"]

# Log Secrets at Metadata only (never log content!)
- level: Metadata
resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["secrets"]

# Log RBAC changes at full detail
- level: RequestResponse
resources:
  - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
    resources: ["roles", "rolebindings", "clusterroles", "clusterrolebindings"]

# Catch-all
- level: Metadata
# Add to kube-apiserver.yaml:
# --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
# --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
# --audit-log-maxage=30
# --audit-log-maxbackup=10
# --audit-log-maxsize=100
#
# Mount both the policy file and log directory as volumes
Explanation

Audit policy rules are evaluated in order — the first matching rule wins. That's why the None rules (skip) come first. For Secrets, use Metadata level to avoid logging Secret values in the audit trail. RBAC changes need RequestResponse level for full forensic detail. The API server needs both --audit-policy-file and --audit-log-path flags, plus volume mounts for both the policy file and the log output directory.

Q39.5
Set up complete namespace isolation for the easypj namespace: enforce the restricted Pod Security Standard, create a default-deny NetworkPolicy, and set a ResourceQuota limiting to 4 CPU cores and 8Gi memory.
Show Answer 
# 1. Label namespace for Pod Security Standard
kubectl label namespace easypj \
pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted

# 2. Default deny NetworkPolicy
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
name: default-deny-all
namespace: easypj
spec:
podSelector: {}
policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
EOF

# 3. ResourceQuota
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
name: easypj-quota
namespace: easypj
spec:
hard:
requests.cpu: "4"
requests.memory: 8Gi
limits.cpu: "4"
limits.memory: 8Gi
pods: "20"
EOF

# Verify all three
kubectl describe namespace easypj
kubectl get networkpolicy -n easypj
kubectl describe resourcequota -n easypj
Explanation

Complete namespace isolation requires three components: Pod Security Standards via namespace labels (enforce=restricted blocks privileged containers, host networking, etc.), NetworkPolicy with empty podSelector and both Ingress/Egress policyTypes creates a default-deny rule, and ResourceQuota limits total resource consumption. On the CKA, you'll often need to combine these. After default-deny, remember to create allow-rules for legitimate traffic (DNS, ingress controller, internal communication).

Policies and the CKA Exam

The CKA tests your ability to enforce security policies at the namespace and cluster level. Pod Security Admission via namespace labels is the most likely exam topic. LimitRange and ResourceQuota questions also appear frequently. Know the difference between them and when to use each.

  • Should Know — ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL), PodDisruptionBudget
